greek_sentence: [Δαμοκράτους περὶ λευκῆς ἐμπλάστρου.] Ἐπεὶ δὲ αἱ διὰ μέτρων ἐγγεγραμμέναι δυνάμεις φαρμάκων εὐμνημόνευτοί εἰσι καὶ διαφυλάττουσαι ἀκριβῆ τὴν συμμετρίαν αὐτῶν, ἔδοξέ μοι κάλλιον καὶ τούτων μνημονεύειν.
english_sentence_A: [Damocrates on the white plaster.] Since the compositions of drugs written down in metre are easy to remember and preserve their proportions exactly, it seemed to me better to make mention of these too.
english_sentence_B: [Damocrates on the white plaster.] Since the preparations (dynameis) of drugs written down in metre are easy to remember and also preserve their exact proportion, it seemed better to me to record these as well.

greek_sentence: γεγραφότος οὖν Δαμοκράτους λευκὰς ἄλλας ἐμπλάστρους καὶ μέντοι καὶ λευκὴν, ἣν ἐπαινεῖ, παραθήσομαι τὴν γραφὴν αὐτοῖς τοῖς ὑπ’ ἐκείνου γεγραμμένοις στίχοις, τῷ τριμέτρῳ καλουμένῳ μέτρῳ.
english_sentence_A: Since, then, Damocrates has written other white plasters, and indeed also a white one which he praises, I shall set out the recipe in the very verses written by him, in the metre called trimeter.
english_sentence_B: Damocrates has written of other white plasters, and indeed also of a white one which he commends; I shall therefore set out the recipe in the very verses written by him, in the metre called trimeter.

greek_sentence: Δεῖ δὲ μετὰ τούτων τοὺς φιλιάτρους ἔχειν Λευκὴν καλὴν ἔμπλαστρον εἰς ἀποσύρματα, Καὶ τὰ πυρίκαυτα καὶ τὰ χωρὶς αἰτίας Ἔξ ἐπιπολῆς γινόμενα φανερᾶς ἕλκεα.
english_sentence_A: Together with these, lovers of the medical art must have a fine white plaster for abrasions, and for burns, and for ulcers that arise on the surface without any evident cause.

lsj_entry_text: λιπαρ-ός, ά, όν, (λίπα) prop. oily, shiny with oil, once in Hom. , anointed, λιπαροὶ κεφαλὰς καὶ καλὰ πρόσωπα Od. 15.332 ; λ. χωρεῖν ἐκ βαλανείου Ar. Pl. 616 ; θεᾶσθαι λιπαρὸν παρὰ τῷ Διονύσῳ Id. Eq. 536 , cf. Nu. 1002 ; σοὶ δὲ μελήσει . . λιπαρῷ (Bentl. for -ρῶς) χωρεῖν ἐπὶ δεῖπνον Id. Ec. 652 ; of oil or oily objects, shiny, Simon. 148.4 , X. Mem. 2.1.31 , Pl. Ti. 60a , 84a , Arist. HA 520a27 . fatty, greasy, ἄρτος Ar. Fr. 109 ; τὰ λ. unctuous dishes, ib. 506.1 ; τὸ λ. fatty substance, Arist. PA 651a24 ; λιπαραί (sc. ἔμπλαστροι), αἱ, oily plasters, Dsc. 1.112 , Gal. 12.468 : sts. opp. τὸ πῖον (which implies resinous substance), Arist. Mete. 387b6 , cf. Col. 791b23 ; of vegetables boiled in grease, Hp. Mul. 1.66 . Adv. -ρῶς, ἕψειν boil in grease, Hp. Mul. l. c.; so λ. ἠρτυμένον Gal. 9.677 ; ἀνατρίβειν massage with a greasy or oily lubricant, Hp. Art. 9 . of the healthy look of the human body or skin, shining, sleek, in Hom. in phrase λιπαροὶ πόδες bright, smooth feet, without a wrinkle on the skin, mostly of men's feet, in the line ποσσὶ δ' ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσιν ἐδήσατο καλὰ πέδιλα Il. 2.44 , al.; of Hera, 14.186 ; of Themis, Hes. Th. 901 ; - ώτεροι ἐγένοντο Hdt. 3.23 ; λ. στῆθος Ar. Nu. 1012 ; θηρία X. Cyr. 1.4.11 ; χείλεα Luc. Am. 13 ; radiant, θυγάτηρ Χρόνου B. 7.1 ; ἄκοιτις Id. 5.169 . of condition or state of life, rich, comfortable, easy, γῆρας Od. 11.136 , 19.368 , Pi. N. 7.99 ; λ. εὐφροσύνη AP 11.63 ( Maced. ). Adv. - ρῶς, γηρασκέμεν Od. 4.210 ; πλήσαντα λ. κύκλον ἐτῶν ἑκατόν Epigr.Gr. 451 . of things, bright, brilliant, λιπαρὴ καλύπτρη Il. 22.406 ; λ. κρήδεμνα Od. 1.334 , etc.; χοροί Hes. Th. 63 ; of city walls, Od. 13.388 ; λ. δόμος B. 15.29 ; νίκα Id. 10.38 ; στέφανοι Id. 1.47 ; λιπαρὰς τελέουσι θέμιστας splendid or rich tribute, Il. 9.156 , 298 ; also, of the oily smoothness of a calm sea, λ. γαλάνα Theoc. 22.19 , cf. Call. Epigr. 6.5 ; also σέλας Theoc. 23.8 ; and of smells, λ. ὀσμή rich, savoury, Arist. de An. 421a30 , cf. Sens. 443b10 . of soil, fat, rich, fruitful, as epith. of places, Χίος, ἣ νήσων λιπαρωτάτη εἰν ἁλὶ κεῖται h.Ap. 38 ; λ. πόλις Thgn. 947 ; λ. Ὀρχομενός, Θῆβαι, Νάξος, Μαραθών, Pi. O. 14.2 , P. 2.3 , 4.88 , O. 13.110 ; λιπαραὶ Ἀθῆναι, favourite epith. with the Athenians, prob. with allusion to the Attic olive, first in Pi. I. 2.20 , Fr. 76 , cf. Ar. Ach. 639 , 640 (where he plays on the double sense of brilliant and greasy), Nu. 300 , Fr. 110 ; λ. τὸ χρῆμα τῆς πόλεως, of Nephelococcygia, Id. Av. 826 ; λ. χεύματα, of rivers, A. Supp. 1028 (lyr.); λ. ὅρμος Call. Del. 155 ; ἄντρον Orph. H. 59.4 (Hermann), etc. Adv. λιπαρῶς, v. supr. 1 , 111 .

lsj_entry_text: σύν-θεσις, εως, ἡ, putting together, composition, combination, Pl. Phd. 93a , R. 611b ; τῶν λίθων Arist. EN 1174a23 , cf. IG 42(1).103.56 (Epid., iv B.C.), 7.3073.92 (Lebad., ii B.C.); τῶν σπονδύλων Sor. 1.102 ; storage, τῶν μήλων (quinces in a ῥίσκος) Phylarch. 10 J. ; but ἐλαιῶν ς. a preserve of olives, Gp. 9.28.2 . in concrete sense, junction, ὀστῶν Arist. PA 658b19 ; συνθέσεις (λέγω τὰς γωνίας) Id. Pr. 910b14 . in various technical senses: in Grammar, composition, γραμμάτων τε συνθέσεις, i.e. syllables and words, A. Pr. 460 , cf. Arist. Metaph. 1092a26 ; ς. ἔκ τε ῥημάτων γιγνομένη καὶ ὀνομάτων, i.e. sentences, Pl. Sph. 263d , cf. Cra. 431c , Arist. Po. 1458a28 , Gal. 15.487 ; περὶ συνθέσεως ὀνομάτων, title of work by D.H. ; also, the juxtaposition of letters in a word, Arist. Rh.Al. 1434b34 ; of an author's composition, Isoc. 10.11 ; so ἡ τῶν μέτρων ς. metrical composition, Arist. Po. 1449b35 ; ἡ τῶν ἐπῶν ς. D.S. 5.74 ; ἡ τοῦ παίωνος ξ. the way the paeon is made up, Plu. 2.1143d ; the constitution of things, Hp. Virg. 1 . Math., synthesis of a problem (opp. ἀνάλυσις), Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.7 , explained in Papp. 634 ; ἡ κατὰ ς. ἀγωγή synthetic procedure, Id. 412.2 . Math., ς. λόγου transformation of a ratio known as componendo, Euc. 5 Def. 14 ; κατὰ -σιν, = componendo, Archim. Aequil. 2.9 . Math., addition, Ph. 1.11 , Plu. 2.1018c , Dioph. 1 Intr.; καθ' ἁντινοῦν -σιν however many times added, i.e. whatever number of times taken (multiplied), Archim. Spir. 1 :—also as Pythag. name for 2 , Anatol. ap. Theol.Ar. 8 . in Logic, union of noun and verb or of two objects of thought in a statement, Arist. Int. 16a12 , de An. 430a27 ; also ὁ παρὰ τὴν ς. [λόγος] the fallacy of composition, opp. διαίρεσις, Id. SE 177a33 . in Physics, composition of substances, parts of organisms, from their elementary constituents, Id. PA 646a12 , Top. 151a23 ; opp μίξις (combination), Id. GC 328a6 . in Medicine, compounding of essences and drugs, τῶν μύρων Thphr. Od. 14 , al., cf. D.S. 4.45 , Aglaïas 8 . combination of parts so as to form a whole, γενέσεις καὶ ς. Pl. R. 533b ; ἡ τῶν στρωμάτων ς. Id. Plt. 280b , cf. Arist. PA 645a35 , Metaph. 1014b37 ; in plants, Thphr. HP 5.5.2 . in concrete sense, a social or political combination, Arist. Pol. 1276b7 ; a military formation, Ael. Tact. 18.5 . agreement, treaty, Pi. P. 4.168 , Fr. 205 ; πὸς τὰς συνθέσις in accordance with the agreements, IG 5(2).343.41 , 60 (Orchom. Arc. , iv B.C.); ἐκ συνθέσεως by arrangement, D.S. 13.112 , etc.; συνθέσεις περὶ γάμων Plu. Sull. 35 . ς. λόγων making up accounts, Stud.Pal. 4.70.391 (i A.D.); so ς. alone, εἰς σύνθεσιν τῷ βασιλεῖ PTeb. 714.6 (ii B.C.). set, service (most freq. in Lat. synthesis): collection of clothes, wardrobe, Dig. 34.2.38.1 ; also, dress, gown, costume, suit, ς. τελείας λευκὰς δεκατρεῖς, γυναικείας ς. PHamb. 10.13 , 21 (ii A.D.), cf. POxy. 1153.23 (i A.D.), 496.4 (ii A.D.), PSI 10.1117.11 , 13 (ii A.D.), Mart. 2.46.4 , 5.79.2 ; synthesinam indutus, Suet. Ner. 51 . service of plate, ς. πινακίων BGU 781 i 5 (i A.D.), cf. Mart. 4.46.15 , Stat. Silv. 4.9.44 .
greek_sentence: Τῆς στυπτηρίας, ἧς ἐμνημόνευσεν, ἡ σύνθεσις ἐν τῷ πέμπτῳ τῆσδε τῆς πραγματείας.
english_sentence_A: The composition of the alum plaster which he mentioned is in the fifth book of this treatise.
english_sentence_B: The compounding of the alum plaster that he mentioned is in the fifth book of this treatise.

greek_sentence: Τῆς προκειμένης πραγματείας σκοπὸν ἐχούσης σὺν τοῖς ἄλλοις καὶ τοῦτον, ὡς ἐὰν ἀπολέσωμέν ποτε τὸ βιβλίον, ἐν ᾧ τῶν φαρμάκων οἷς χρώμεθα τὰς συνθέσεις γεγραμμένας ἔχομεν, αὐτοὺς ἡμᾶς δύνασθαι συντιθέναι παραπλήσια τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι, πρῶτον μὲν ἡμᾶς καθόλου τινὰ τύπον ὁδοῦ μεμαθηκέναι, δι’ ἧς εὑρήσομεν ὃ προεθέμεθα.
english_sentence_A: Since the present treatise has, together with its other aims, also this one, namely that if we should ever lose the book in which we have the compositions of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely similar to those that have been lost, it is necessary, first, that we should have learned some general outline of a method by which we shall discover what we have set out to find.
english_sentence_B: Since the present treatise has, among its other aims, this one as well, that if we should ever lose the book in which we keep the compounding of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely resembling those that are lost, it is necessary, first, that we have learned in general some outline of a way by which we shall find what we have set before ourselves.

greek_sentence: Τῆς προκειμένης πραγματείας σκοπὸν ἐχούσης σὺν τοῖς ἄλλοις καὶ τοῦτον, ὡς ἐὰν ἀπολέσωμέν ποτε τὸ βιβλίον, ἐν ᾧ τῶν φαρμάκων οἷς χρώμεθα τὰς συνθέσεις γεγραμμένας ἔχομεν, αὐτοὺς ἡμᾶς δύνασθαι συντιθέναι παραπλήσια τοῖς ἀπολλυμένοις ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι, πρῶτον μὲν ἡμᾶς καθόλου τινὰ τύπον ὁδοῦ μεμαθηκέναι, δι’ ἧς εὑρήσομεν ὃ προεθέμεθα.
english_sentence_A: Since the present treatise has, together with its other aims, also this one, namely that if we should ever lose the book in which we have the compositions of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely similar to those that have been lost, it is necessary, first, that we should have learned some general outline of a method by which we shall discover what we have set out to find.
english_sentence_B: Since the present treatise has, among its other aims, this one as well, that if we should ever lose the book in which we keep the compounding of the drugs we use written down, we ourselves should be able to compound drugs closely resembling those that are lost, it is necessary, first, that we have learned in general some outline of a way by which we shall find what we have set before ourselves.

greek_sentence: δεινὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ συμβὰν ἤδη τισὶν ὧν ἐγὼ γινώσκω δυσὶν ἰατροῖν.
english_sentence_A: Terrible too is what has already befallen certain persons whom I know, two physicians: for the one, wasted away by grief at the loss of such writings, died, while the other withdrew from medical practice.
english_sentence_B: Terrible, too, is what has already befallen certain people, two physicians whom I know.

greek_sentence: ὁ μὲν γὰρ ὑπὸ λύπης ἐπὶ τῇ τῶν τοιούτων γραφῶν ἀπωλείᾳ συντακεὶς ἀπέθανεν, ὁ δὲ ἀπέστη τῶν ἰατρικῶν ἔργων.

english_sentence_B: For the one, wasting away from grief at the loss of such writings, died, and the other withdrew from medical practice.

greek_sentence: ὑπάρχει δὲ τοῖς γυμνασθεῖσιν, ὡς ἐγὼ λέγω, πρὸς τῷ δύνασθαι συντιθέναι φάρμακα χρήσιμα καὶ τὸ κριτικοῖς εἶναι τῶν γεγραμμένων τοῖς πρὸ ἡμῶν ἰατροῖς, ἐπιτηδείως τε χρῆσθαι πᾶσι τοῖς ὑπ’ ἐκείνων γεγραμμένοις, οἷς τ’ ἂν αὐτὸς εὕρῃ κατὰ τὴν διδαχθησομένην μέθοδον.
english_sentence_A: But those who have been trained, as I say, possess, in addition to being able to compose useful drugs, also the capacity to be discriminating judges of what has been written by the physicians before us, and to make suitable use both of everything written by them and of whatever one may oneself discover according to the method that is going to be taught.
english_sentence_B: Those who have been trained in the way I describe have, besides being able to compound useful drugs, also the capacity to be critical judges of what was written by the physicians before us, and to make suitable use both of everything written by them and of whatever one discovers oneself according to the method that is going to be taught.

english_sentence_A: In this book, the one now before us, there will be discussion of the green plasters and the quince-yellow and the tawny and the grey and the reddish ones, among which are also those called two-coloured, and between these others, some of them bearing names, such as the whitish-quince-yellow and the blackish-green and the dirty-coloured and the sky-blue-tinged and the dark-blue-tinged, while some are altogether nameless.

english_sentence_A: But to record those that are alike in colour is not the practice of people who look to likeness according to the art; [461] rather, since some of the very powerful men sometimes order us to make for them a quince-yellow plaster that is agglutinative of wounds, or cicatrizing, or emollient of parts that are becoming hardened, or able to effect something of this sort, some of the more recent physicians have been compelled, in writing one after another those that are alike in colour, to add to each its proper professed effects.
english_sentence_B: But recording together those that are similar in colour is not the practice of people who look to a technical similarity [461]. However, some men of great power sometimes order us to make them a quince-yellow plaster that is agglutinative of wounds, or cicatrizing, or emollient of parts that are becoming hardened, or able to accomplish something else of that kind.

lsj_entry_text: σαρκ-ωτικός, ή, όν, making flesh grow, Id. 1.261 , 11.799 ; πληγῶν ς. interpol. in Dsc. 1.126 ; κόλπων ς. Id. 1.1.2 .
greek_sentence: γράφω γὰρ πρῶτον μὲν τὰς σαρκωτικὰς τῶν κοίλων ἑλκῶν, ὧν αἱ πλεῖσται χλωραὶ κατὰ χρόαν εἰσὶν, ἐπισημαινόμενος ὅσαι τε κολλητικαὶ τούτων ὑπάρχουσι καὶ ὅσαι τῶν κακοηθευομένων ἰατρικαὶ καί τι τῶν τοιούτων ἄλλο δυνάμεναι διαπράττεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: For I write first the flesh-producing plasters for hollow ulcers, most of which are green in colour, indicating which of these are agglutinative as well, and which are curative of ulcers that are turning malignant, and which are able to accomplish something else of this kind.
english_sentence_B: I shall therefore try to make my teaching a kind of mixture, beginning from the more technical arrangement. For first I write the flesh-producing plasters for hollow wounds, most of which are green in colour, noting which of them are also agglutinative, which are curative of wounds turning malignant, and which can accomplish something else of that kind.

lsj_entry_text: συνούλ-ωσις, εως, ἡ, complete cicatrization, soundness, LXX Je. 40(33).6 , Orib. 44.13.3 ; of plants, Gp. 4.13.4 .
greek_sentence: δευτέρας δὲ τὰς κολλητικὰς, οὐ μόνον τῶν προσφάτων ἑλκῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν κόλπων, ἐν αἷς εἰσι καὶ μέχρι συνουλώσεως ἄγουσαι πολλαί.
english_sentence_A: Second, the agglutinative ones, not only for recent wounds but also for sinuses, among which there are also many that lead right up to cicatrization.
english_sentence_B: Second, I write the agglutinative ones, not only of fresh wounds but also of sinuses, among which there are also many that carry the healing through to cicatrisation.

lsj_entry_text: φαιός, ά, όν, grey, of any colour mixed of black and white, Pl. Ti. 68c , cf. Arist. Cat. 12a18 , Top. 106b6 , al.: opp. to both μέλας and λευκός, in a negative sense, Pl. greek_sentence: καὶ τούτων ἁπασῶν ἕνα μὲν στίχον ποιήσομαι τῶν μηλίνων, ἕτερον δὲ τῶν βαρβάρων ὀνομαζομένων, ἕτερον δὲ φαιῶν, ἐπί τε τῶν ἄλλων χρωμάτων ὁμοίως.
english_sentence_A: And of all these I shall make one series of the quince-yellow ones, another of those called barbarian, another of the grey ones, and likewise for the other colours.
english_sentence_B: And of all these I shall make one row of the quince-yellow ones, another of those called 'barbarian', another of the grey ones, and likewise for the other colours.

lsj_entry_text: χρῶμα, ατος, τό, (χρώννυμι) skin, esp. of the human body, κάθαρσις διὰ τοῦ χρώματος Hp. english_sentence_A: And I shall also state, in one other book [462] without similarities of colour, all those that treat the wounds that are hard to cicatrize, which they also call Chironian.
english_sentence_B: I shall also speak, in one further book [462], without regard to similarities of colour, of those that treat ulcers which are difficult to cicatrise, which they also call Chironian.

greek_sentence: καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο καθ’ ἕτερον βιβλίον, ὅσαι καὶ ταῦτα καὶ ἄλλ’ ἄττα πολύχρηστοι λεγόμεναί τε καὶ οὖσαι.
english_sentence_A: And after this, in yet another book, all those that treat both these and certain other things, being both called and actually being polychrēsta (of many uses).
english_sentence_B: And after this, in another book, of those that treat both these and certain other conditions, which are called polychrest and are so in fact.

english_sentence_A: And after all these I shall try to go through by method whatever remains to be known of the plasters according to their powers.
english_sentence_B: And after all these I shall attempt to go through by method whatever remains to be known of the plasters classified according to their faculties.

greek_sentence: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν προείρηται κοινόν τι προοίμιον ἁπασῶν τῶν προσγραφησομένων ἐμπλάστρων, ἐπὶ δὲ τὰς ἐν τούτῳ τῷ βιβλίῳ γεγραμμένας μεταβήσομαι, προτάξας αὐτῶν τινα λόγον κοινὸν, ὡς εἰ καὶ μηδὲν ἤδη μοι προείρητο.
english_sentence_A: These things, then, have been said beforehand as a kind of common preface to all the plasters that are going to be written up hereafter; and I shall pass over to those written in this book, having set before them a certain common account, as if nothing had already been said beforehand by me.
english_sentence_B: These things, then, have been said beforehand as a kind of common preface to all the plasters that are to be recorded; but I shall now pass on to those written in this book, placing before them a common account, as if nothing had already been said by me beforehand.

greek_sentence: φαρμάκων συνθέσεις παμπόλλων ἀξίων ἐπαίνου πρῶτος ὧν οἶδα Μαντείας ὁ Ἡροφίλειος ἔγραψεν, οὗ μαθητὴς γενόμενος Ἡρακλείδης ὁ Ταραντῖνος οὐ μόνον ἐν τῇ τῶν φαρμάκων χρήσει φαίνεται μιμούμενος ἐκεῖνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὸ διαιτητικὸν μέρος τῆς τέχνης.
english_sentence_A: Compositions of a very great many drugs worthy of praise were written, first of those I know, by Mantias the Herophilean, whose pupil Heraclides of Tarentum appears to imitate him not only in the use of drugs but also in the dietetic part of the art.
english_sentence_B: The first, of those I know, to write down the compositions of very many drugs worthy of praise was Mantias the Herophilean; Heracleides of Tarentum, who became his pupil, is seen to imitate him not only in the use of drugs but also in the dietetic part of the art.

lsj_entry_text: μικρός and σμικρός, ά, όν, Dor. , Ion. μικκός (q.v.): σμικρός is corroborated by metre in Il. 17.757 , Hes. Op. 361 , and might be restored in Il. 5.801 , Od. 3.296 (μικρός codd.); it is prob. the only form in Hdt. ( μικρός Hdt. 2.74 codd.): freq. in Lyr. and prob. always in Trag. (exc. where metre requires μικρός, as S. Aj. 161 (anap., Comp. )); most freq. in Pl. ; but in Th. , also Ar. and other Com., μικρός prevails, σμικρός being found Th. 4.13 , 7.75 , 8.81 , Ar. Ach. 523 , V. 5 ; Att. Inscrr. have σμικρός IG 12.313.111 , al., μικρός ib. 369.10 , al.:—small, little, in Size, μ. ἔην δέμας Il. 5.801 ; μ. λίθος Od. 3.296 ; κίρκον, ὅ τε σμικρῇσι φόνον φέρει ὀρνίθεσσιν Il. 17.757 ; σμ. ἄστεα Hdt. 1.5 ; μεγάθεϊ σμικροί Id. 2.74 : with Dims., μ. πολίχνιον, γῄδιον, παιδάρια, Isoc. 5.145 , X. Cyr. 8.3.38 , Ages. 1.21 : as a Com. exaggeration, δικαστηρίδιον μ. πάνυ Ar. V. 803 ; σκαλαθυρμάτι' ἄττα μ. Id. Nu. 630 , etc.: c. inf., μικροὶ δ' ὁρᾶν Id. Pax 821 : as a term of reproach, Κλειγενὴς ὁ μικρός Id. Ra. 709 , cf. Pl. Prt. 323d , Arist. EN 1123b7 , Alex. 98.7 ; Ἀμύντας ὁ μ. Arist. Pol. 1311b3 ; οἱ ἐν μικρῷ μεγάλοι short but stoutly built, Philostr. Gym. 36 ; ὁ μ. δάκτυλος SIG 1172.4 (Lebena). in Quantity, σμικρὸν ἐπὶ σμικρῷ καταθεῖναι Hes. Op. 361 ; μέλιτος μικρόν Ar. V. 878 ; μ. ὄψον, ἀργυρίδιον, X. Mem. 3.14.1 , Ar. Pl. 240 , cf. Antiph. 44 . in Amount or Importance, petty, trivial, slight, σμ. πρόφασις Thgn. 323 ; ἔπος, ἔγκλημα, ῥοπή, etc., S. OC 443 , Tr. 361 , OT 961 , etc.; ἐκ σμικροῦ λόγου on some slight pretext, Id. OC 620 ; ἐν σμικρῷ λόγῳ παρῆκεν as of small account, ib. 569 ; αἰτίας μικρᾶς πέρι E. Andr. 387 , etc.; οὐδὲ μικρόν, = οὐδὲ γρῦ , D. 19.37 ; of persons, of small account, opp. μέγας, σμ. ἐν σμικροῖς, μέγας ἐν μεγάλοις Pi. P. 3.107 ; ἄριστ' ἂν καὶ μέγας ὀρθοῖθ' ὑπὸ μικροτέρων S. Aj. 161 (anap.), etc.; σμ. τίθησί με Id. OC 958 ; βίος ὁ μ., = μέτριος , E. Fr. 504 ; τίνος σμικροτάτου μεταβαλόντος, σμικρότατος τὴν δύναμιν, Pl. R. 473b ; of the mind, οὐ σμικρὸν φρονεῖ S. Aj. 1120 ; of style, mean, [ Φίλιστοσ] μικρὸς ταῖς ἐκφράσεσιν D.H. Vett.Cens. 3.2 ; of festivals, of lesser importance, Ἁλίεια τὰ μεγάλα καὶ τὰ μ. SIG 1067.14 (Cedreae). of Time, short, Pi. O. 12.12 , Ar. Pl. 126 , etc.; εἰς μ. χρόνον Pl. R. 498d ; ἐν μικρῷ (sc. χρόνῳ) shortly, X. Cyn. 5.32 , Eq. 8.7 ; πρὸ μικροῦ Poll. 1.72 ; ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ καταλιθοβολήσουσί με LXX Ex. 17.4 . of Age, young, Ostr.Bodl. i237 (ii B.C.), etc. Adverbial usages, regul. Adv. σμικρῶς, but little, Pl. Criti. 107d ; μικρῶς by a little, prob. in Archim. Stom. 1 : Sup. σμικρότατα X. Mem. 3.11.12 . σμικροῦ or μικροῦ within a little, almost, Id. Cyr. 1.4.8 , D. 18.151 , etc.; in full, μικροῦ δεῖν, v. δεῖ 11 , δέω (B) 1 ; μικροῦ τινος ἀπελείφθη τοῦ μή . . Ach.Tat. 7.13 ; but μικροῦ πρίασθαι for a little, cheap, X. Mem. 2.10.4 . σμικρῷ by a little, with Comp. , Pl. Plt. 262c , etc.; also σμικρῷ πρόσθεν a little before, Id. Lg. 719b , etc.; μικρῷ ἄνωθεν D. 44.6 . μικρόν a little, σμικρὸν ὑπολείπεσθαι, σμ. τι παρακλίνειν, X. An. 5.4.22 , Pl. Cra. 410a ; of Time, X. An. 3.1.11 , etc.; repeated, μικρὸν μικρόν Antiph. 10 : pl., of Degree, σμικρὰ γεωμετρίας ἔμπειροι Pl. R. 527a , etc.; σμίκρ' ἄττα διατρίψαντες Id. Prt. 316a ; μικρὰ διακινήσω σε περὶ τοῦ πράγματος Sosip. 1.22 ; περιπάτησον μικρὰ μετ' ἐμοῦ Men. Sam. 243 , cf. Plu. Luc. 31 . with Preps., ἐπὶ σμικρόν but a little, S. El. 414 , Antipho 6.18 , Hdt. 4.129 . κατὰ μικρόν into small pieces, X. An. 7.3.22 ; so κατὰ μικρὰ γενομένης τῆς δυνάμεως ib. 5.6.32 ; also, little by little, κατὰ μικρὸν ἀεί Ar. V. 702 , cf. Nu. 741 ; opp. συλλήβδην, Pl. R. 344a ; καὶ κατὰ σμ. or μ. ever so little, Id. Sph. 241c , Isoc. 3.10 , D. 2.22 . παρὰ μικρόν within a little, παρὰ μ. ἐλθεῖν c. inf., to be within an ace of doing, E. Heracl. 295 (anap.), cf. Isoc. 7.6 , etc.; παρὰ μ. ἦλθον ἀποθανεῖν Id. 17.42 ; τὸ παρὰ μ. ὥσπερ οὐδὲν ἀπέχειν δοκεῖ Arist. Ph. 197a30 ; but τὸ παρὰ μ. σῴζεσθαι to be only just saved, Id. Rh. 1371b11 , cf. Simp. in Ph. 344.10 ; gradual, imperceptible change, Arist. Pol. 1303a20 ; οὐδὲ παρὰ μ. ἦν κρεῖττον c. inf., Plb. 12.20.7 ; [ ἡ τύχη] παρὰ μ. εἰς ἑκάτερα ποιεῖ μεγάλας ῥοπάς Id. 15.6.8 , cf. Isoc. 4.59 ; but also παρὰ μ. ποιεῖσθαι, ἡγεῖσθαι, to think little of . . , D. 61.51 , Isoc. 5.79 . μετὰ μικρόν a little after, Ev.Matt. 26.73 . besides regul. Comp. and Sup. μικρότερος, -ότατος ( Ar. Eq. 789 , D. Prooem. 48 , etc.), there are the irreg. ἐλάσσων, ἐλάχιστος, from ἐλαχύς, and μείων, μεῖστος, also μειότερος; v. μείων. [ι by nature; ι only in late Poetry, Epigr. ap. Phleg. Fr. 36.17 J. ] (Perh. cf. Lat. mīca, mīcidus, OHG. smāhi, ONorse smár 'little'.)

M. 1.25 . experience, ξυγκαταινέω . . τὸν λογισμόν, ἤνπερ ἐκ περιπτώσιος ποιέηται τὴν ἀρχήν Hp. Praec. 1 ; οὔτε πεῖρα οὔτε π. Plu. 2.918c tit. ; ἄλογος τριβὴ καὶ π. ib. 44o a ; κατὰ περίπτωσιν ἐγνωσμένον Stoic. 2.29 , al., cf. Phld. Rh. 2.164S. , Diog.Oen. 10 (pl.).
greek_sentence: οὔτε δὲ τούτων τις οὔτε ἄλλος ἔγραψε τὸν λογισμὸν τῆς συνθέσεως ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο θαῤῥαλεώτερον οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἀποφαίνονται, καίτοι γε ἀδιανόητα λέγοντες, εἰς περίπτωσιν γὰρ ἀναφέρουσι τὴν εὕρεσιν τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων.

lsj_entry_text: συντίθημι, used by Hom. only in Med. , v. infr.:— Pass. (v. infr.), but σύγκειμαι is more freq. as Pass. :— place or put together, τὴν οὐρὴν καὶ τὸν σπλῆνα . . συνθεὶς ὁμοῦ Hdt. 2.47 , cf. 4.67 ; ὅπλα ἐν τῷ ναῷ X. HG 2.3.20 ; ἅπαντα εἰς ἕν E. IT 1016 ; ἐν ὀλίγῳ πάντα Id. Supp. 1126 (lyr.); ὁ πρῶτος συνθεὶς εἰς ταὐτὸν τὰ δύο ταῦτα βιβλίδια Gal. 15.109 ; ς. ἱμάτια, opp. ἀνασείειν, fold them together, X. Oec. 10.11 ; ς. σκέλη, opp. ἐκτείνειν, Id. Cyn. 5.10 ; opp. διαιρεῖσθαι, Pl. Sph. 252b ; ς. ἄρθρα στόματος close the lips, E. Cyc. 625 ; εἰς τὸ οὖλον (αυλον cod.) ς. τὴν κόμην, = calamistrat, Gloss. :— Pass. , τὸ συντίθεσθαι καθ' ὁντινοῦν τρόπον ῥῖγος οὐκ ἀγαθόν ἐστι any sort of combination of shivering (with other symptoms), Gal. 16.746 . technical uses, Math., add together, of numbers, Hdt. 3.95 ( Pass. ); τό τε ἀρχαῖον καὶ τὸ ἔργον principal and interest, D. 27.17 , cf. 29.30 : Geom., of lines and figures, Archim. Spir.Praef. , Papp. 70.4 . Math. also, of the transformation of a ratio componendo, Arist. EN 1131b8 ( Pass. ), Euc. 5.18 , 24 ( Pass. ). Logic, combine the terms of a proposition, Arist. Rhet., accumulate, joined with ἐποικοδομεῖν (to form a climax), ib. 1365a16 . ς. λόγον make up an account, PHib. 1.48.15 (iii B.C.). put together constructively, so as to make a whole, πεντηκοντέρους καὶ τριήρεας (as a bridge) Hdt. 7.36 ; λίθους, of builders, Th. 4.4 , IG 42(1).103.59 (Epid., iv B.C.); πλίνθους, ξύλα, X. Mem. 3.1.7 , etc.; τὰ ὄστρακα IG 42(1).121.82 (Epid., iv B.C.); τὰ κομισθέντα Sor. 2.64 ; ἐκ τούτων τὰ μέγιστα . . συνθεὶς τοῦτον . . τὸν λόγον ποιήσομαι Hippias Eleus 6 D. ; συλλαβάς Pl. Cra. 424e . construct, frame, τὸ θνητὸν γένος Pl. Ti. 69d ; ὁ συνθείς the creator, ib. 33d :— Pass. , to be constructed, of the material universe, opp. διαλύεσθαι, Arist. Cael. 304b30 . ς. τι ἀπό τινος compose or make one thing of or from another, Hdt. 4.23 ; τὸ ἐκ τῶν νεῶν καὶ τοῦ πεζοῦ πλῆθος συντιθέμενον Id. 7.184 ; ἐξ ὧν [συλλαβῶν] τὰ ὀνόματα συντίθενται Pl. greek_sentence: οὔτε δὲ τούτων τις οὔτε ἄλλος ἔγραψε τὸν λογισμὸν τῆς συνθέσεως ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο θαῤῥαλεώτερον οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἀποφαίνονται, καίτοι γε ἀδιανόητα λέγοντες, εἰς περίπτωσιν γὰρ ἀναφέρουσι τὴν εὕρεσιν τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων.
english_sentence_A: But neither any of these men nor anyone else wrote the reasoning behind the composition of each of the drugs, and for this reason those of the empirical school make their pronouncements with greater boldness, even though what they say is inconceivable, for they refer the discovery of compound drugs to chance encounter.
english_sentence_B: But neither any of these nor anyone else wrote out the reasoning behind the composition of each of the drugs, and for this reason those from experience [the Empiricists] make their pronouncements more boldly, although what they say is unintelligible, for they refer the discovery of compound drugs to accidental encounter (periptōsis).

english_sentence_A: They have taken courage from the fact that none of the dogmatic physicians has written out in articulated form the method of their composition.

greek_sentence: ὅταν γὰρ οἱ δογματίζοντες ἐρωτώμενοι τὸν λόγον, ᾧ σύγκειται τῶν φαρμάκων ἕκαστον οἷς χρῶνται, μηδὲν ἔχωσι λέγειν, ἀπολέσαντές τε τὰς γραφὰς αὐτῶν ἀδυνατῶσιν αὐτοσχεδιάζειν ἑτέρας συνθέσεις, αὐτοί τε εἰκότως καταφρονοῦνται, τούς τε ἐμπειρικοὺς ἐργάζονται [464] τολμηροτέρους εἰς ἀντιλογίαν.
english_sentence_A: For when those who dogmatize, on being asked the rationale by which each of the drugs they use is composed, have nothing to say, and, if they have lost their written recipes for them, are unable to improvise other compositions, they are themselves deservedly despised, and they make the Empiricists [464] bolder in contradiction.
english_sentence_B: For when the dogmatists, asked for the reasoning by which each of the drugs they use is compounded, have nothing to say, and, having lost their written formulas, are unable to improvise other compoundings, they are themselves rightly despised, and they make the Empiricists [464] bolder in contradiction.

greek_sentence: εἰ δ’ ἠπίσταντο τὴν ἑκάστου πάθους ὧν θεραπεύουσι φύσιν ἐγίγνωσκόν τε μέθοδον, ὡς ἐξ αὐτῆς ἐξευρίσκειν τόν τε σκοπὸν τῆς θεραπείας, ἑκάστου τε τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων τὴν δύναμιν, οὐκ ἂν ἠγνόουν τὸν λόγον τῆς συνθέσεως· οἷον αὐτίκα κοῖλον ἕλκος ἀπερίστατον, οὐδὲν γὰρ χεῖρον, ὡς ἔνιοι καλοῦσι, συντόμου διδασκαλίας ἕνεκεν οὕτως καὶ ἡμᾶς ὀνομάσαι, πῶς ἄν τις ἰάσαιτο προκείσθω σκοπεῖν, ὡς εἰ καὶ μήπω μηδὲν εὕροιτο φάρμακον ἐπιτήδειον εἰς αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: But if they understood the nature of each affection among those they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the rationale of the composition. For example, to begin with, let it be set before us to consider how one might heal a hollow uncomplicated ulcer (for it is no worse that we too should name it thus, as some call it, for the sake of concise teaching), as if no drug suitable for it had yet been discovered.
english_sentence_B: But if they understood the nature of each affection that they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the reasoning of compounding. greek_sentence: εἰ δ’ ἠπίσταντο τὴν ἑκάστου πάθους ὧν θεραπεύουσι φύσιν ἐγίγνωσκόν τε μέθοδον, ὡς ἐξ αὐτῆς ἐξευρίσκειν τόν τε σκοπὸν τῆς θεραπείας, ἑκάστου τε τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων τὴν δύναμιν, οὐκ ἂν ἠγνόουν τὸν λόγον τῆς συνθέσεως· οἷον αὐτίκα κοῖλον ἕλκος ἀπερίστατον, οὐδὲν γὰρ χεῖρον, ὡς ἔνιοι καλοῦσι, συντόμου διδασκαλίας ἕνεκεν οὕτως καὶ ἡμᾶς ὀνομάσαι, πῶς ἄν τις ἰάσαιτο προκείσθω σκοπεῖν, ὡς εἰ καὶ μήπω μηδὲν εὕροιτο φάρμακον ἐπιτήδειον εἰς αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: But if they understood the nature of each affection among those they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the rationale of the composition. For example, to begin with, let it be set before us to consider how one might heal a hollow uncomplicated ulcer (for it is no worse that we too should name it thus, as some call it, for the sake of concise teaching), as if no drug suitable for it had yet been discovered.
english_sentence_B: But if they understood the nature of each affection that they treat, and knew a method such that from it they could discover both the aim of the treatment and the power of each of the simple drugs, they would not be ignorant of the reasoning of compounding. For instance, let it be proposed to consider how one would cure a hollow ulcer that is uncomplicated (for there is no harm in our also naming it so, as some call it, for the sake of concise teaching), as though no drug suitable for it had yet been found.

greek_sentence: διδαχθέντες γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου τὴν τῶν κοίλων ἑλκῶν ἴασιν γίγνεσθαι γιγνομένης σαρκὸς ἀντὶ τῆς ἀπολωλυίας ἑτέρας, ἐξ αὐτῆς δηλονότι βλαστανούσης τῆς ὑποκειμένης σαρκὸς, ἐνενοήσαμεν ἀδύνατον εἶναι γενέσθαι τοῦτο, ῥύπου κατὰ τὸ ἕλκος ἢ πολλῆς ὑγρότητος ὑποκειμένης.
english_sentence_A: For having been taught by reason that the healing of hollow ulcers comes about when other flesh is generated in place of that which has been lost, sprouting evidently from the underlying flesh itself, we realized that it is impossible for this to happen when filth or much moisture lies in the ulcer.
english_sentence_B: For, having been taught by reason that the healing of hollow ulcers comes about when other flesh is generated in place of that which has been destroyed, sprouting evidently from the underlying flesh itself, we have realised that this cannot come about while there is filth in the ulcer or much moisture present.

greek_sentence: καὶ πολλάκις γε ὅτι κατὰ μεσοῦσαν ἑκάστην τούτων ἢ ἀρχομένην ἢ τελευτῶσαν, ὡς εἶναι δώδεκα τάξεις τῶν κατ’ ἐπικράτειαν ἡντιναοῦν λεγομένων φαρμάκων.
english_sentence_A: It is necessary, then, to know the materials of such drugs, not simply by kind, as Dioscorides wrote in a different manner, but as we did in the books on simple drugs, [465] writing not only that this particular drug heats or cools or produces some other such effect, but also that the drug is of such a kind at the first remove from the mean, or the second or the third or the fourth; and often, indeed, that it is at the middle of each of these, or at its beginning or its end, so that there are twelve orders of the drugs that are spoken of according to any predominance whatsoever.
english_sentence_B: And often, too, we wrote that it is so at the middle of each of these, or at its beginning, or at its end, so that there are twelve ranks of the drugs named according to any predominance whatever.

greek_sentence: τοῦτο γὰρ, ὡς ἔφην, ἔστι τὸ μάλιστα χρήσιμον, ὥστε ἐάν ποτε δέηταί τις ἰσχυροτέρου φαρμάκου, γινώσκειν ἐφ’ ὃ μεταβήσεται, μὴ παρόντος δὲ τῶν ἁπλῶν μηδενὸς, ἐπὶ τὸ σύνθετον ἐρχόμεθα.
english_sentence_A: For this, as I said, is the most useful thing: so that, if ever someone needs a stronger drug, he knows to which one he will pass over; but when none of the simples is at hand, we come to the compound.
english_sentence_B: For this, as I said, is the most useful thing: that if ever one needs a stronger drug, one knows what to pass on to; and when none of the simples is at hand, we come to the compound.

greek_sentence: καὶ πρῶτόν γε ὑποκείσθω κηρὸν ἔχειν ἡμᾶς καὶ ἰὸν, ἄλλο δὲ μηδὲν τῶν ἁρμοττόντων ἄντικρυς ἕλκει κοίλῳ, λιβανωτὸν λέγω καὶ ἴριν καὶ ἀριστολοχίαν, ἄλευρόν τε τὸ τῶν ὀρόβων καὶ πάνακος ῥίζαν, ὅσα τ’ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα.
english_sentence_A: And first let it be supposed that we have wax and verdigris, but nothing else of the things directly suited to a hollow ulcer—I mean frankincense and iris and aristolochia, and the flour of bitter vetch and the root of panax, and whatever other such things there are.

english_sentence_A: Knowing, then, that if wax alone is applied the ulcer will be found sordid, inasmuch as wax is able neither to cleanse nor to dry, whereas if verdigris is applied it will be bitten and eaten away and will become inflamed, we shall decline each of these, and shall make from both another, intermediate one, weaker than verdigris but stronger than wax.
english_sentence_B: We know, then, that if wax alone is applied the ulcer will be found foul, since wax can neither cleanse nor dry, whereas if verdigris is applied the ulcer will be bitten and eroded and will become inflamed.

english_sentence_A: Knowing, then, that if wax alone is applied the ulcer will be found sordid, inasmuch as wax is able neither to cleanse nor to dry, whereas if verdigris is applied it will be bitten and eaten away and will become inflamed, we shall decline each of these, and shall make from both another, intermediate one, weaker than verdigris but stronger than wax.

V. 878 ; μ. ὄψον, ἀργυρίδιον, X. Mem. 3.14.1 , Ar. Pl. 240 , cf. Antiph. 44 . in Amount or Importance, petty, trivial, slight, σμ. πρόφασις Thgn. 323 ; ἔπος, ἔγκλημα, ῥοπή, etc., S. OC 443 , Tr. 361 , OT 961 , etc.; ἐκ σμικροῦ λόγου on some slight pretext, Id. OC 620 ; ἐν σμικρῷ λόγῳ παρῆκεν as of small account, ib. 569 ; αἰτίας μικρᾶς πέρι E. Andr. 387 , etc.; οὐδὲ μικρόν, = οὐδὲ γρῦ , D. 19.37 ; of persons, of small account, opp. μέγας, σμ. ἐν σμικροῖς, μέγας ἐν μεγάλοις Pi. P. 3.107 ; ἄριστ' ἂν καὶ μέγας ὀρθοῖθ' ὑπὸ μικροτέρων S. Aj. 161 (anap.), etc.; σμ. τίθησί με Id. OC 958 ; βίος ὁ μ., = μέτριος , E. Fr. 504 ; τίνος σμικροτάτου μεταβαλόντος, σμικρότατος τὴν δύναμιν, Pl. R. 473b ; of the mind, οὐ σμικρὸν φρονεῖ S. Aj. 1120 ; of style, mean, [ Φίλιστοσ] μικρὸς ταῖς ἐκφράσεσιν D.H. Vett.Cens. 3.2 ; of festivals, of lesser importance, Ἁλίεια τὰ μεγάλα καὶ τὰ μ. SIG 1067.14 (Cedreae). of Time, short, Pi. O. 12.12 , Ar. Pl. 126 , etc.; εἰς μ. χρόνον Pl. R. 498d ; ἐν μικρῷ (sc. χρόνῳ) shortly, X. Cyn. 5.32 , Eq. 8.7 ; πρὸ μικροῦ Poll. 1.72 ; ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ καταλιθοβολήσουσί με LXX Ex. 17.4 . of Age, young, Ostr.Bodl. i237 (ii B.C.), etc. Adverbial usages, regul. Adv. σμικρῶς, but little, Pl. Criti. 107d ; μικρῶς by a little, prob. in Archim. Stom. 1 : Sup. σμικρότατα X. Mem. 3.11.12 . σμικροῦ or μικροῦ within a little, almost, Id. Mem. 2.10.4 . σμικρῷ by a little, with Comp. , Pl. Plt. 262c , etc.; also σμικρῷ πρόσθεν a little before, Id. An. 3.1.11 , etc.; repeated, μικρὸν μικρόν Antiph. 10 : pl., of Degree, σμικρὰ γεωμετρίας ἔμπειροι Pl. R. 527a , etc.; σμίκρ' ἄττα διατρίψαντες Id. Prt. 316a ; μικρὰ διακινήσω σε περὶ τοῦ πράγματος Sosip. 1.22 ; περιπάτησον μικρὰ μετ' ἐμοῦ Men. Sam. 243 , cf. Plu. Luc. 31 . with Preps., ἐπὶ σμικρόν but a little, S. greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν οὖν σκληρὰ σώματα πλέονος ἰοῦ τῇ κηρωτῇ μιγνυμένου σαρκοῦται, τὰ μαλακὰ δὲ ἐλάττονος.
english_sentence_A: Hard bodies, then, are made to grow flesh when more verdigris is mixed with the cerate, soft bodies when less.
english_sentence_B: Hard bodies, then, fill with flesh when more verdigris is mixed into the cerate, soft bodies when less.

greek_sentence: ἐὰν δ’ ἐλλιπέστερον, αὐξάνειν αὐτοῦ τὴν δύναμιν, ὥσπερ γε καὶ καθαιρεῖν, ἡνίκα περαιτέρω τοῦ προσήκοντος ἐνήργησεν.
english_sentence_A: For if it appears to have accomplished what is needed, it is proper to continue with it; but if it falls somewhat short, to increase its power, just as also to reduce it, whenever it has acted beyond what is proper.
english_sentence_B: For if it appears to have done what is required, one should persist with it; but if it has acted rather deficiently, one should increase its potency, just as one should also reduce it whenever it has acted beyond what is fitting.

lsj_entry_text: κηρωτή, ἡ , ʽκηρόὠ = κήρωμα 1 , cerate or salve, used medically, Hp. Off. 12 , Art. 14 , Ar. Ach. 1176 , Ph. Bel. 96.18 ; κ. οἰνανθίνη, ῥοδίνη, Dsc. 1.109 , 2.110 ; κ. ὑγρά Gal. 11.391 ; used as a cosmetic, Ar. Fr. 320.1 .
greek_sentence: οἷον ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ προκειμένου διὰ τῆς κηρωτῆς καὶ ἰοῦ φαρμάκου, σκοπεῖσθαι πότερον ἐσαρκώθη τὸ ἕλκος ἢ σὰρξ μὲν οὐκ ἐγεννήθη, ῥυπαρὸν δὲ εὑρέθη καὶ μεστὸν ὑγρότητος, ἢ πρὸς τῷ μὴ σεσαρκῶσθαι [469] δήξεώς τις αἴσθησις ἐγένετο τῷ κάμνοντι, καὶ θερμότερον ἢ ἐρυθρότερόν γε τὸ ἡλκωμένον ἐφάνη.
english_sentence_A: For example, in the case of the drug now before us, the one made from cerate and verdigris, one must consider whether the ulcer has been filled with flesh, or whether flesh was not generated but the ulcer was found foul and full of moisture, or whether, in addition to its not having been filled with flesh, [469] some sensation of biting arose in the patient and the ulcerated part appeared hotter, or at any rate redder.
english_sentence_B: For example, in the case of the very drug under discussion, the one made of cerate and verdigris, one must consider whether the ulcer has been filled with flesh; or whether flesh has not been generated, but the ulcer has been found dirty and full of moisture; or whether, besides not having been filled with flesh, [469] the patient has had some sensation of biting, and the ulcerated part has appeared hotter or at any rate redder.

greek_sentence: ἐὰν μὲν οὖν ἀσθενέστερον φανεῖται, μίξει μέλιτος ἢ ἰοῦ τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ παραυξήσεις, ἐὰν δ’ ἰσχυρότερον, ἔλαιον ἢ ῥόδινον μίξεις μαλάττων τὸ μέλλον ἀναλαμβάνεσθαι τοῖς μοτοῖς φάρμακον.
english_sentence_A: If, then, it appears weaker, you will increase its power by the admixture of honey or verdigris; but if stronger, you will mix in olive oil or rose-oil, softening the drug that is to be taken up on the lint pledgets.
english_sentence_B: If, then, the drug appears too weak, you will increase its potency by an admixture of honey or of verdigris; but if too strong, you will mix in oil or rose-oil, softening the drug that is to be taken up on the lint-plugs.

english_sentence_A: On an occasion of need, then, cerate and verdigris are mixed in this way, just as I said they were once mixed by me.
english_sentence_B: On the occasion itself, cerate and verdigris are mixed in this way, just as I said they were once mixed by me.

lsj_entry_text: ἔμ-πλαστρος, ἡ, salve or plaster, Dsc. 1.32 ; said to be later form of ἔμπλαστος, Gal. 13.372 ; also ἔμπλαστρον, τό, Hierocl. Facet. 221 , PSI 3.297 (V A. D. ).
greek_sentence: παρασκευὴ δ’ ἔστω τοῖς ἰατρεύουσιν ἐμπλάστρου γεγονυίας ἣν ἀπὸ τῆς χρόας ὀνομάζουσι χλωρὰν, ἱκανῆς μὲν καὶ τὰ πρόσφατα τραύματα θεραπεύειν, ὅσα μὴ μεγάλα, δυναμένης δὲ καὶ διὰ ῥοδίνου τήκεσθαι πρὸς σύστασιν ἐμμέσου φαρμάκου.
english_sentence_A: But let those who practise medicine have in readiness a prepared plaster, the one they name 'green' from its colour, which is sufficient also to treat fresh wounds, those that are not large, and which can also be melted with rose-oil to the consistency of a drug of intermediate (ἐμμέσου) character.
english_sentence_B: But let those who practise medicine have in readiness a plaster already made, which they name 'the green' from its colour. It is sufficient to treat fresh wounds, those that are not large, and it can also be melted down with rose-oil to the consistency of a drug applied on lint.

Th. 367 ; ἕτερον τοσοῦτον as much again, Hdt. 2.149 ; ἑτέρου τοσούτου χρόνου for as long again, Isoc. 4.153 ; ἕ. τοιαῦτα other things of like kind, Hdt. 1.120 , 191 ; ἑτέρων τοιῶνδε (sc. ἀνθρώπων) ἄρχεις ib. 207 ; τῷ αὐτῷ τρόπῳ . . τῷ ἑτέρῳ in the same way over again, Id. 2.127 ; ἄλλα τε τοιαῦθ' ἕτερα μυρία Ar. Pl. Prt. 333a , D. 10.44 , etc.; ἕτερον, ἕτερα ἢ . . , E. Or. 345 , X. Cyr. 1.6.2 ; παρὰ ταῦτα πάντα ἕτερόν τι Pl. Phd. 74a ; ἕτερα πολιτείας εἴδη παρὰ μοναρχίαν Arist. Pol. 1294a25 , cf. 1286b21 . other than should be, euphem. for κακός, παθεῖν μὲν εὖ, παθεῖν δὲ θάτερα S. Ph. 503 ; ἀγάθ' ἢ θάτερα, ἵνα μηδὲν εἴπω φλαῦρον D. 22.12 : abs., δαίμων ἕ. Pi. P. 3.34 ; λέκτρα, συμφοραί, E. Med. 639 (lyr.), HF 1238 ; ἐὰν τὰ ἕ. ψηφίσωνται οἱ δικασταί D. 48.30 ; πλέον θάτερον ἐποίησαν did more harm (than good), Isoc. 19.25 , cf. Pl. Phd. 114e , Euthd. 280e , Aristid. 2.117 J. Special Phrases: elliptical, mostly in dat. fem., τῇ ἑτέρᾳ (sc. χειρί), Ep. ἑτέρῃ or ἑτέρηφι, with one hand (v. sub init.); with the left hand, Od. 3.441 , Il. 22.80 , Theoc. 24.45 : hence prov., οὐ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ληπτός not to be caught with one hand, Pl. Sph. 226a ; ἐκ δ' ἑτέρης A.R. 1.1115 , AP 9.650 ( Leont. ). θατέρᾳ (sc. ἡμέρᾳ) on the morrow, S. OT 782 , E. Rh. 449 ; τῆς ἑτέρας Pl. Cri. 44a ; but τῇ ἑτέρᾳ on the following (i.e. the third) day, X. Cyr. 4.6.10 . (sc. ὁδῷ) in another or a different way, καὶ τῇδε φῦναι χἀτέρᾳ S. OC 1444 ; another way, τρέπεσθαι Ar. Nu. 812 ; ἑτέρᾳ πῃ Id. Eq. 35 ; τότ' ἄλλοσ' . . , θατέρᾳ δὲ . . S. Tr. 272 ; θατέρᾳ . . , θατέρᾳ . . in one way . . , in the other . . , Henioch. 5.16 ; ἑτέρηφι Hes. Op. 216 : acc. ἑτέραν ἐκτρέπεσθαι Luc. Tim. 5 . adverb. with Preps.: ἐπὶ θάτερα to the one or the other side, one or the other way, ἐπὶ μὲν θάτερα . . , ἐπὶ θ. δὲ . . Hp. Art. 7 ; τότε μὲν ἐπὶ θάτερα, τότε δ' ἐπὶ θ. Pl. Sph. 259c : also with another Prep., ἐς τὰ ἐπὶ θάτερα to or on the other side, Th. 1.87 ; ἐκ τοῦ ἐπὶ θάτερα from the other side, Id. 7.37 ; ἐκ μὲν τοῦ ἐπὶ θ., ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἐπὶ θ. Pl. Prt. 314e : c. gen., ἐς τὰ ἐπὶ θ. τοῦ ποταμοῦ Th. 7.84 ; εἰς τἀπὶ θ. τῆς πόλεως X. HG 6.2.7 ; τὸ ἐπὶ θάτερον τῆς ῥινός Hp. Art. 35 . κατὰ θάτερα on the one or other side, κατὰ θ. ἀστός D. 57.30 ; ψόφου κατὰ θ. προσπεσόντος Plu. Brut. 51 , etc.; but καθ' ἕτερα at other points, Th. 7.42 . Adv. ἑτέρως in one or the other way, opp. ἀμφοτέρως, Pl. Tht. 181e ; ἑ. τε καὶ ἑ., = ἀμφοτέρως , Id. Phdr. 235a ; τοῦ σκέλους ἑ. ἔχειν, = ἑτεροσκελὴς εἶναι , Philostr. VA 3.39 . differently, rarely in Poetry, οὐχ ἑ. τις ἐρεῖ Theoc. Ep. 10.3 ; ἑ. ἔχειν to be different, Ar. Pl. 371 : freq. in Prose, ὡς ἑ. in the other way (cf. ὡς) , ἢν ἡ ἑτέρη γνάθος ἐκστῇ ὡς ἑ. χρὴ τὴν ἐπίδεσιν ἄγειν Hp. Art. 34 , cf. Pl. Sph. 266a , etc.; ἐάν τε καλῶς, ἐάν θ' ὡς ἑ. D. 18.85 , cf. 212 : c. gen., differently from, ἑ. πως τῶν εἰωθότων Pl. Plt. 295d ; ἑ. ἤπερ . . Ael. NA 12.28 . otherwise than should be, badly, wrongly, once in Hom. , ἑ. ἐβόλοντο Od. 1.234 ; εἰ καὶ ἑ. τοῦτο ἀπέβη SIG 851.10 (Marc.Aur.); εἴ τι ἑ. φρονεῖτε Ep.Phil. 3.15 .

english_sentence_A: If, then, anyone asks you which of these green plasters is best, remember what is often said by me, and answer that all are best for the one who knows the conditions to which each is suited, just as all are also bad for the one who does not know.

greek_sentence: ἡ δ’ ὑφισταμένη τοῖς τὴν πευκίνην ῥητίνην περιέχουσι κεραμείοις ὑγρὰ ῥητίνη κατὰ μὲν τὴν σύστασιν καὶ τὴν χρόαν ἀκριβῶς ἔοικε τῇ τερμινθίνῃ, τῇ δ’ ὀσμῇ καὶ τῇ γεύσει διενήνοχεν, ἀηδεστέρα μὲν οὖσα κατὰ τὴν ὀσμὴν, ὥσπερ καὶ δριμυτέρα, καὶ κατὰ τὴν γεῦσιν δακνωδεστέρα· διὸ καὶ κάλλιόν ἐστι τὴν τερμινθίνην μιγνύειν ἅπασι τοῖς μέλλουσι ἕλκη καλῶς ἰάσασθαι φαρμάκοις, ἐπειδὴ πρῶτός τε καὶ ἄριστος ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐστι σκοπὸς ἄδηκτον εἶναι τὸ προσφερόμενον.
english_sentence_A: The liquid resin that settles at the bottom of the earthenware vessels containing pine resin exactly resembles the terebinth in consistency and colour, but differs in smell and taste, being more unpleasant in smell, as also more pungent, and more biting in taste; wherefore it is also better to mix the terebinth into all the drugs that are to heal ulcers well, since the first and best aim among them is that what is applied be non-biting.
english_sentence_B: The liquid resin that settles at the bottom of the earthenware vessels holding pine resin resembles terebinth exactly in consistency and colour, but differs from it in smell and taste: it is more unpleasant in smell, and also more pungent, and more biting in taste. For this reason it is better to mix terebinth into all drugs that are meant to heal ulcers well, since the first and foremost aim in these is that what is applied should be non-biting.

greek_sentence: ἐπὶ τὴν προκειμένην οὖν ἀνέλθωμεν ἔμπλαστρον, εἰς ἣν ὁ Ἀνδρόμαχος ἐμβαλεῖν κελεύει τῆς στροβιλίνης ῥητίνης τὰς δραχ.τ΄.
english_sentence_A: Let us return, then, to the plaster before us, into which Andromachus orders that three hundred drachmas of stone-pine resin be put, mixed with the hundred drachmas of wax, neither he himself nor whoever composed it having aimed accurately at either its consistency or its power.
english_sentence_B: Let us go back, then, to the plaster under discussion. Into it Andromachus directs one to put 300 drachms of strobiline resin mixed with the hundred drachms of wax.

greek_sentence: οὔτε γὰρ ἐχέκολλος ἔσται καὶ δριμεῖα γενήσεται, βοήθημα δ’ αὐτῇ πρὸς ἄμφω καλῶς ἐποίησε τὸν λιβανωτὸν μίξας, ἀλλ’ ὡς [477] πρὸς τὸ πλῆθος ἐκείνων ὀλίγον ἔμιξε καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅτι τοῦ ἰοῦ δραχ.ν΄.
english_sentence_A: For it will not be adhesive, and it will become acrid; and he rightly provided it with a remedy against both by mixing in frankincense, but, [477] relative to the quantity of those ingredients, he mixed in little, and especially because he puts in fifty drachms of verdigris, and these are an eighth part of the four hundred that are made up from the wax and the resin.
english_sentence_B: For it will not be adhesive, and it will turn out acrid.

english_sentence_A: It is better, in the composition, to grind the verdigris with sharp vinegar for several days in a hot sun; for its biting quality will be mitigated, while nothing of its power will be diminished.
english_sentence_B: For its biting quality will be softened, while its power will be diminished not at all.

lsj_entry_text: μίσυ, υος and εως, τό, a copper ore found in Cyprus, Hp. Mul. 1.103 , Gal. 12.241 , 15.32 , Dsc. 5.100 , cf. 74 . truffle, Tuber aestivum, growing near Cyrene, Thphr. Fr. 167 .
greek_sentence: μεμνῆσθαι γὰρ ὑμᾶς νομίζω καὶ τούτου πολλάκις εἰρημένου τῶν μὲν ἰσχυρῶν φαρμάκων, ὁποῖός ἐστιν ὅ τε ἰὸς καὶ τὸ μίσυ καὶ ἡ χαλκῖτις καὶ τὸ σῶρυ καὶ ἡ λεπὶς ἥ τε χάλκανθος ἐν ὄξει λειουμένων ἡμέραις πλείοσι, τὴν μὲν δῆξιν ἀμβλύνεσθαι, τὴν δ’ ἀρετὴν αὐξάνεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: For I think you remember this too, which has often been said, that in the case of the strong drugs, such as verdigris, misy, chalcitis, sory, scale and chalcanthum, when they are ground in vinegar for several days, the bitingness is blunted while the virtue is increased.

greek_sentence: ὅπως οὖν γένηται λεπτομερέστερα τὴν διὰ τῆς τρίψεως καὶ τοῦ ὄξους αὐτοῖς κατεργασίαν χρὴ προστίθεσθαι· διὰ ταύτης γὰρ ἀκριβῶς λεπτουργηθέντα [479] μέχρι τοῦ βάθους καταδύεται.
english_sentence_A: In order, then, that they may become more fine-particled, one must add to them the working-up by means of trituration and vinegar; for having been thoroughly refined through this, they sink down [479] as far as the depth.
english_sentence_B: So, in order that they may become finer-particled, one must apply to them the processing by means of trituration and vinegar; for when they have been thoroughly refined by this, [479] they sink down to the depth.

greek_sentence: προσέρχεται δέ τι καὶ ἄλλο χρηστὸν ἐν ταῖς τοιαύταις παρασκευαῖς τῶν φαρμάκων, ἀκριβῶς γὰρ κατεργασθέντα διεξέρχεται τοὺς κατὰ τὸ σῶμα πόρους, μηδαμόθεν κατὰ τὴν ὁδοιπορίαν ἰσχόμενα καὶ διὰ τοῦτο, κᾂν ᾖ θερμότερα φύσει, χωρὶς τοῦ δάκνειν ἐνεργεῖ.
english_sentence_A: And there accrues also another benefit in such preparations of drugs: for having been thoroughly worked up, they pass through the pores in the body, being held back nowhere on their journey, and for this reason, even if they are hotter by nature, they act without biting.
english_sentence_B: And there accrues also another benefit in such preparations of drugs: for, when thoroughly processed, they pass through the pores throughout the body, being held back nowhere on their passage, and for this reason, even if they are hotter by nature, they act without biting.

lsj_entry_text: δῆξις, εως, ἡ, (δάκνω) bite, biting, Arist. HA 623a1 ; δήξιες σπλάγχνων gnawings, Hp. VM 19 : metaph., of mental anguish, pangs, Zeno Stoic. 1.51 (pl.), Chrysipp.ib. 3.119 , Phld. D. 3 . Fr. 22 ; also, biting jokes, Plu. Lyc. 14 .
greek_sentence: καὶ τῶν χυμῶν οὖν αὐτῶν κατὰ τὸ σῶμα γεννωμένων οἱ μὲν λεπτοὶ διαπνέονται ῥᾳδίως ἄνευ δήξεως, οἱ παχύτεροι δὲ κατεχόμενοί τε καὶ σφηνούμενοι λυποῦσιν, ὅταν ὦσι δακνώδεις.
english_sentence_A: And so too of the humours themselves that are generated in the body, the thin ones are easily dispersed by transpiration without bitingness, whereas the thicker ones, being retained and wedged in, cause distress, when they are biting.
english_sentence_B: So too, of the humours themselves that are generated in the body, the thin ones are readily dispersed by transpiration without biting, whereas the thicker ones, being retained and wedged in, cause distress whenever they are biting.

greek_sentence: ὁ δ’ αὐτὸς λόγος ἐστὶ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν καυθέντων μεταλλικῶν φαρμάκων, ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνα μὲν ἐκ τῆς τοῦ πυρὸς ὁμιλίας διασώζει τι δακνῶδες, ὃ κατὰ τὰς πλύσεις ἀποθέμενα παντάπασι ἄδηκτα γίνεται.

Ap. 41d , etc.; ψυχῆς ἀγαθῆς πατρὶς ὁ ξύμπας κόσμος Democr. 247 : freq. with other Adjs., ὁ πιστὸς κἀ. S. Tr. 541 ; δικαίων κἀ. ib. 1050 :—ironical, τὸν ἀ. Κρέοντα Id. Ant. 31 . ὦ ἀγαθέ, my good friend, as a term of gentle remonstrance, Pl. Prt. 311a , etc. ἀ. δαίμων, v. sub δαίμων; ἀ. τύχη, v. sub τύχη; ἀ. θεός = Lat. bona dea, Plu. Caes. 9 , Cic. 19 . of things, good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη . . ἀ. κουροτρόφος Od. 9.27 , etc.; ἀ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει X. Cyn. 13.17 : c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀ. good for it, Id. HP 9.11.1 . of outward circumstances, αἰδὼς οὐκ ἀ. κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι Od. 17.347 ; εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν to good purpose, Il. 9.102 ; ὁ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀ. περ for his own good end, 11.789 ; οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη 2.204 :—ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it is good to do so and so<*> Il. 7.282 , 24.130 , Od. 3.196 , etc. morally good, πρῆξις Democr. 177 ; ἔργα Emp. 112.2 , cf. Ep.Rom. 2.7 , etc. ἀγαθόν, τό, good, blessing, benefit, of persons or things, ὦ μέγα ἀ. σὺ τοῖς φίλοις X. Cyr. 5.3.20 ; φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀ. εἶναί φασι Id. Mem. 2.4.2 , cf. Ar. Ra. 74 , etc; as term of endearment for a baby, blessing!, treasure!, Men. Sam. 28 :— ἀγαθόν τινα δεδρακέναι, πεποιηκέναι confer a benefit on . . , Th. 3.68 , Lys. 13.92 ; ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ τινος for one's good, Th. 5.27 , X. Cyr. 7.4.3 ; ἐπ' ἀ. τοῖς πολίταις Ar. HG 5.2.35 :—in pl., ἡ ἐπ' ἀγαθοῖς γεναμένη (sic) κατασπορά PFlor. 21.10 (iii A.D.):—τὸ ἀ. or τἀ., the good, Epich. 171.5 , cf. Pl. R. 506b , 508e , Arist. english_sentence_A: For to harder bodies, whether through natural temperament or through age or through region or pursuits, one must apply drugs that dry more, and to moister bodies those that dry less.

english_sentence_A: For if the hollow ulcer is found to be free of inflammation and [485] clean, one should make no innovation; but if it is moister or fouler, one should intensify the drying and cleansing drug; and if it is more hollow than before, one should relax it.

lsj_entry_text: μικρός and σμικρός, ά, όν, Dor. , Ion. μικκός (q.v.): σμικρός is corroborated by metre in Il. 17.757 , Hes. Op. 361 , and might be restored in Il. 5.801 , Od. 3.296 (μικρός codd.); it is prob. the only form in Hdt. ( μικρός Hdt. 2.74 codd.): freq. in Lyr. and prob. always in Trag. (exc. where metre requires μικρός, as S. Aj. 161 (anap., Comp. )); most freq. in Pl. ; but in Th. , also Ar. and other Com., μικρός prevails, σμικρός being found Th. 4.13 , 7.75 , 8.81 , Ar. Ach. 523 , V. 5 ; Att. Inscrr. have σμικρός IG 12.313.111 , al., μικρός ib. 369.10 , al.:—small, little, in Size, μ. ἔην δέμας Il. 5.801 ; μ. λίθος Od. 3.296 ; κίρκον, ὅ τε σμικρῇσι φόνον φέρει ὀρνίθεσσιν Il. 17.757 ; σμ. ἄστεα Hdt. 1.5 ; μεγάθεϊ σμικροί Id. 2.74 : with Dims., μ. πολίχνιον, γῄδιον, παιδάρια, Isoc. 5.145 , X. Cyr. 8.3.38 , Ages. 1.21 : as a Com. exaggeration, δικαστηρίδιον μ. πάνυ Ar. V. 803 ; σκαλαθυρμάτι' ἄττα μ. Id. Nu. 630 , etc.: c. inf., μικροὶ δ' ὁρᾶν Id. Pax 821 : as a term of reproach, Κλειγενὴς ὁ μικρός Id. Ra. 709 , cf. Pl. Prt. 323d , Arist. EN 1123b7 , Alex. 98.7 ; Ἀμύντας ὁ μ. Arist. Pol. 1311b3 ; οἱ ἐν μικρῷ μεγάλοι short but stoutly built, Philostr. Gym. 36 ; ὁ μ. δάκτυλος SIG 1172.4 (Lebena). in Quantity, σμικρὸν ἐπὶ σμικρῷ καταθεῖναι Hes. Op. 361 ; μέλιτος μικρόν Ar. V. 878 ; μ. ὄψον, ἀργυρίδιον, X. Mem. 3.14.1 , Ar. Pl. 240 , cf. Antiph. 44 . in Amount or Importance, petty, trivial, slight, σμ. πρόφασις Thgn. 323 ; ἔπος, ἔγκλημα, ῥοπή, etc., S. OC 443 , Tr. 361 , OT 961 , etc.; ἐκ σμικροῦ λόγου on some slight pretext, Id. OC 620 ; ἐν σμικρῷ λόγῳ παρῆκεν as of small account, ib. 569 ; αἰτίας μικρᾶς πέρι E. Andr. 387 , etc.; οὐδὲ μικρόν, = οὐδὲ γρῦ , D. 19.37 ; of persons, of small account, opp. μέγας, σμ. ἐν σμικροῖς, μέγας ἐν μεγάλοις Pi. P. 3.107 ; ἄριστ' ἂν καὶ μέγας ὀρθοῖθ' ὑπὸ μικροτέρων S. Aj. 161 (anap.), etc.; σμ. τίθησί με Id. OC 958 ; βίος ὁ μ., = μέτριος , E. Fr. 504 ; τίνος σμικροτάτου μεταβαλόντος, σμικρότατος τὴν δύναμιν, Pl. R. 473b ; of the mind, οὐ σμικρὸν φρονεῖ S. Aj. 1120 ; of style, mean, [ Φίλιστοσ] μικρὸς ταῖς ἐκφράσεσιν D.H. Vett.Cens. 3.2 ; of festivals, of lesser importance, Ἁλίεια τὰ μεγάλα καὶ τὰ μ. SIG 1067.14 (Cedreae). of Time, short, Pi. O. 12.12 , Ar. Pl. 126 , etc.; εἰς μ. χρόνον Pl. R. 498d ; ἐν μικρῷ (sc. χρόνῳ) shortly, X. Cyn. 5.32 , Eq. 8.7 ; πρὸ μικροῦ Poll. 1.72 ; ἔτι μικρὸν καὶ καταλιθοβολήσουσί με LXX Ex. 17.4 . of Age, young, Ostr.Bodl. i237 (ii B.C.), etc. Adverbial usages, regul. Adv. σμικρῶς, but little, Pl. Criti. 107d ; μικρῶς by a little, prob. in Archim. Stom. 1 : Sup. σμικρότατα X. Mem. 3.11.12 . σμικροῦ or μικροῦ within a little, almost, Id. Cyr. 1.4.8 , D. 18.151 , etc.; in full, μικροῦ δεῖν, v. δεῖ 11 , δέω (B) 1 ; μικροῦ τινος ἀπελείφθη τοῦ μή . . Ach.Tat. 7.13 ; but μικροῦ πρίασθαι for a little, cheap, X. Mem. 2.10.4 . σμικρῷ by a little, with Comp. , Pl. Plt. 262c , etc.; also σμικρῷ πρόσθεν a little before, Id. Lg. 719b , etc.; μικρῷ ἄνωθεν D. 44.6 . μικρόν a little, σμικρὸν ὑπολείπεσθαι, σμ. τι παρακλίνειν, X. An. 5.4.22 , Pl. Cra. 410a ; of Time, X. An. 3.1.11 , etc.; repeated, μικρὸν μικρόν Antiph. 10 : pl., of Degree, σμικρὰ γεωμετρίας ἔμπειροι Pl. R. 527a , etc.; σμίκρ' ἄττα διατρίψαντες Id. Prt. 316a ; μικρὰ διακινήσω σε περὶ τοῦ πράγματος Sosip. 1.22 ; περιπάτησον μικρὰ μετ' ἐμοῦ Men. Sam. 243 , cf. Plu. Luc. 31 . with Preps., ἐπὶ σμικρόν but a little, S. El. 414 , Antipho 6.18 , Hdt. 4.129 . κατὰ μικρόν into small pieces, X. An. 7.3.22 ; so κατὰ μικρὰ γενομένης τῆς δυνάμεως ib. 5.6.32 ; also, little by little, κατὰ μικρὸν ἀεί Ar. V. 702 , cf. Nu. 741 ; opp. συλλήβδην, Pl. R. 344a ; καὶ κατὰ σμ. or μ. ever so little, Id. Sph. 241c , Isoc. 3.10 , D. 2.22 . παρὰ μικρόν within a little, παρὰ μ. ἐλθεῖν c. inf., to be within an ace of doing, E. Heracl. 295 (anap.), cf. Isoc. 7.6 , etc.; παρὰ μ. ἦλθον ἀποθανεῖν Id. 17.42 ; τὸ παρὰ μ. ὥσπερ οὐδὲν ἀπέχειν δοκεῖ Arist. Ph. 197a30 ; but τὸ παρὰ μ. σῴζεσθαι to be only just saved, Id. Rh. 1371b11 , cf. Simp. in Ph. 344.10 ; gradual, imperceptible change, Arist. Pol. 1303a20 ; οὐδὲ παρὰ μ. ἦν κρεῖττον c. inf., Plb. 12.20.7 ; [ ἡ τύχη] παρὰ μ. εἰς ἑκάτερα ποιεῖ μεγάλας ῥοπάς Id. 15.6.8 , cf. Isoc. 4.59 ; but also παρὰ μ. ποιεῖσθαι, ἡγεῖσθαι, to think little of . . , D. 61.51 , Isoc. 5.79 . μετὰ μικρόν a little after, Ev.Matt. 26.73 . besides regul. Comp. and Sup. μικρότερος, -ότατος ( Ar. Eq. 789 , D. Prooem. 48 , etc.), there are the irreg. ἐλάσσων, ἐλάχιστος, from ἐλαχύς, and μείων, μεῖστος, also μειότερος; v. μείων. greek_sentence: [487] καλλίων δὲ σύνθεσις ἔσται τὸ μὲν ὄγδοον μέρος ἰοῦ μιξάντων τῇ διὰ τοῦ κηροῦ καὶ τῆς ῥητίνης συνθέσει, προλειωσάντων δὲ πλείοσιν ἡμέραις τὸν ἰὸν μετὰ ὄξους δριμυτάτου.
english_sentence_A: [487] But a finer composition will result if one mixes the eighth part of verdigris with the composition made from wax and resin, having first triturated the verdigris for several days with the most acrid vinegar.
english_sentence_B: [487] A finer composition will result if one mixes an eighth part of verdigris into the composition made with wax and resin, having first ground the verdigris for several days with the most acrid vinegar.

english_sentence_A: Of oil you will mix in, whenever you prepare the drug without vinegar and frankincense, cyathi equal in number to the ounces of verdigris; but whenever you mix in frankincense and vinegar, if the phryktē (roasted resin) is somewhat fattier and softer and you are preparing it in summer, you will mix in none; but when it is hard and it is winter, one cyathus.
english_sentence_B: But when you mix in frankincense and vinegar, if the roasted [resin] is somewhat fattier and softer and you are preparing it in summer, you will mix in none; but when it is hard, and in winter, one cyathus.

english_sentence_A: You will mix in, of the most liquid resin, a third of the weight of the wax, and of the less liquid, a half.
english_sentence_B: Of the most liquid you will mix in a third of the weight of the wax, and of the less liquid one a half.

greek_sentence: τὸν κηρὸν καὶ τὴν ῥητίνην τήξας καὶ ψύξας μῖξον ἰοῦ μέρει ποτὲ μὲν ὀγδόῳ, ποτὲ δὲ δεκάτῳ, ποτὲ δὲ δωδεκάτῳ, γιγνώσκων ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν σκληρῶν σωμάτων τήν τε πρώτην συμμετρίαν ἁρμόττειν, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μαλακῶν τὴν τρίτην, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μέσων τὴν μέσην.
english_sentence_A: The composition will evidently turn out to be something like this: having melted the wax and the resin and cooled them, mix them with a part of verdigris, sometimes an eighth, sometimes a tenth, sometimes a twelfth, knowing that for hard bodies the first proportion is suitable, for soft ones the third, and for intermediate ones the intermediate.

english_sentence_B: If you should wish to make the drug milder, put in a weight of frankincense half of that which you used of the verdigris.

lsj_entry_text: ἔμ-πλαστρος, ἡ, salve or plaster, Dsc. 1.32 ; said to be later form of ἔμπλαστος, Gal. 13.372 ; also ἔμπλαστρον, τό, Hierocl. Facet. 221 , PSI 3.297 (V A. D. ).
greek_sentence: αὗται μὲν οὖν αἱ πρῶται συνθέσεις ἐμπλάστρου χλωρᾶς, κολλητικῆς μὲν ἐναίμων τραυμάτων, ὅσα μὴ μεγάλα καὶ μέχρι συνουλώσεως δὲ τἄλλα δυναμένης ἰᾶσθαι καὶ σαρκούσης, εἰ τακείη μετά τινος ἐλαιώδους ὑγροῦ, λέγω δὲ ἐλαιώδη τό τε ῥόδινον, ᾧ μάλιστα χρῆσθαι προσήκει καθ’ ὃν εἴρηκα τρόπον ἐσκευασμένῳ, καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο τῷ μυρσίνῳ καὶ τῷ κυπρίνῳ καὶ τῷ σχινίνῳ, αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ ἔλαιον, ἐφ’ ὧν μὲν βούλει θερμότητός τι προσθεῖναι τῷ τηκομένῳ φαρμάκῳ τὸ κοινὸν τοῦτο μίξεις.
english_sentence_A: These, then, are the first compositions of the green plaster, which is agglutinative of bloody wounds, those that are not large, and which is able to heal the others as far as cicatrization and to produce flesh, if it is melted with some oily liquid.
english_sentence_B: These, then, are the first compositions of the green plaster: agglutinative of bloody wounds, such as are not large, and able to heal the other [lesions] up to cicatrisation, and fleshing, if it is melted with some oily liquid. By 'oily' I mean rose-oil, which it is most fitting to use, prepared in the way I have described, and after this myrtle-oil, cyprus-oil and mastic-oil.

english_sentence_A: And in the boiling the verdigris must not be put in together with the things being united over the fire, but be mixed with them, once united, in the mortar, if you wish the drug to remain green in colour.
english_sentence_B: As for the boiling, the verdigris should not be added to the ingredients while they are being united over the fire; it should be mixed with them in the mortar once they have been united, if you want the drug to stay green in colour.

english_sentence_A: But since what is appropriate has been said about their colour, [498] I shall pass again to the discussion of their powers, having recalled the point from which I first set out in this book.

greek_sentence: ὡρμήθην δὲ, εἴ τι μεμνήμεθα, περὶ τῶν σαρκωτικῶν φαρμάκων εἰπεῖν, ὧν ὁ μὲν τῆς δυνάμεως σκοπός ἐστιν ἐν τῷ μετρίως τε καὶ ἀδήκτως ῥύπτειν τε καὶ ξηραίνειν.
english_sentence_A: I set out, if we remember, to speak about the flesh-producing drugs, whose aim with respect to their power lies in cleansing and drying moderately and without biting; but the compositions according to species are different, being varied according to the materials of the simple drugs.
english_sentence_B: I set out, if we remember at all, to speak about the flesh-producing drugs, the aim of whose power lies in cleansing and drying moderately and without biting.

PA 658b19 ; συνθέσεις (λέγω τὰς γωνίας) Id. Pr. 910b14 . in various technical senses: in Grammar, composition, γραμμάτων τε συνθέσεις, i.e. syllables and words, A. Pr. 460 , cf. Arist. Metaph. 1092a26 ; ς. ἔκ τε ῥημάτων γιγνομένη καὶ ὀνομάτων, i.e. sentences, Pl. Sph. 263d , cf. Cra. 431c , Arist. Po. 1458a28 , Gal. 15.487 ; περὶ συνθέσεως ὀνομάτων, title of work by D.H. ; also, the juxtaposition of letters in a word, Arist. D.S. 5.74 ; ἡ τοῦ παίωνος ξ. the way the paeon is made up, Plu. 2.1143d ; the constitution of things, Hp. Virg. 1 . Math., synthesis of a problem (opp. ἀνάλυσις), Archim. Math., addition, Ph. 1.11 , Plu. 2.1018c , Dioph. 1 Intr.; καθ' ἁντινοῦν -σιν however many times added, i.e. whatever number of times taken (multiplied), Archim. Spir. 1 :—also as Pythag. name for 2 , Anatol. ap. Theol.Ar. 8 . in Logic, union of noun and verb or of two objects of thought in a statement, Arist. Int. 16a12 , de An. 430a27 ; also ὁ παρὰ τὴν ς. P. 4.168 , Fr. 205 ; πὸς τὰς συνθέσις in accordance with the agreements, IG 5(2).343.41 , 60 (Orchom. Arc. , iv B.C.); ἐκ συνθέσεως by arrangement, D.S. 13.112 , etc.; συνθέσεις περὶ γάμων Plu. Ner. 51 . service of plate, ς. πινακίων BGU 781 i 5 (i A.D.), cf. Mart. 4.46.15 , Stat. Silv. 4.9.44 .
greek_sentence: αἱ δὲ κατ’ εἴδη συνθέσεις διάφοροι κατὰ τὰς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων ὕλας ὑπαλλαττόμεναι.
english_sentence_A: I set out, if we remember, to speak about the flesh-producing drugs, whose aim with respect to their power lies in cleansing and drying moderately and without biting; but the compositions according to species are different, being varied according to the materials of the simple drugs.
english_sentence_B: Their compoundings by species, however, are various, varying according to the materials of the simple drugs.

english_sentence_A: It is evident that those properly and primarily called flesh-producing are flesh-producing for uncomplicated ulcers, that is, those which are hollow but do not have filth or inflammation attending them, and still less an influx of bad humours, nor dyscratic flesh in the hollow ulcer.
english_sentence_B: It is evident that the drugs properly and primarily called flesh-producing are flesh-producing for uncomplicated wounds, that is, those which are hollow but do not have filth or inflammation present with them, and still more, have no influx of bad fluids, nor badly tempered flesh in the hollow wound.

english_sentence_A: And it is quite evident that, in the case of inflamed parts, one must cure the inflammation [499], while in the case of parts whose flesh is dyscratic, one must render it eucratic; and since it becomes dyscratic in four simple modes and in four other composite ones, the cure will be effected by means of the opposite qualities.
english_sentence_B: It is quite clear that, in the case of inflamed parts, one must also [499] heal the inflammation, and in the case of parts that have their flesh badly tempered, one must make it well tempered. english_sentence_A: If, then, there should be some suspicion that a still slight inflammation is mingled with the sinus, let the drug by all means be melted in rose-oil; but if it is free of inflammation, in olive oil, and if it tolerates without biting the admixture of old oil, let the drug be melted in that.

english_sentence_A: If, then, there should be some suspicion that a still slight inflammation is mingled with the sinus, let the drug by all means be melted in rose-oil; but if it is free of inflammation, in olive oil, and if it tolerates without biting the admixture of old oil, let the drug be melted in that.
english_sentence_B: But if the sinus is free of inflammation, let it be melted in oil; and if it tolerates the admixture of old oil without being bitten, let the drug be dissolved in that.

english_sentence_A: And just as sinuses need the more liquid drugs, since the thicker ones cannot be injected, so those of the hollow ulcers that lie on the surface require a thicker drug, because the liquids flow off them quickly and the lint-plugs are left dry.

english_sentence_A: And just as sinuses need the more liquid drugs, since the thicker ones cannot be injected, so those of the hollow ulcers that lie on the surface require a thicker drug, because the liquids flow off them quickly and the lint-plugs are left dry.

english_sentence_B: For you, then, who remember these things and have heard the method both of the composition and of the use of all such drugs, I shall write down in what follows the drugs that have been tested by experience at the hands of the reputable physicians, with a view to knowledge of the best drugs.

greek_sentence: πρώτων δὲ τῶν περὶ Μαντίαν καὶ τὸν μαθητὴν αὐτοῦ τὸν Ταραντῖνον Ἡρακλεί δην πολλὰ φάρμακα γραψάντων, ἃ τοῖς μετὰ ταῦτα διὰ πείρας ἀφικόμενα διωρίσθη.
english_sentence_A: Mantias and his pupil Heraclides of Tarentum were the first to write down many drugs, which, having come to the test of experience among those who followed them, were sorted out (διωρίσθη); and the best among them these men in turn wrote down again, while those that seemed to act less effectively than the others they left aside.
english_sentence_B: First came Mantias and his pupil Heraclides of Tarentum, who wrote down many drugs; these, having come down to their successors, were sifted by experience.

english_sentence_A: And for this reason it is proper to put into the cauldron first [518] the litharge, which is to be boiled until it reaches a glutinous consistency, next the verdigris, and after it, if any of the metallic substances is being put in, such as burnt copper and its scale, and when it has thickened, at that point wax and resin, if the drug takes these too, and at the end frankincense and myrrh and aloe and whatever other such things, as in the case of the most renowned of the tawny plasters, which they call the one 'through dittany', it too being one of those named 'sacred', like the Isis, since they say that they were brought from the temples in Egypt.
english_sentence_B: And for this reason one should put into the pot first [518] the litharge, which is to be boiled until it reaches a glutinous consistency; next the verdigris; and after it, if any of the metallic substances is being added, such as burnt copper and copper flake, these; and when the mixture has thickened, then the wax and resin, if the drug also takes these; and at the end frankincense, myrrh, aloe and all other such things. english_sentence_A: More desiccative than the tawny plasters prepared in this way are those which have no resin and wax at all, but are composed solely of the so-called metallic substances, just as certain others among earlier writers have recorded such plasters, and the one which I always use, composed by me and boiled in the following manner.
english_sentence_B: More drying than the tawny plasters prepared in this way are those which contain no resin and wax at all, but are compounded only of the so-called metallics, such as some others of our predecessors wrote down, and such as the one which I use constantly, compounded by me and boiled in the following manner.

english_sentence_A: It is clear, then, that, being of such a kind, it will not produce flesh in the ulcer nor fill up the hollow of the flesh, but will rather melt it away and diminish it; and for this reason the drugs that cleanse much [554] filth, about which I spoke earlier, are not always able to produce flesh, but only when, having been melted down either with a larger quantity of oil or with rose-oil, as in the case of the oily one and the one made with papyrus, the vehemence of their detergent action has been curbed, or when they become non-biting through admixture of cerate.
english_sentence_B: It is clear, then, that being of this kind it will not incarnate the ulcer nor fill up the hollow of the flesh, but will both melt it down and diminish it; and for this reason the drugs that cleanse much filth [554], about which I spoke earlier, are not always able to incarnate, but only when, having been melted either with a larger quantity of oil or with rose oil, as are both the 'oily' drug and the one made with papyrus, the vehemence of their detergent action is curbed, or when through the admixture of cerate they become non-biting.

lsj_entry_text: δύναμις [υ], ἡ , gen. εως, Ion. ιος, Ion. dat. δυνάμι : (δύναμαι):— power, might, in Hom. , esp. of bodily strength, εἴ μοι δ. γε παρείη Od. 2.62 , cf. Il. 8.294 ; οἵη ἐμὴ δ. καὶ χεῖρες Od. 20.237 ; ἡ δ. τῶν νέων Antipho 4.3.2 , etc.: generally, strength, power, ability to do anything, πὰρ δύναμιν beyond one's strength, Il. 13.787 ; in Prose, παρὰ δ. τολμηταί Th. 1.70 , etc.; ὑπὲρ δ. D. 18.193 ; opp. κατὰ δ. as far as lies in one, Hdt. 3.142 , etc. ( κὰδ δ. Hes. Op. 336 ); εἰς δύναμιν Cratin. 172 , Pl. R. 458e , etc.; πρὸς τὴν δ. Id. Phdr. 231a . outward power, influence, authority, A. Pers. 174 (anap.), Ag. 779 (lyr.); καταπαύσαντα τὴν Κύρου δ. Hdt. 1.90 ; δυνάμει προὔχοντες Th. 7.21 , etc.; ἐν δ. εἶναι, γενέσθαι, X. HG 4.4.5 , D. 13.29 . force for war, forces, δ. ἀνδρῶν Hdt. 5.100 , cf. Pl. Mx. 240d , Plb. 1.41.2 , LXX Ge. 21.22 , OGI 139.8 (ii B. C.); μετὰ δυνάμεων ἱκανῶν Wilcken Chr. 10 (ii B. C.), etc.; δ. καὶ πεζὴ καὶ ἱππικὴ καὶ ναυτική X. An. 1.3.12 ; πέντε δυνάμεσι πεφρουρημένον, of the five projecting rows of sarissae in the phalanx, Ascl. Tact. 5.2 ,al. a power, quantity, χρημάτων δ. Hdt. 7.9 .ά. means, κατὰ δύναμιν Arist. EE 1243b12 ; opp. παρὰ δ., 2 Ep.Cor. 8.3 ; κατὰ δ. τῶν ὑπαρχόντων BGU 1051.17 (Aug.). power, faculty, capacity, αἱ ἀμφὶ τὸ σῶμα δ. Hp. VM 14 ; αἱ τοῦ σώματος δυνάμεις Pl. Tht. 185e ; ἡ τῆς ὄψεως δ. Id. R. 532a ; ἡ τῶν λεγόντων δ. D. 22.11 : c. gen. rei, capacity for, τῶν ἔργων Arist. Pol. 1309a35 ; τοῦ λέγειν Id. Rh. 1362b22 ; τοῦ λόγου, τῶν λόγων, Men. 578 , Alex. 94 ; δ. στρατηγική Plb. 1.84.6 ; δ. ἐν πραγματείᾳ Id. 2.56.5 ; δ. συνθετική D.H. Comp. 2 : abs., any natural capacity or faculty, that may be improved and may be used for good or ill, Arist. Top. 126a37 , cf. MM 1183b28 . elementary force, such as heat, cold, etc., Hp. VM 16 , Arist. PA 646a14 ; ἡ τοῦ θερμοῦ δ.ib. 650a5 ; θερμαντικὴ δ. Epicur. Fr. 60 , cf. Polystr. p.23 W. property, quality, ἰδίην δύναμιν καὶ φύσιν ἔχειν Hp. VM 13 , cf. Nat.Hom. 5 , Vict. 1.10 ; esp. of the natural properties of plants, etc., αἱ δ. τῶν φυομένων, τῶν σπερμάτων, X. Cyr. 8.8.14 , Thphr. HP 8.11.1 ; productive power, τῆς γῆς Id. Oec. 16.4 ; μετάλλων Id. Vect. 4.1 : generally, function, faculty, δύναμις φυσική, ζωική, ψυχική, Gal. 10.635 ; περὶ φυσικῶν δ., title of work by Galen. in pl., agencies, ὑπάρχειν ἐν τῇ φύσει τὰς τοιαύτας δυνάμεις (sc. the gods) Polystr. p.10 W. function, meaning, of part in whole, Id. p.17 W. in Music, function, value, of a note in the scale, δ. ἐστι τάξις φθόγγου ἐν συστήματι Cleonid. Harm. 14 , cf. Aristox. Harm. p.69M. ; μέση κατὰ δύναμιν, opp. κατὰ θέσιν, Ptol. Harm. 2.5 . faculty, art, or craft, Pl. R. 532d , Arist. Metaph. 1018a30 , EN 1094a10 , Arr. Epict. 1.1.1 ; δ. σκεπτική the doctrine of the Sceptics, S.E. M. 7.1 . a medicine, Timostr. 7 , etc.; δ. ἁπλαῖ Hp. Decent. 9 , Aret. CD 1.4 , etc.; δ. πολυφάρμακοι Plu. 2.403c , Gal. 13.365 : in pl., collection of formulae or prescriptions, Orib. 10.33 . action of medicines, περὶ τῆς ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δ., title of work by Galen; also, potency, δυνάμει θερμά, ψυχρά, Id. 1.672 , al. magically potent substance or object, PMag.Leid.V. 8.12 : in pl., magical powers, Hld. 4.7 . force or meaning of a word, Lys. 10.7 , Pl. Cra. 394b , Diog.Oen. 12 , Phld. Sign. 31 , etc. phonetic value of sounds or letters, Plb. 10.47.8 , D.H. Comp. 12 , Luc. Jud.Voc. 5 , etc. worth or value of money, Th. 6.46 , 2.97 , Plu. Lyc. 9 , Sol. 15 . capability of existing or acting, potentiality, opp. actuality (ἐνέργεια), Arist. Metaph. 1047b31 , 1051a5 , etc.: hence δυνάμει as Adv., virtually, ὕστερον ὂν τῇ τάξει, πρότερον τῇ δυνάμει . . ἐστί D. 3.15 ; opp. ἐνεργείᾳ, Arist. APo. 86a28 , al.; opp. ἐντελεχείᾳ, Id. Ph. 193b8 , al. Math., power, κατὰ μεταφορὰν ἡ ἐν γεωμετρίᾳ λέγεται δ. Id. Metaph. 1019b33 ; usu. second power, square, κατὰ δύναμιν in square, Pl. Ti. 54b , cf. Theol.Ar. 11 , etc.: chiefly in dat., [εὐθεῖα] δυνάμει ἴση a line the square on which is equal to an area, ἡ BA ἐλάσσων ἐστὶν ἢ διπλασίων δυνάμει τῆς AK the square on BA is less than double of the square on AK, Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.9 : εὐθεῖαι δ. σύμμετροι commensurable in square, Euc. 10 Def. 2 ; ἡ δυνάμει δεκάς the series 12 + 22 . . . + 102 , Theol.Ar. 64 . square number, Pl. Ti. 32a . square of an unknown quantity ( x2 ), Dioph. Def. 2 , al. square root of a number which is not a perfect square, surd, opp. μῆκος, Pl. Tht. 147d . product of two numbers, ἡ ἀμφοῖν (sc. τριάδος καὶ δυάδος) δ. ἑξάς Ph. 1.3 , cf. Iamb. in Nic. p.108 P.; δυνάμει in product, Hero Metr. 1.15 , Theol.Ar. 33 . concrete, powers, esp. of divine beings, αἱ δ. τῶν οὐρανῶν LXX Is. 34.4 , cf. 1 Ep.Pet. 3.22 , al., Ph. 1.587 , Corp.Herm. 1.26 , Porph. Abst. 2.34 : sg., Act.Ap. 8.10 , PMag.Par. 1.1275 ; πολυώνυμος δ., of God, Secund. Sent. 3 . manifestation of divine power, miracle, Ev.Matt. 11.21 , al., Buresch Aus Lydien 113 , etc.

greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν ὑγρὰ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μαλακὰ, καθάπερ τὰ τῶν γυναικῶν καὶ παιδίων εὐνούχων τε καὶ γυναικείως βιούντων, ἀσθενεστέρων δεῖται φαρμάκων, τὰ δὲ τῶν ἀνδρῶν, καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅσοι δι’ ἐνεργειῶν ἀνδρικῶν καὶ ἡλίου σκληρὰν εἰσήγοντο τὴν ἕξιν τοῦ σώματος, ὑπὸ τῶν ἀσθενῶν οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖται.
english_sentence_A: Those that are moist and for this reason soft, such as those of women and children and eunuchs and those who live in a womanish manner, require weaker drugs; but those of men, and especially of all who through manly activities and the sun have acquired a hard habit of body, derive no benefit from the weak ones.
english_sentence_B: Those that are moist, and for this reason soft, such as those of women and small children, and of eunuchs and of those who live in a womanish manner, require weaker drugs; but those of men, and especially of all who through manly activities and the sun have acquired a hard habit of body, are not benefited at all by the weak ones.

lsj_entry_text: κολλ-ητικός, ή, όν, glutinous, Arist. Pr. 928a5 ( Comp. ), Plu. 2.952b ; δύναμις κ. τραυμάτων closing up wounds, Dsc. 3.85 ; κ. φάρμακον Gal. 11.439 ; κ. ἔργα plumber's work, PLond. 3.1177.283 (ii A.D.): Dor. κολλατικόν, τό, = κόλλα , IG 42(1).102.69 (Epid.).
greek_sentence: διὰ τοῦτ’ οὖν οὐδὲ τὰ κολλητικὰ κοινὰ τῶν σωμάτων ἑκατέρων ἐστὶν, ἀλλ’ ὅσα μὲν διὰ λιθαργύρου καὶ ἐλαίου [555] σκευάζεται καὶ ὄξους, περὶ ὧν ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ λόγῳ διῆλθον, ἀσθενοῦς καὶ μαλακῆς σαρκός ἐστι κολλητικά· τὰ δὲ δι’ ἀσφάλτου καὶ ἰοῦ καὶ λεπίδος, ἀλόης τε καὶ σμύρνης, ἰσχυρᾶς τε καὶ σκληρᾶς.
english_sentence_A: For this reason, then, not even the agglutinative drugs are common to both kinds of bodies; rather, those which are prepared from litharge and oil [555] and vinegar, which I went through in the first book, are agglutinative of weak and soft flesh, whereas those made from asphalt and verdigris and scale, and aloe and myrrh, are agglutinative of strong and hard flesh.
