Hdt. 3.158 ; so in Att. , Ar. Pl. 785 , Pl. Prt. 327e , etc. ; ὅτι ἕκαστος ἐπίστασθε ἀγαθόν X. Smp. 3.3 : sg. in apposition with pl. greek_sentence: ὅσα δ’ ἄμφω δρᾷν πέφυκε, προσεπισκεπτομένους ἐκ ποίας τάξεως ἕκαστόν ἐστιν, ὃ μέγιστον μὲν ὑπάρχει τῶν εἰς τὴν θεραπείαν διαφερόντων, ὠλιγώρηται δὲ τοῖς γράψασι τὰ περὶ ὕλης βιβλία.

lsj_entry_text: Λημνιασταί, οἱ, worshippers of the Lemnian deities, IG 12(1).43 (Rhodes, i B.C.). Λήμνιος, v. Λῆμνος .
greek_sentence: ξηραίνει τοίνυν μετρίως ἥ τε Λημνία σφραγὶς καὶ ἡ καδμεία καὶ μᾶλλον ταύτης ἡ αὐτοφυὴς ἄνευ τοῦ μεταβάλλεσθαι κατὰ τοὺς χειμάῤῥούς τε καὶ ῥύακας καὶ ἐν τοῖς τῶν Κυπρίων ὄρεσιν εὑρισκομένη καὶ κατὰ τὰ ἄλλα χωρία, μάλιστα δὲ ἐν οἷς ἐστι τὰ μεταλλικά.
english_sentence_A: Moderately drying, then, are the Lemnian seal and cadmia, and more so than the latter the naturally occurring kind, which, without undergoing any transformation, is found in the winter torrents and streams and in the mountains of the Cyprians, and in other regions too, but especially in those where the mines are.
english_sentence_B: Now, Lemnian seal dries moderately, and so does cadmia; and more than this the natural [cadmia], which has not undergone transformation and is found in torrents and streams, in the mountains of the Cypriots, and in other places, but especially in those where there are mines.

( v.l. σφράγιν ), Eust. 265.18 :—seal, signet, Hdt. 1.195 , 3.41 , PHib. 1.72.19 (iii B.C.), Numen. ap. Eus. PE 14.7 , etc.; distd. from δακτύλιος, Ar. Fr. 320.12 , Pl. IG 22.204.40 , Str. 9.3.1 ; τὸν στρατηγὸν καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ς. keeper of the privy seal, IGRom. 4.1712 (Samos, ii B.C.). gem or stone for a ring, Hdt. 7.69 , cf. Arist. Mete. 387b17 , Thphr. Ind. 8 . impression of a signet-ring, seal, ς. δακτυλίου Lex Solonis ap. D.L. 1.57 ; σφραγῖδος ἕρκος S. Tr. 615 , cf. El. 1223 , E. IA 155 (anap.), Th. 1.129 ; παρασημήνασθαι σασθαι ς. to counterfeit it, ib. 132 ; warrant attached to a camel, οἴσομεν ὑμῖν τὴν ς. καὶ οὐδὲν ζητηθήσεται πρὸς ἡμᾶς PBasel 2.11 (ii A.D.): metaph., σφρηγὶς ἐπικείσθω τοῖσδ' ἔπεσιν, as a warrant, Thgn. 19 ; but ἀρρήτων ἐπέων γλώσσῃ ς. ἐπικείσθω (for secrecy) Luc. english_sentence_A: Sprinkling, then, all these drugs dry upon malignant ulcers, you will see them wonderfully dried without biting, as also the burnt shells of whelks, of purple-shells and of oysters, and all other such things.

english_sentence_A: And the so-called transparent stone, which the Romans name specularium, is, when burnt, among the things that dry without biting, being useful for ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, though not for malignant ones; for it dries more moderately than is required for these.

english_sentence_A: Of the same power as it are also burnt glass and the fiery deposit that forms in the copper heating-vessels.

greek_sentence: μετὰ δὲ τοῦ ξηραίνειν ἔτι καὶ στυπτικὴν ἔχει δύναμιν ὁ καρπὸς τῆς Αἰγυπτίας ἀκάνθης ἥ τε ὀμφακῖτις κηκὶς καὶ τὸ ῥῆον καὶ τὰ σίδια, οὐκ ὀλίγαι τε [664] ῥίζαι καὶ πόαι.

Ch. 391 (lyr.). of things which affect the eyes or taste, keen, pungent, acrid, of smoke, δριμύτατος καπνῶν Ar. V. 146 ; of radish, etc., opp. γλυκύς, X. Mem. 1.4.5 , cf. Pl.Com. 154 ( Sup. ); χυμός Arist. de An. 422b13 ; ὀσμαί ib. 421a30 ; δριμέσιν ἰητρεύειν with pungent drugs, Hp. Fract. 27 ; δ. οἶνος Luc. Merc.Cond. 18 . Adv. -έως: Comp. δριμύτερον, ὄζειν Arist. Pr. 907a13 ; ῥεύματος δριμύτερον γενομένου Hp. VM 18 . metaph., of persons, bitter, fierce, ἀλάστωρ A. Ag. 1501 (lyr.); ἄγροικος Ar. Eq. 808 , etc.; also, keen, shrewd, κρόταλον E. Cyc. 104 ; ἔντονοι καὶ δ. Pl. Tht. 173a ; δ. καὶ δικανικός ib. 175d ; δ. ἐν τῷ ἀποκρίνεσθαι Arist. Top. 156b37 ; λόγος δριμύτατος Id. SE 182b37 (but λέξις and λόγος δ. of striking turns of phrase, Hermog. Id. 1.2 , 2.5 ): neut. as Adv., δριμὺ βλέπειν look bitter, Ar. Ra. 562 ; but also to look sharply, keenly, Pl. R. 519a , Luc. Symp. 16 ; ἐνορᾶν Id. Cat. 3 , Ael. VH 14.22 , D.C. 59.26 :—regul. Adv. δριμέως, Anaxandr. 15.3 ; ἐρασθῆναι Ael. NA 7.15 ; δριμύτατα ἀλγεῖν Id. VH 12.1 .
greek_sentence: καὶ κατ’ ἄλλον αὖ τρόπον τὰ δριμέα, πέπερι, ζίγγιβερ, νᾶπυ, κάγχρυ καὶ πολὺ πλῆθος ἑτέρων τοιούτων.

lsj_entry_text: φάρμακον [v. sub fin.], τό, drug, whether healing or noxious: in Hom. the sense is freq. determined by an epith., φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ . . , πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά Od. 4.230 ; τόδε φ. ἐσθλόν 10.287 , cf. 292 ; φ. ἤπια, ὀδυνήφατα (v. infr. 2 ); κακὰ φ. ib. 213 ; φ. λυγρά ib. 236 ; φ. οὐλόμενον ib. 394 ; ἀνδροφόνον 1.261 ; θυμοφθόρα φ. 2.329 ; so, after Hom. , προσανέα φ. Pi. P. 3.52 ; παιώνια A. Ag. 848 ; χρήσιμον Pl. R. 382c ; θανάσιμα Ph. Bel. 103.31 ; ὀλέθριον Luc. Herm. 62 . healing remedy, medicine, in Hom. mostly of those applied outwardly, ἐπιθήσει φάρμαχ' ἅ κεν παύσῃσι μελαινάων ὀδυνάων Il. 4.191 ; ἐπ' ἄρ' ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσε ib. 218 ; ὀδυνήφατα φ. πάσσων 5.401 , 900 , cf. 11.515 , 830 , 15.394 ; προσάλειφεν ἑκάστῳ φ. Od. 10.392 ; φ. περιαλείφειν Ar. Eq. 906 ; also of potions, πιὼν φάρμακ' Od. 10.326 ; φ. πεπωκώς Hdt. 4.160 , cf. Pi. l. c.; παρὰ τοῦ ἰατροῦ Pl. R. 406d , cf. Grg. 467c ; φ. χριστόν E. Hipp. 516 ; ἔγχριστον Theoc. 11.1 ; ἐπίχριστον Str. 17.1.10 ; ἐπίπαστον Theoc. l. c.; καταπλαστόν Ar. Pl. 716 ; ποτόν E. Hipp. l.c.; freq. in Medic. writers, Sor. 1.4 , Gal. 6.265 , etc.; of medicines for cattle, PFlor. 222.11 (iii A. D.). c. gen. (v. infr. 11 ), φ. νόσου a medicine for it, remedy against it, A. Pr. 251 , 606 (lyr.); βηχός Phryn.Com. 60 : κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Pl. Chrm. 155b ; στραγγουρίας Arist. HA 612b16 , cf. 624a16 ; μέθης Amphis 37 ; δίψης AP 6.170 ( Thyill. ); but ὑγιείας φ. a medicine to restore or maintain health, Aristid. Or. 37(2).11 . enchanted potion, philtre: hence, charm, spell, Od. 4.220 sq., Ar. Pl. 302 , Theoc. 2.15 , PSI 1.64.20 (i B. C.); φαρμάκοις τὸν ἄνδρ' ἔμηνεν Ar. Th. 561 ; τοιαῦτα ἔχω φ. such charms have I, Hdt. 3.85 , cf. Apoc. 9.21 . poison, S. Tr. 685 , E. Med. 385 ; πιεῖν τὸ φ. Antipho 6.15 , Pl. Phd. 57a , 115a ; φάρμακα ἐσβεβληκέναι ἐς τὰ φρέατα Th. 2.48 ; φ. δηλητήρια SIG 37 A 1 (Teos, v B. C.); τοξικὸν φ. BGU 21 ii 14 (iv A. D.). lye for laundering, Stud.Pal. 22.56.12 (iii A. D.). generally, remedy, cure, Hes. Op. 485 , Alc. 35 , etc.; μεῖζον . . τῆς νόσου τὸ φ. the cure too strong for, i. e. worse than, the disease, S. Fr. 589.4 , cf. Com.Adesp. 455 ; φ. πραΰ, of a bridle, Pi. O. 13.85 ; φ. τινι for a thing, Thgn. 1134 (pl.), Archil. 9 ; πρός τι Arist. Pol. 1321a16 ; ποττὸν ἔρωτα Theoc. 11.1 ; but most freq. φ. τινός remedy against . . χλαῖνα . . φ. ῥίγευς Hippon. 19 ; Ζεὺς πάντων φ. μοῦνος ἔχει Simon. 87 ; τὸ σιγᾶν φ. βλάβης ἔχω A. Ag. 548 ; φ. πόνων, λύπης, E. Ba. 283 , Fr. 1079 ; δόλοι . . χρείας ἀνάνδρου φ. ib. 288 ; φόβου Pl. Lg. 647e ; λήθης φάρμακα (of γράμματα) E. Fr. 578.1 ; v. εὐδιανός. c. gen. also, a means of producing something, φ. σωτηρίας Id. Ph. 893 ; μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φ. Pl. Phdr. 274e ; ὑπομνήσεως ib. 275a , cf. 230d ; ἀθανασίας Antiph. 86.6 ; ἡσυχίας Arist. english_sentence_A: Whenever, therefore, we are about to sprinkle on them one of the dry drugs, one must first wipe them out with a linen cloth that is soft, clean and dry, and, having filled the hollow of the ulcer with the drug, apply on the outside a flat piece (platysma) of a plaster that thins the lips, and over this again, on the outside, a linen cloth equal on every side, and over it a sponge from water or wine.

english_sentence_B: If the parts around the ulcer also show something phlegmonous, one should apply over the flat spread, on the outside, extending over a wide area [667], a liquid drug made from my palm plaster (phoinikinē), not simply melted, but having taken up as much astringent wine as possible.

lsj_entry_text: ἐρυθρότης, ητος, ἡ, redness, ruddiness, τῆς χρόας Gal. 1.582 , cf. Phlp. in Cat. 148.5 .
greek_sentence: οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ διὰ τοῦ τυχόντος ἐλαίου τήκειν αὐτὴν προσήκει, ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν ἐρυθρότης τις ἢ ὅλως θερμότης ἐπικρατεῖ κατὰ τὰ πέριξ τοῦ ἕλκους, διά τινος τῶν στυφόντων καὶ ψυχόντων· ἔστι δὲ τοιαῦτα μύρσινόν τε καὶ μήλινον· εἰ δὲ μὴ παρείη ταῦτα, τὸ καλούμενον ὀμφάκινόν τε καὶ ὠμοτριβὲς ἔλαιον· εἰ δὲ σκληρότης ἐπικρατεῖν φαίνοιτο, δι’ ἐλαίου παλαιοῦ τηκτέον ἢ διὰ κικίνου τὴν αὐτὴν φοινικίνην.
english_sentence_A: Nor indeed is it proper to melt it in any oil whatever; rather, if some redness, or in general heat, prevails in the parts around the ulcer, in one of the astringent and cooling oils—such are myrtle oil and quince oil; and if these are not at hand, the oil called omphakine and omotribes (of unripe olives); but if hardness appears to prevail, the same phoinikine must be melted in old oil or in castor oil (kikinon).
english_sentence_B: Nor indeed is it fitting to melt it with any oil that comes to hand. Rather, if some redness, or heat generally, prevails in the parts around the ulcer, it should be melted with one of the astringent and cooling oils; such are myrtle oil and quince oil; and if these are not available, the so-called omphacine oil and omotribes oil (oil of unripe olives).

english_sentence_A: It once happened, when such a [668] vein had been excised, that the ulcer was immediately cicatrized, even though it was a year old, but that in its place, at the incision from which the vein was excised, a malignant ulcer arose, which could not be cicatrized.

english_sentence_A: It is better, therefore, in such cases, having observed the strength of the patient under treatment, to begin with phlebotomy, and next to purge with a drug that evacuates the melancholic humour and, together with it, the phlegmatic as well, since this too sometimes flows in together with the melancholic in the generation of varices.

greek_sentence: εἶθ’ ἑξῆς αὐτὴν κατὰ τὸ μῆκος σχάσαι τὴν ὑπερκειμένην τοῦ ἕλκους φλέβα καὶ κενώσαντα δαψιλὲς, αὐτὴν ταύτην πρότερον ἰᾶσθαι τὴν γενομένην διαίρεσιν τῆς φλεβὸς, ὅταν δ’ ἀκριβῶς ἤδη φαίνηται συνουλουμένη, τηνικαῦτα τῇ θεραπείᾳ τοῦ κακοήθους ἕλκους ἐπιχειρεῖν, ὡς προείρηται.
english_sentence_A: Then, next, to scarify lengthwise the vein itself that lies above the ulcer and, having evacuated in abundance, first to heal this very incision that has been made in the vein; and when it already appears to be perfectly cicatrizing over, then to undertake the treatment of the malignant ulcer, as has been said before.
english_sentence_B: Then, next, one should lance lengthwise the vein itself that lies above the ulcer and, having evacuated in abundance, first heal this very division made in the vein; and when it already appears to be cicatrising completely, only then undertake the treatment of the malignant ulcer, as has been said before.

english_sentence_A: And the spleen too, when it is in a bad condition, sometimes becomes the cause of such cacochymy (κεκοχυμίας, presumably for κακοχυμίας), just as the liver does also; having first made provision for these, one should in this way undertake the cure of the ulcer.
english_sentence_B: The spleen too, when it is in a bad condition, sometimes becomes the cause of such cacochymy, as indeed does the liver as well; one must first take care of these, and only then undertake the healing of the ulcer.

english_sentence_A: And in the very course of treating the ulcer by means of the dry drugs, at each unbinding one must attend to the action that has been produced by it upon the part, knowing and remembering that those which dry without cleansing — and such are those in which the astringent quality prevails — do not render the ulcer clean; whereas those which, in addition to drying, also possess the power of cleansing, render the whole ulcerated part not only dry but also clean.
english_sentence_B: And in the very course of treating the ulcer by means of the dry drugs, at each removal of the dressing one must attend to the action that the drug has produced on the part. One must know and remember that drugs which dry without deterging do not make the ulcer clean; such are those in which the astringent quality predominates.

english_sentence_A: One must also know that clean ulcers are bitten by drugs by which they were previously not bitten at all, when they were foul.
english_sentence_B: One must also know that clean ulcers are stung by drugs by which they were not stung at all before, when they were foul.

greek_sentence: μεταβαίνειν οὖν ἀπὸ τῶν ἰσχυρότερον ῥυπτόντων ἐπὶ τὸ πρᾳότερον καὶ ἀδηκτότερον, καθ’ ὃν ἂν καιρὸν ἀκριβῶς καθαρὸν εὑρέθη τὸ ἕλκος, ὥσπερ γε πάλιν ἐπὶ τῶν ῥυπαρῶν, ἐπανέρχεσθαι ἐπὶ τὰ ῥυπτικώτερα, πλὴν εἰ μὴ διὰ τὸ δηχθῆναι ῥυπαρὸν ἐφάνη.
english_sentence_A: One must therefore pass from the drugs that cleanse more strongly to what is milder and less biting, at whatever moment the ulcer is found to be perfectly clean, just as, conversely, in the case of foul ulcers, one must return to the more cleansing drugs — unless it appeared foul because of having been bitten.
english_sentence_B: One must therefore pass from the more strongly deterging drugs to the milder and less stinging kind at whatever moment the ulcer is found to be thoroughly clean. Conversely, in foul ulcers one must go back to the more detergent drugs, unless the ulcer has appeared foul because it has been stung.

english_sentence_A: For this has sometimes deceived even physicians who are reputed to be good, so that they passed over to another drug, more detergent and more acrid, by which the ulcer, being eroded again, [670] appeared at the next undoing of the dressing equally foul or even more so, the flesh that had been melted down by the drug fouling it.
english_sentence_B: For this has sometimes deceived even those reputed to be good physicians, so that they changed over to another drug, more cleansing and more acrid, by which the ulcer, eaten away again, [670] appeared at the next removal of the dressing equally foul, or even more so, the flesh melted down by the drug fouling it.

greek_sentence: λύεται μὲν γὰρ εἰς ἰχῶρας μοχθηροὺς ἡ συντηκομένη σὰρξ, αὐτῶν δὲ τούτων ὅσον μὲν λεπτομερέστερόν ἐστι κατὰ τὴν σύστασιν, ὑπὸ τοῦ φαρμάκου διαφορεῖται, τὸ λοιπὸν δ’ αὐτόθι περιπηγνύμενον τοῖς ἕλκεσι ῥύπος αὐτοῖς γίγνεται.
english_sentence_A: For the flesh that is being melted down is dissolved into vicious ichors, and of these, whatever is more fine-particled in its consistency is dispersed by the drug, while the remainder, congealing there around the ulcers, becomes filth for them.

greek_sentence: τάχα μὲν οὖν περιττὸν εἴη ἐν τῇ προκειμένῃ πραγματείᾳ τὸν τρόπον τῆς χρήσεως τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων προσγράφειν· εἴρηται γὰρ ἐν τῇ θεραπευτικῇ μεθόδῳ· τὰ δ’ ἀναγκαῖα καὶ μεγάλην φέροντα βλάβην εἰ παροφθείη, βέλτιόν ἐστι καὶ δὶς καὶ τρὶς λέγειν ἀναμνήσεως ἕνεκα.

greek_sentence: προσκείσθω τοιγαροῦν ἔτι καὶ τοῦτο κατὰ τὸν λόγον, ἐν τῇ θεραπείᾳ τῶν τοιούτων ἑλκῶν, εἰ μὲν εἴη [671] δυνατὸν ἄνευ τῆς τοῦ παντὸς σώματος βλάβης ἀλουτεῖν τὸν θεραπευόμενον ἀνατριβόμενόν τε σινδόσιν ἐπὶ πλέον, ἐφεξῆς τε δι’ ἐλαίου, κᾄπειτα δι’ ἁλτήρων γυμναζόμενον, εἰ σκέλος εἴη τὸ πεπονθὸς ἢ διὰ δρόμων ἐπὶ τῶν ὑπερκειμένων.
english_sentence_A: Let this, then, also be added to the account: in the treatment of such ulcers, if it should be [671] possible, without harm to the whole body, for the patient to go without bathing, being rubbed down with linen cloths for a longer time, and next with oil, and then exercising with jumping-weights (halteres) if the affected part is a leg, or by running if it is in the parts above.
english_sentence_B: Let this, then, also be added to the account: in the treatment of such ulcers, if it should be [671] possible, without harm to the whole body, for the patient to go unbathed, being rubbed down at some length with linen cloths, and next with oil, and then exercising with jumping-weights, if the affected part is a leg, or by running in the case of the parts lying above.

greek_sentence: εἰ δὲ ἀλουτεῖν ἀδύνατον εἴη τῷ θεραπευομένῳ χωρὶς βλάβης ὅλου τοῦ σώματος, οὐ χρὴ λύειν τὴν ἐπίδεσιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐπιδέδεται λουσάμενον, ἐκθλίψαντα τὸ τοῦ σπόγγου θερμὸν ὕδωρ, εὐθέως ἄλλο καταχεῖν ψυχρὸν, ὡς μηδεμίαν ὑπολείπεσθαι θερμότητα κατὰ τὴν ἐπίδεσιν.
english_sentence_A: But if it is impossible for the patient to go without bathing without harm to the whole body, one must not undo the bandaging, but, having bathed just as he has been bandaged, and having squeezed out the hot water of the sponge, one should at once pour on other, cold, water, so that no heat is left behind in the bandaging.
english_sentence_B: But if it should be impossible for the patient to go unbathed without harm to the whole body, one must not undo the bandaging; rather, when he has bathed bandaged as he is, one should squeeze the warm water out of the sponge and at once pour other, cold water over it, so that no heat is left behind in the bandaging.

greek_sentence: εἰ δὲ φαίνοιτο προχωρεῖν ἡ θεραπεία, καὶ χωρὶς ἐπιδέσεως σπόγγου θεραπεύεσθαι, τῆς ὑγρᾶς φοινικίνης ἐπιβαλλομένης ἔξωθεν ὡς εἴρηται· καὶ χωρὶς ἐπιθέσεως σπόγγου καταλαμβανομένης ἐπιδέσμοις καταγματικῷ τρόπῳ περιελιττομένης τῷ θεραπευομένῳ μέρει τοῦ σώματος.
english_sentence_A: And if the treatment should appear to be progressing, he may also be treated without the bandaging of a sponge, the moist phoinikine being applied externally, as has been said, and, without the application of a sponge, being secured with bandages wound around the part of the body being treated in the manner of a fracture.
english_sentence_B: And if the treatment appears to be making progress, he may also be treated without the bandaging-on of a sponge, the moist phoenicine being laid on from outside as has been said; that is, without the application of a sponge, the drug being held in place by bandages wound round the treated part of the body in the fracture manner.

greek_sentence: αὐτῶν δὲ τῶν μεταλλικῶν ἧττόν τε καὶ μᾶλλον ἀδήκτων τε καὶ ξηραντικῶν ὄντων, ἐπιταθήσεται μὲν ἐν τοῖς ξηραντικωτέροις ἡ δύναμις, ἐκλυθήσεται δ’ ἐν τοῖς ἧττον ξηραίνουσιν, ὥσπερ γε πάλιν, ἀσφαλεστέρα μὲν ἡ χρῆσις ἔσται διὰ τῶν ἀδηκτοτέρων σφαλερωτέρα δὲ διὰ τῶν δακνωδεστέρων.

english_sentence_A: But in the case of Chironian ulcers, when it has been mixed with the other [681] drugs, it is itself so far released from the vehemence of its power, while it increases that of those others, that the drug compounded from all of them becomes a most excellent one.

greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ αἱ γραφαὶ τῶν ὑπολοίπων ἓξ φαρμάκων τοῖς κακοήθεσιν ἁρμόττουσι διαφέρουσαι κατ’ ἰσχὺν ἀλλήλων, αἷς δυοῖν θάτερον ἐχρῆν, ἤτοι λογικὴν καὶ μεθοδικὴν ποιούμενον τὴν διδασκαλίαν προσγεγραφέναι τὴν κατὰ σφοδρότητα διαφορὰν, ὡς ἡμῶν νοησάντων, ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν κακοηθεστέρων ἑλκῶν τοῖς ἰσχυροτέροις χρῆσθαι φαρμάκοις, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μετριωτάτων τοῖς ἀσθενεστέροις· ἢ τοῖς ἐμπειρικοῖς ὁμοίως γράψαι, τοῖς μὲν φαγεδαινικοῖς καὶ ὅλως τοῖς ἀναβιβρωσκομένοις καὶ νεμομένοις ἐπιτήδεια τάδε τινὰ τῶν φαρμάκων εἶναι, τοῖς δὲ κοίλοις τάδε τινὰ, καὶ τοῖς μὲν ἱκανῶς ῥυπαροῖς ταυτὶ, τοῖς δὲ μετὰ φλεγμονώδους ἢ σκιῤῥώδους διαθέσεως ἢ τῶν χειλῶν τοῦ ἕλκους σκληρῶν ἢ ὀχθωδῶν ἢ μελάνων ἤ τινα ἄλλην χροιὰν ἐχόντων, ἴδια ἑκάστου.
english_sentence_A: But the prescriptions of the remaining six drugs are suited to malignant ulcers, differing from one another in strength; and for these one of two things was required: either, making his teaching rational and methodical, to have written in addition the difference according to intensity, so that we would understand that on the more malignant ulcers the stronger drugs are to be used, and on the mildest the weaker; or, in the manner of the Empiricists, to write that for phagedaenic ulcers, and in general for those being eaten away and spreading, such-and-such of the drugs are suitable, for hollow ones such-and-such, and for the considerably sordid ones these, and for those accompanied by an inflammatory or scirrhous condition, or where the lips of the ulcer are hard or bank-like (ὀχθωδῶν) or black or have some other colour, the drugs proper to each.
english_sentence_B: Either, giving his teaching in a rational and methodical way, he should have added the difference in vehemence, so that we would understand that the stronger drugs are to be used on the more malignant ulcers and the weaker on the most moderate ones. Or, like the Empirics, he should have written that these particular drugs are suitable for phagedaenic ulcers and in general for those being eaten away and spreading, these others for hollow ones, these for very foul ones, and, for those with an inflammatory or scirrhous condition, or where the lips of the ulcer are hard or ridged or black or have some other colour, ones peculiar to each.

english_sentence_A: And when it is deep, the whole of its hollow is filled up in addition, the drug being inserted into it.
english_sentence_B: After this another flat spread is laid on, taking in the lips as well.

english_sentence_A: And after this another flat piece (platysma) is laid on in turn, encompassing the lips too.
english_sentence_B: Then over this a piece of linen soaked in cold water, again of such a size, is laid over the whole, so as to cover the drug.

english_sentence_A: And then upon this in turn a linen cloth soaked in cold water is laid over the whole, of such a size as to cover the drug; then, on the outside, a soft sponge, secured by a bandage of linen cloth wound once or twice in a circle around the affected part, of such a width that the whole ulcer is encompassed together with the lips, and also something of the parts lying above and below them; and let the bandaging be done 'from two heads'—they call it so when the whole middle of the band is laid upon the affected place, and each of the heads is drawn away toward the opposite side.
english_sentence_B: Then, on the outside, a soft sponge, held in place by a bandage of linen cloth wound in a circle around the affected part either once or twice, and of such a breadth that the whole ulcer is taken in together with its lips, and also something of the parts lying above and below them. Let the bandaging be done 'from two starting-points': they call it this when the whole middle of the band is laid upon the affected place, and each of the heads is led away towards the opposite side.

greek_sentence: εἶτα ἐὰν μὲν ἰσχυρὸν ᾖ τὸ ὀθόνιον, ὡς διὰ μιᾶς ἐπιβολῆς ἀσφαλῶς κατέχειν τὸν σπόγγον, αὐτόθι που συῤῥαφήσεται διὰ τῶν περάτων, ἀφαιρουμένου ψαλίδι τοῦ περιττεύοντος· ἐὰν δὲ ἀσθενὲς, αὖθις ἀχθήσεται τῶν κεφαλῶν ἑκάτερον ὁμοτόνως ἑλκόμενον ἐπὶ τὸ πεπονθὸς, ὅπερ ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα φυλακτέον ἐστὶ κατά τε τὴν πρώτην ἐπιβολὴν, [686] οὐχ ἥκιστα δὲ καὶ κατὰ τὴν δευτέραν.
english_sentence_A: Then, if the linen bandage is strong enough to hold the sponge securely with a single turn, it will be sewn together there at its ends, the excess being cut away with scissors; but if it is weak, each of the heads will be brought once more over the affected part, drawn with equal tension—which is among the things most to be observed both in the first turn [686] and no less also in the second.
english_sentence_B: Then, if the linen strip is strong enough to hold the sponge securely with a single turn, it will be stitched together somewhere right there through its ends, the excess being cut away with scissors; but if it is weak, each of the two heads will be brought round again, drawn with equal tension towards the affected part. This must be guarded above all in the first turn, [686] and not least in the second as well.

english_sentence_A: And you will also be able easily to alter the first one itself: if you wish to make it milder, by mixing in, while kneading it, a little of one of the astringent oils, either myrtle oil or rose-oil or quince oil or lentisk oil or mastic oil or henna oil; but if stronger, either some of the scale or of the verdigris—for let a little of each of these be prepared for you, ground perfectly fine, so that you may add it while kneading.
english_sentence_B: You will also be able easily to modify the first drug itself. If you wish to make it milder, mix in, while softening it, a little of one of the astringent oils: myrtle-oil, rose-oil, quince-oil, lentisk-oil, mastic-oil or oil of cypros.

english_sentence_A: And you will also be able easily to alter the first one itself: if you wish to make it milder, by mixing in, while kneading it, a little of one of the astringent oils, either myrtle oil or rose-oil or quince oil or lentisk oil or mastic oil or henna oil; but if stronger, either some of the scale or of the verdigris—for let a little of each of these be prepared for you, ground perfectly fine, so that you may add it while kneading.

english_sentence_A: But the scale is a stronger, more roughening and more biting drug, and for this reason the man who composed the drug mixed in litharge, viewing with suspicion [689] the violent character of the scale and wishing to relax it by the admixture of the softer drug.

greek_sentence: [698] ἀνασμνῆσαι δὲ καὶ νῦν ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τοῦ πολλάκις πολλοῖς εἰρημένου περὶ τῶν αὐστηρῶν καὶ στρυφνῶν καὶ ὅλως στυφόντων οἴνων τε καὶ σιτίων καὶ φαρμάκων, ἔτι δὲ πρότερον ὑπὲρ τῶν κατὰ τὰς εἰρημένας φωνὰς σημαινομένων.
english_sentence_A: [698] It is necessary now too to recall what has often been said to many people concerning austere and harsh wines, foods and drugs, and in general astringent ones, and, before that, concerning what is signified by the terms just mentioned.

greek_sentence: ἐκ μὲν γὰρ τῆς αὐστηρὸν τὸ μετρίως στῦφον σημαίνεται παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν, ἐκ δὲ τῆς στρυφνὸν τὸ βιαίως καὶ σφοδρῶς.
english_sentence_A: For by the word 'austere' is signified, among the Greeks, that which is moderately astringent, and by 'harsh' that which is violently and intensely so.

english_sentence_A: For this reason some physicians have rightly devised the mixing with such drugs of others that are fine-parted and possess a sharp power, in order that through these the powers of the astringents may be conducted, under their guidance, into the depth of the body.

greek_sentence: αὐτίκα χοῦν ἐν αὐτοῖς τοῖς φαρμάκοις, ὅσα πρὸς δυσεπούλωτα καὶ κακοήθη συντεθείκασι, λεπίδος ἁπλῶς γεγραμμένης χωρὶς τοῦ προσκεῖσθαι χαλκοῦ καὶ σχιστῆς χωρὶς στυπτηρίας καὶ τὸ τερμινθίνης χωρὶς τοῦ προσκεῖσθαι τὸ ῥητίνης· προσυπακούομεν αὐτοῖς τὰ παραλελειμμένα κατὰ τὴν λέξιν οὕτως, ὥσπερ καὶ νῦν ἐπὶ τῆς ἀσβέστου τὴν τίτανον.
english_sentence_A: Thus, to take an immediate example, in these very drugs which they have composed for ulcers hard to cicatrize and malignant ones, when 'scale' is written simply, without 'of copper' being added, and 'split' without 'alum', and 'terebinth' without 'resin' being added, we supply in thought for them the words omitted in the expression in this way, just as now too, in the case of 'unslaked', we supply 'lime'.
english_sentence_B: For instance, in the very drugs which they have composed for hard-to-cicatrise and malignant [sores], 'scale' (lepis) is written simply, without 'of copper' being added, and 'split' (schistē) without 'alum', and 'terebinth' without 'resin' being added. english_sentence_B: When I add the word 'some', you must understand, besides what is called oil in the proper and unqualified sense, also the oil named with a qualification: rose-oil or myrtle-oil or oil of cypros or something of this sort.

english_sentence_A: For sometimes I made haste to compound the drug from simples few in number, [701] sometimes from more, and there are times when I did so from very many or from all those of the same genus.
english_sentence_B: For sometimes I was eager to compound the drug from simples few in number, [701] sometimes from more, and at times even from very many, or from all those of the same genus.

english_sentence_A: And moreover, because I had some in abundance and others not at all or in very small quantity at that particular time, I turned to the composition of the drug from those I had, since the need was pressing; then, having found it approved by experience, I used it thus ever after.
english_sentence_B: And indeed also, because at that particular time I had some of them in abundance and others not at all or only very little, I turned to the composition of the drug from those I had, since need was pressing; then, having found it approved by trial, I always used it thus.

greek_sentence: πολλάκις δ’ ἑκὼν ἔνια μὲν ἰσχυρότερα τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων, ἔνια δὲ ἀσθενέστερα ποιῆσαι προθέμενος, ὡς πρὸς πλείονας ἔχειν διαθέσεις ἁρμόττοντα φάρμακα, διαφερούσας ἐποιησάμην τὰς συνθέσεις, καὶ μέντοι κᾀκ τοῦ πλειόνων χρῄζειν δυνάμεων τὸ τὴν ἕλκωσιν ἔχον μόριον, ὥσπερ ὅταν ἅμα τε κοῖλον καὶ πλαδαρὸν καὶ ῥυπαρὸν ὀχθῶδές τε τοῖς χείλεσι καὶ ῥευματιζόμενον ἐκ τῶν ὑπερκειμένων.
english_sentence_A: And often, deliberately setting out to make some of the compound drugs stronger and some weaker, so as to have drugs suited to a greater number of conditions, I made the compositions differ; and moreover also because the part that has the ulceration requires a greater number of powers, as when it is at once hollow and flabby and dirty, callous at its lips, and afflicted with flux from the parts lying above it.
english_sentence_B: Often, too, I deliberately set out to make some of the compound drugs stronger and some weaker, so as to have drugs suited to more conditions, and so I made the compoundings different. Indeed it was also because the part that has the ulceration needs more faculties, as when it is at once hollow and flabby and foul, raised and ridged at the lips, and receiving a flux from the parts lying above.

lsj_entry_text: σύν-θεσις, εως, ἡ, putting together, composition, combination, Pl. Phd. 93a , R. 611b ; τῶν λίθων Arist. EN 1174a23 , cf. IG 42(1).103.56 (Epid., iv B.C.), 7.3073.92 (Lebad., ii B.C.); τῶν σπονδύλων Sor. 1.102 ; storage, τῶν μήλων (quinces in a ῥίσκος) Phylarch. 10 J. ; but ἐλαιῶν ς. a preserve of olives, Gp. 9.28.2 . in concrete sense, junction, ὀστῶν Arist. PA 658b19 ; συνθέσεις (λέγω τὰς γωνίας) Id. Pr. 910b14 . in various technical senses: in Grammar, composition, γραμμάτων τε συνθέσεις, i.e. syllables and words, A. Pr. 460 , cf. Arist. Metaph. 1092a26 ; ς. ἔκ τε ῥημάτων γιγνομένη καὶ ὀνομάτων, i.e. sentences, Pl. Sph. 263d , cf. Cra. 431c , Arist. Po. 1458a28 , Gal. 15.487 ; περὶ συνθέσεως ὀνομάτων, title of work by D.H. ; also, the juxtaposition of letters in a word, Arist. Rh.Al. 1434b34 ; of an author's composition, Isoc. 10.11 ; so ἡ τῶν μέτρων ς. metrical composition, Arist. Po. 1449b35 ; ἡ τῶν ἐπῶν ς. D.S. 5.74 ; ἡ τοῦ παίωνος ξ. the way the paeon is made up, Plu. 2.1143d ; the constitution of things, Hp. Virg. 1 . Math., synthesis of a problem (opp. ἀνάλυσις), Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.7 , explained in Papp. 634 ; ἡ κατὰ ς. ἀγωγή synthetic procedure, Id. 412.2 . Math., ς. λόγου transformation of a ratio known as componendo, Euc. 5 Def. 14 ; κατὰ -σιν, = componendo, Archim. Aequil. 2.9 . Math., addition, Ph. 1.11 , Plu. 2.1018c , Dioph. 1 Intr.; καθ' ἁντινοῦν -σιν however many times added, i.e. whatever number of times taken (multiplied), Archim. Spir. 1 :—also as Pythag. name for 2 , Anatol. ap. Theol.Ar. 8 . in Logic, union of noun and verb or of two objects of thought in a statement, Arist. Int. 16a12 , de An. 430a27 ; also ὁ παρὰ τὴν ς. [λόγος] the fallacy of composition, opp. διαίρεσις, Id. SE 177a33 . in Physics, composition of substances, parts of organisms, from their elementary constituents, Id. PA 646a12 , Top. 151a23 ; opp μίξις (combination), Id. GC 328a6 . in Medicine, compounding of essences and drugs, τῶν μύρων Thphr. Od. 14 , al., cf. HP 5.5.2 . in concrete sense, a social or political combination, Arist. Pol. 1276b7 ; a military formation, Ael. Tact. 18.5 . agreement, treaty, Pi. P. 4.168 , Fr. 205 ; πὸς τὰς συνθέσις in accordance with the agreements, IG 5(2).343.41 , 60 (Orchom. Arc. , iv B.C.); ἐκ συνθέσεως by arrangement, D.S. 13.112 , etc.; συνθέσεις περὶ γάμων Plu. greek_sentence: ἔστι δὲ τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ἑλκῶν, ἐφ’ ὧν αὐτὸ τὸ πεπονθὸς μόριον ἐν καχεξίᾳ τοσαύτῃ γέγονεν, ὡς κᾂν εὔπεπτον ᾖ τὸ παραγιγνόμενον ἐπ’ αὐτὸ τροφῆς ἕνεκεν αἷμα, μεταβάλλειν τε καὶ διαφθείρειν, ἐάν τε κακόχυμον ᾖ τὸ ἐπιῤῥέον εἰς τοσοῦτον, ὡς εἰ καὶ μηδὲν ἐπεπόνθει τὸ μόριον, ὑπ’ ἐκείνου γοῦν αὐτοῦ μόνου διαβιβρώσκεσθαι.

english_sentence_B: Such ulcers are those in which the affected part itself has come into so great a cachexia that, even if the blood arriving at it for the sake of nourishment is well concocted, it alters and corrupts it; and if what flows in is cacochymous to such a degree that, even if the part had suffered nothing at all, it would be eaten through by that alone.

greek_sentence: τῆς μὲν σχιστῆς στυπτηρίας καὶ τῶν σιδίων, ὡς σφοδρότατα στυφόντων, ἔλαττον ἐνέβαλεν, ἑκκαίδεκα δραχμαῖς ἑκατέρου μίξας εἰς ταὐτὸ, τοῦ σώρεως δὲ τὸ ἡμιόλιον ἑκατέρου, τουτέστι τέσσαρας ἐπὶ ταῖς εἴκοσι, ἧττον μὲν στύφοντος, οὐχ ἧττον δὲ ξηραίνοντος, ἴσον δὲ συναμφοτέρου, τῆς τε σχιστῆς καὶ τῶν σιδίων, ἐνέβαλλε τῆς κηκί δος ἐπὶ ταῖς τριάκοντα δραχμαῖς δύο προσθεὶς, ὡς ἀσθροισθῆναι τὰς πάσας ἐκ τῶν φαρμάκων ὀκτὼ καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα.
english_sentence_A: Of the split alum and the pomegranate rinds, since they are most vehemently astringent, he put in less, mixing sixteen drachms of each together into the same; but of sory half as much again as of each of these, that is twenty-four, since it is less astringent but no less drying; and an amount equal to both of them together, the split alum and the pomegranate rinds, he put in of oak-gall, adding two to the thirty drachms, so that the total from the drugs came to eighty-eight.
english_sentence_B: Of the split alum and of the pomegranate rinds, as being the most strongly astringent, he put in less, mixing sixteen drachms of each together; of the sory one and a half times the amount of each, that is, twenty-four, since it is less astringent but no less drying; and of the oak-gall he put in an amount equal to both together, the split [alum] and the pomegranate rinds, adding two to the thirty drachms, so that the total from the drugs comes to eighty-eight.

greek_sentence: τῶν τοιούτων ἐστὶ καὶ ἡ πίττα, κατά γε τὴν τοῦ ξηραίνειν καὶ ὑγραίνειν ἀντίθεσιν, ἀποκεχωρηκυῖα σαφῶς ἤδη τῶν μέσων, κατὰ τὴν ἑτέραν ἀντίθεσιν τῶν θερμαινόντων καὶ ψυχόντων φαρμάκων οὐκ ἔτι· θερμαίνει γὰρ μετρίως καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τοῖς ἐκπυΐσκουσι φαρμάκοις μίγνυται, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ προκείμενον φάρμακον ἡ μὲν ξηρὰ [710] πίττα τῶν μέσων ἐστὶ καὶ λιθάργυρος ἔτι μᾶλλον, τά τ’ ἄλλα τῶν ξηραντικῶν.
english_sentence_A: Pitch too is among such things, at least with respect to the opposition of drying and moistening, since it has already clearly departed from the intermediate drugs, but with respect to the other opposition, that of heating and cooling drugs, not yet; for it heats moderately, and for this reason it is also mixed with the drugs that bring things to suppuration, so that in the drug under discussion the dry [710] pitch is among the intermediate ones, and litharge still more so, and the others are among the drying drugs.
english_sentence_B: Pitch too is among such substances, at least with respect to the opposition between drying and moistening, though it has already clearly departed from the middle ones; with respect to the other opposition, that between heating and cooling drugs, it is no longer of this kind. For it heats moderately, and for this reason it is also mixed into drugs that bring to suppuration.

Fr. 578.1 ; v. εὐδιανός. c. gen. also, a means of producing something, φ. σωτηρίας Id. Ph. 893 ; μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φ. Pl. Phdr. 274e ; ὑπομνήσεως ib. 275a , cf. 230d ; ἀθανασίας Antiph. 86.6 ; ἡσυχίας Arist. english_sentence_A: But since a misunderstanding can arise here too, I shall discuss it, having first recalled a theorem useful for many purposes, which has been stated by me in other treatises as well, but has been sufficiently worked out in the treatise on simple drugs and in that of the therapeutic method.
english_sentence_B: So in the drug before us the dry [710] pitch is among the middle substances, and litharge still more so, as are the other drying substances. Since a misapprehension can arise here too, I shall discuss it, but first I shall recall a theorem useful for many purposes.

greek_sentence: θερμὸν γὰρ καὶ ψυχρὸν, ὑγρόν τε καὶ ξηρὸν ὀνομάζομεν φάρμακον, ὅ τι περ ἀνθρώπου σῶμα θερ μαίνειν ἢ ψύχειν ἢ ξηραίνειν ἢ ὑγραίνειν δύνηται, πρὸς τὴν ἀρίστην κρᾶσιν ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ τὴν ἀναφορὰν ποιούμενοι.
english_sentence_A: For we call a drug hot and cold, moist and dry, whichever is able to heat or cool or dry or moisten the human body, making our reference to the best temperament in a human being.
english_sentence_B: I have stated it in other treatises as well, but it has been worked out sufficiently in the treatise On Simple Drugs and in that of the Therapeutic Method. We call a drug hot or cold, moist or dry, whatever is able to heat or cool or dry or moisten the body of a human being, making the reference to the best mixture in a human being.

english_sentence_A: And this is a kind of mean among the blameworthy temperaments, which for this very reason we call hot or cold or moist or dry, naming them derivatively from what predominates in them, whether you wish to call it quality or power or substance or temperament.
english_sentence_B: This mixture is a kind of middle among the faulty ones. For this very reason we call those hot or cold or moist or dry, naming them derivatively from whatever predominates in them, whether you wish to call it a quality or a power or a substance or a mixture.

lsj_entry_text: στοιχεῖον, τό: in a form of sun-dial, the shadow of the gnomon, the length of which in feet indicated the time of day, ὅταν ᾖ δεκάπουν τὸ ς. when the shadow is ten feet long, Ar. Ec. 652 , v. Sch.; ὁπηνίκ' ἂν εἴκοσι ποδῶν . . τὸ ς. ᾖ Eub. 119.7 , cf. Philem. 83 . element, a simple sound of speech, as the first component of the syllable, Pl. Cra. 424d ; τὸ ῥῶ τὸ ς. ib. 426d ; γραμμάτων ς. καὶ συλλαβάς Id. Tht. 202e ; ς. ἐστι φωνὴ ἀδιαίρετος Arist. Po. 1456b22 ; φωνῆς ς. καὶ ἀρχαὶ δοκοῦσιν εἶναι ταῦτ' ἐξ ὧν σύγκεινται αἱ φωναὶ πρώτων Id. Metaph. 998a23 , cf. Gal. 15.6 :—στοιχεῖα therefore, strictly, were different from letters (γράμματα), Diog.Bab.Stoic. 3.213 , Sch.D.T. p.32 , al., but are freq. not clearly distd. from them, as by Pl. Tht. l.c., Cra. 426d ; τὰ ς. τῶν γραμμάτων τὰ τέτταρα καὶ εἴκοσι Aen.Tact. 31.21 ; ς. ε letter ε (in a filing-system), BGU 959.2 (ii A.D.); ἀκουόμενα ς. letters which are pronounced, A.D. Adv. 165.17 ; γράμματα and ς. are expressly identified by D.T. 630.32 ; the ς. and its name are confused by A.D. Synt. 29.1 , but distd. by Hdn.Gr. ap. Choerob. in Theod. 1.340 , Sch. D.T. l.c.:— κατὰ στοιχεῖον in the order of the letters, alphabetically, AP 11.15 ( Ammian. ); dub.sens.in Plu. 2.422e . in Physics, στοιχεῖα were the components into which matter is ultimately divisible, elements, reduced to four by Empedocles, who called them ῥιζὤματα, the word στοιχεῖα being first used (acc. to Eudem. ap. Simp. in Ph. 7.13 ) by Pl. , τὰ πρῶτα οἱονπερεὶ ς, ἐξ ὧν ἡμεῖς τε συγκείμεθα καὶ τἄλλα Tht. 201e ; τὰ τῶν πάντων ς. Plt. 278d ; αὐτὰ τιθέμενοι ς. τοῦ παντός Ti. 48b , cf. Arist. GC 314a29 , Metaph. 998a28 , Thphr. Sens. 3 , al., D.L. 3.24 ; ς. σωματικά Arist. Mete. 338a22 , Thphr. Fr. 46 ; ἄτομα ς. Epicur. Ep. 2p.36U. ; equivalent to ἀρχαί, Thales ap. Plu. 2.875c , Anaximand. ap. D.L. 2.1 , Anon. ap. Arist. Ph. 188b28 , Metaph. 1059b23 , al.; but Arist. also distinguishes ς. from ἀρχή as less comprehensive, ib. 1070b23 ; τὰ ς. ὕλη τῆς οὐσίας ib. 1088b27 ; τρία τὰ ς. Id. Ph. 189b16 ; distd. from ἀρχή on other grounds by Stoic. 2.111 ; ς. used in three senses by Chrysipp., ib. 136 , cf. Zeno ib. 1.24 , al.; in Medicine, Gal. 6.3 , 420 , al., 15.7 , al.; Αἰθέρ, κόσμου ς. ἄριστον Orph. H. 5.4 ; ἀνηλεὲς ς., of the sea, Babr. 71.4 ; τὸ ς., of the sea, Polem. Cyn. 44 ; ἄμφω τὰ ς., i.e. land and sea, ib. 11 , cf. Hdn. 3.1.5 , Him. Ecl. 2.18 . the elements of proof, e.g. in general reasoning the πρῶτοι συλλογισμοί, Arist. Metaph. 1014b1 ; in Geometry, the propositions whose proof is involved in the proof of other propositions, ib. 998a26 , 1014a36 ; title of geometrical works by Hippocrates of Chios, Leon, Theudios, and Euclid, Procl. in Euc. pp.66,67 , 68F. : hence applied to whatever is one, small, and capable of many uses, Arist. Metaph. 1014b3 ; to whatever is most universal, e.g. the unit and the point, ib. 6 ; the line and the circle, Id. Top. 158b35 ; the τόπος (argument applicable to a variety of subjects), ib. 120b13 , al., Rh. 1358a35 , al.; στοιχεῖα τὰ γένη λέγουσί τινες Id. Metaph. 1014b10 ; τὸ νόμισμα ς. καὶ πέρας τῆς ἀλλαγῆς coin is the unit . . of exchange, Id. Pol. 1257b23 ; in Grammar, ς. τῆς λέξεως parts of speech, D.H. Comp. 2 ; but also, the letters composing a word, A.D. Synt. 313.7 ; letters of the alphabet, Diog. Bab. Stoic. 3.213 ; ς. τοῦ λόγου the elements of speech, viz. words, or the kinds of words, parts of speech, Thphr. ap. Simp. in Cat. 10.24 , Chrysipp.Stoic. 2.45 , A.D. Synt. 7.1 , 313.6 . generally, elementary or fundamental principle, ἀρξάμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν ς. X. Mem. 2.1.1 ; ς. χρηστῆς πολιτείας Isoc. 2.16 ; τὸ πολλάκις εἰρημένον μέγιστον ς. Arist. greek_sentence: καὶ τοῖς ἰσχυροῖς φαρμάκοις οὐ μικρὰ διαφορὰ τῆς ἐνεργείας, ἣν ποιεῖται κατὰ τὰ μαλακὰ καὶ σκληρὰ σώματα, καὶ γὰρ θᾶττον ἅπτεται τῶν μαλακῶν καὶ σφοδρότερον ἀνιᾷ καὶ φλεγμονὰς ἐπεγείρει μείζονας.
english_sentence_A: Now those which have the strongest powers seem to display the same activity upon all bodies, whereas the weak ones show the difference clearly; but if you pay attention there will appear no less, in the strong drugs too, a considerable difference in the activity which they produce upon soft and upon hard bodies; for they take hold of soft bodies more quickly, distress them more violently, and arouse greater inflammations.
english_sentence_B: Now, those that have the strongest powers seem to display the same action on all bodies, whereas the weak ones show the difference clearly; yet if you pay attention it will appear no less: even in the strong drugs there is no small difference in the action they exert on soft and on hard bodies, for they lay hold of the soft ones more quickly, cause more violent pain, and arouse greater inflammations.

greek_sentence: ὁπότ’ οὖν ταῦτά μοι χρησίμως οὐκ εἰς τὰ παρόντα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς ἄλλα πολλὰ τῶν κατὰ τήνδε τὴν πραγματείαν [713] εἴρηται, πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον ἀφίξομαι φάρμακον, ἐφ’ οὗ τῆς μὲν ξηρᾶς πίττης ἔφην ὑπὸ τοῦ Κρίτωνος γεγράφθαι δραχ.
english_sentence_A: Since, then, these things have been said by me usefully not only for the present matters but also for many others in this treatise, [713] I shall return again to the drug under discussion, in which I said that 100 drachms of dry pitch had been written by Criton, and 3 litrae of litharge—neither of them being able, from its own proper power, to heal a malignant ulcer, but having reasonably been mixed with the beneficial ingredients so that the drug being compounded might become a plaster.
english_sentence_B: Since, then, I have said these things usefully not only for the present matters but also for many others in this treatise, [713] I shall return again to the drug under discussion.

greek_sentence: οὐδετέρου μὲν αὐτῶν ἐκ τῆς οἰκείας δυνάμεως ἰᾶσθαι δυναμένου κακόηθες ἕλκος, ἵνα δ’ ἔμπλαστον γένηται τὸ συντιθέμενον φάρμακον, εὐλόγως μιχθέντων τοῖς ὠφελοῦσιν.
english_sentence_A: Their quantity, taken by a conjecture grounded in art, came out at the weight mentioned just now, the compounder taking care neither to mix so little of each with the strong drugs that the biting and corrosive ones became painful to those being treated, nor so much in both bulk and weight as to dissolve their power; for the scale of copper dries and cleanses strongly, and verdigris still more than it, and it does both these things and also eats through the flesh.
english_sentence_B: Neither of them is able by its own proper power to heal a malignant ulcer, but they were reasonably mixed with the beneficial ingredients so that the drug being compounded might become emplastic.

english_sentence_A: Burnt copper, however, needs neither to be intensified by anything nor to be relaxed, being of moderate power for the present purposes.
english_sentence_B: Their quantity, arrived at by technical estimation, came to the weight just stated. The compounder took care neither to mix so little of each with the strong drugs that the biting and erosive ones would become painful to those being treated, nor so much in both bulk and weight as to slacken their power.

english_sentence_B: Their quantity, arrived at by technical estimation, came to the weight just stated. english_sentence_A: [714] And for this reason Criton also added the boiling for them, writing somewhat as follows, in these very words: boil litharge and oil until it thickens to some degree, then the scale of copper and the verdigris until it thickens and becomes of good colour, then add the pitch, then, having cooled it, the ladanum made smooth with wine, taking care that it does not boil over when this is thrown in; then, having united them over a gentle fire, pour it out and knead it.

greek_sentence: αὐτίκα γέ τοι τῆς μυρσίνης κηρωτῆς ἔξεστιν ἔλαττόν τε καὶ πλέον μίξαντα ποτὲ μὲν ὑγροτέρῳ τε καὶ μαλακωτέρῳ χρῆσθαι τῷ φαρμάκῳ, ποτὲ δὲ σκληροτέρῳ καὶ ξηροτέρῳ, κατὰ μὲν τὴν πρώτην ἐπίθεσιν ἐν πλατεῖ στοχασμῷ, καθάπερ εἴρηται πρόσθεν, ἐν δὲ τῇ δευτέρᾳ χρήσει πλησιαίτερον ἀφικνουμένου, ὡς ἐδείχθη.

lsj_entry_text: ὑγρός, ά, όν: Comp. ὑγρότερος Pl. Tht. 162b , etc.: Sup. -ότατος X. Eq. 7.7 , etc.:—wet, moist, fluid (opp. ξηρός), ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον, i. e. olive-oil, opp. fat or tallow, Il. 23.281 , Od. 6.79 ; ὑ. πίσσα, νᾶπυ, raw pitch, liquid mustard, SIG 1171.14 (Lebena, i B. C.), IG 42(1).126.22 (Epid., ii A. D.); τὸ ὑ. ξύλον, opp. τὸ ξηρόν, Ev.Luc. 23.31 ; ὑγρὸν ὕδωρ Od. 4.458 ; ἄνεμοι ὑγρὸν ἀέντες winds blowing moist or rainy, 5.478 , 19.440 , Hes. Op. 625 , Th. 869 ; ὑ. ἅλς, πέλαγος, θάλασσα, Pi. O. 7.69 . P. 4.40 , A. Supp. 259 ; ὑγρὰ νύξ a wet night, Pl. Criti. 112a ; ἐφ' ὑγροῖς ζωγραφεῖν paint on a wet ground, Plu. 2.759c . ὑγρά, Ion. ὑγρή, ἡ, the moist, i.e. the sea, ἐπὶ τραφερήν τε καὶ ὑγρήν Il. 14.308 ; ἠμὲν ἐφ' ὑγρὴν ἠδ' ἐπ' ἀπείρονα γαῖαν 24.341 , Od. 1.97 ; ἐφ' ὑγρᾷ Ar. V. 678 ; πουλὺν ἐφ' ὑγρήν Il. 10.27 ; so ὑγρὰ κέλευθα the watery ways, i. e. the sea, 1.312 , Od. 3.71 . τὸ ὑ. and τὰ ὑ. wet, moisture, Hdt. 1.142 , Hp. Loc.Hom. 9 , Liqu. tit.; Liquid, Hdt. 4.172 ; γῆ ὑγρῷ φυραθεῖσα Pl. Tht. 147c ; ἐξερρύα συχνὸν ὑγρόν a quantity of fluid, IG 42(1).122.4 (Epid., iv B. C.); μετρεῖν τὰ ὑγρά liquids, ib. 22.1013.10 ; ἐπὶ ὑγροῖς οὐκ ἐξὸν δανείζειν PGnom. 232 (ii A. D.). μέτρα ὑγρὰ καὶ ξηρά liquid and dry measure, Pl. Lg. 746e . θῆρες ὑ. water-animals, opp. πεζοί, AP 9.18 ( Germ. ); οἱ ὄρνιθες οἱ ὑ. Philostr. Im. 1.9 ; ὑ. ἀοιδός, of a frog, AP 6.43 (Plato). of the bowels or faeces, loose, Hp. Aph. 2.20 , Arist. HA 617a1 . ὑ. σφυγμός a damp pulse, defined by Gal. 19.405 . soft, pliant, supple, of the eagle's back, Pi. P. 1.9 ; of the limbs and body, ὑγραῖς ἐν ἀγκάλαις E. Fr. 941 , cf. Babr. 34.7 ; ὑγρὸς τὸ εἶδος, of Ἔρως, Pl. Smp. 196a ; νεώτερος καὶ ὑγρότερος, opp. σκληρός, Id. Tht. 162b ; χορῷ . . ἔτερπον κέαρ ὑγροῖσι ποσσί B. 16.108 ; ὑ. ὀρχηστής Poll. 4.96 , cf. Arist. PA 655a24 ( Comp. ); ὑγρὰ ἔχειν τὰ σκέλη, of a horse, X. Eq. 1.6 ; of a horse's neck, Id. Cyn. 4.1 (so in Adv. of colts, γόνατα ὑγρῶς κάμπτειν, ὑγρῶς τοῖς σκέλεσι χρῆσθαι, Id. Eq. 1.6 , 10.15 ); of the hare, Id. Cyn. 5.31 ; of the jackal, ταχυτῆτι διαφέρει διὰ τὸ ὑγρὸς εἶναι καὶ πηδᾷ πόρρω Arist. HA 580a30 ; also of plants, ὑ. ἄκανθος Theoc. 1.55 ; ὑ. χολάδες Babr. 1.10 ; σῶμα ὑγρὸν κείμενον lying in an easy position, Hp. Prog. 3 ; ὑγρὸν χύτλασον σεαυτόν Ar. V. 1213 ; κέρας ὑ., of a bow, Theoc. 25.206 . languid, feeble, of one dying, ἐς ὑγρὸν ἀγκῶνα . . παρθένῳ προσπτύσσεται S. Ant. 1236 ; κἀπιθεὶς ὑγρὰν χέρα E. Ph. 1439 . of substance, flaccid, flabby, σάρκες Arist. HA 598a9 , 603b32 , al. tender, νεοττοί Ael. NA 7.9 ; βρέφος Nonn. D. 1.4 . moist with wine, tipsy, ὑγρὴν τὴν ψυχὴν ἔχειν Heraclit. 117 ; ἡ διάνοια ὑ. γεγενημένη Plu. 2.713a ; οἰνοβαρὴς . . ὑγρὸν ἀείδων, οὐ μάλα νγφάλιον κλάζων μέλος Opp. H. 2.412 . of the eyes, melting, languishing, ὑ. βλέμμα Anacreont. 15.21 ; ὑγρὰ δερκομένοισιν ἐν ὄμμασιν AP 7.27 (Antip. Brut. 29 ( Comp. ). soft, dainty, luxurious, voluptuous, Id. 2.751a ; ὑ. πρὸς τὴν δίαιταν Id. Sol. 3 ; βίου . . , ὃν πάντες εἰώθασιν ὀνομάζειν ὑγρόν Alex. 203 ; cf. ὑγρότης 11.2 . of the vowels α ι υ, sometimes long and sometimes short, S.E. greek_sentence: ἑνὸς γὰρ ὄντος ἅπασιν αὐτοῖς κοινοῦ τοῦ δυσεπουλώτοις εἶναι, τινὰ μὲν ἐκ τοῦ θεραπεύεσθαι κακῶς ἢ μαλακῶς διαιτᾶσθαι τὸν θεραπευόμενον οὐκ ἐπουλοῦται, μηδεμίαν οἰκείαν αὐτὰ κακοήθειαν ἔχοντα, τινὰ δὲ δι’ ἑαυτὰ δυσθεράπευτά ἐστιν, ἤτοι διὰ τὸ χυμοὺς ἐπιῤῥεῖν αὐτοῖς μοχθηροὺς [735] ἢ διὰ τὸ τοιαύτην ἤδη διάθεσιν ἐσχηκέναι τὸν ἡλκωμένον τόπον, ὡς, κᾂν χρηστὸν ᾗ τὸ ἐπιῤῥέον αἷμα, διαφθείρειν αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: For while there is one thing common to all of them, namely that they are hard to cicatrize, some of them fail to cicatrize because they are badly treated or because the person under treatment lives on a soft regimen, though they themselves have no malignancy of their own; others are hard to treat in themselves, either because bad humors flow into them [735] or because the ulcerated place has already acquired such a disposition that, even if the blood flowing in is good, it corrupts it.
english_sentence_B: For while one thing is common to all of them, namely that they are hard-to-cicatrise, some do not cicatrise because they are treated badly or because the patient under treatment follows a soft regimen, though they have no malignancy of their own; others are hard-to-treat on their own account, either because noxious humours flow in upon them [735] or because the ulcerated place has already acquired such a condition that, even if the blood flowing in is wholesome, it corrupts it.

greek_sentence: ταύτην μὲν οὖν τὴν ἔμπλαστρον ὁ Ἥρας ἔγραψε, μαρτυρήσας αὐτῇ τὸ ἐπὶ τῶν δυσεπουλώτων ἁρμόττειν, ἄλλας δὲ πολυχρήστους κατὰ τὴν αὐτὴν βίβλον γράψας, ἐπὶ πολλοῖς ἔργοις αὐτῶν καὶ τὸ τοῖς δυσεπουλώτοις ἢ καὶ κακοήθεσιν ἢ χειρωνείοις ἀρήγειν προσέγραψε.

english_sentence_A: For all have praised both the plaster called by him Aribarzaneios, as curing malignant, spreading [751] and hard-to-heal ulcers, and the Isis, as circumscribing gangrenes; and a third in addition to these, which he began with the following wording: "of good colour, for fresh wounds (enaimos), cicatrizing," saying that it also helps Chironian ulcers; and a fourth, which he himself names panacea; and a fifth, that of Hicesius.

english_sentence_A: And in the case of [761] inveterate ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, which are also called Chironian, we apply not only the drug itself undiluted, but also, melted in old oil or castor oil and applied on a pledget (ἔμμοτον), even if no pus, not even the least amount, had ever previously formed in the ulcer, it both concocts it and produces pus, and it renders the pus thick.
english_sentence_B: And on inveterate ulcers that are hard to bring to a scar, which are also called cheironian, [761] we not only apply the drug itself unmixed; melted in old oil or in castor oil and applied on lint (emmoton), even if no pus at all, not even the least, had ever formed in the ulcer before, it concocts the ulcer and makes pus, and makes the pus thick.

greek_sentence: δευτέρας δὲ τὰς ἑπομένας αὐταῖς, ὑπὲρ ὧν ἐπὶ πλέον ἐν τῷ πέμπτῳ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων πραγματείας διῆλθον, ἐπιδεικνὺς ἔνια μὲν τῶν φαρμάκων οὐ μόνων τῶν συνθέτων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν αὐτοφυῶν μαλάττειν, ἔνια δὲ σκληρύνειν, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐμπλάττειν, τὰ δὲ ἐκφράττειν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐπιτρέφειν ῥύπον, τὰ δὲ καὶ τὸν ἐπικείμενον ἀποῤῥύπτειν, καὶ τὰ μὲν λεπτύνειν, τὰ δὲ παχύνειν, καὶ τὰ μὲν πυκνοῦν, τὰ δὲ ἀραιοῦν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἀνατρέφειν σάρκα, τὰ δὲ ἀνακαθαίρειν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐπουλοῦν, τὰ δὲ ἑλκοῦν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ἕλκειν, τὰ δὲ ἀποκρούεσθαι, ἑτέρας τε τοιαύτας ἐν αὐτοῖς διαφοράς.
english_sentence_A: It is quite evident that by 'primary' I mean heat and cold and dryness [764] and moisture, and those compounded from these according to any conjugation whatsoever; and by 'secondary' those that follow upon these, about which I went through at greater length in the fifth book of the treatise on simple drugs, showing that some drugs, not only of the compound ones but also of the naturally occurring ones, soften, while others harden, just as also some plug up and others unblock, and some breed filth upon the part while others cleanse away even the filth already lying upon it, and some thin, others thicken, and some condense, others rarefy, and some regenerate flesh, others cleanse it away, and some cicatrize, others ulcerate, and some draw, others repel, and other such differences among them.
english_sentence_B: I discussed these at greater length in the fifth book of my treatise on simple drugs, where I showed that some drugs, not only among the compound ones but also among the natural ones, soften, while others harden. In the same way some block up the passages and others clear obstructions; some generate dirt in addition, while others even cleanse away the dirt lying on the surface; some make thin and others thicken; some condense and others rarefy; some regenerate flesh and others clean it away; some cicatrize and others ulcerate; some draw and others repel; and there are other such differences among them.

english_sentence_A: [On those written by Heras.] Since, then, a certain plaster that works excellently against such ulcers has been recorded in the book of drugs by Heras the Cappadocian, I shall begin from it, transcribing the man's wording, which runs roughly as follows.

english_sentence_A: For you learned, in the treatise on simple drugs, the difference between acrid and bitter drugs: the acrid ones being irritant and biting and hot and bringing fluxes upon the affected parts, [770] while the bitter ones are drying without biting and heating, and for this reason suitable for ulcerated parts.
english_sentence_B: For you learned in the treatise on simple drugs the difference between acrid and bitter drugs: the acrid ones are irritant, biting and hot, and cause a flux into the affected parts [770]; the bitter ones are drying without biting and heating, and for this reason are suitable for ulcerated parts.

english_sentence_A: Of galbanum, at any rate, Heras wrote six drachms and one and a half obols, whereas others wrote ten and a half drachms, just as others again [774] wrote twenty-five, having increased the other ingredients proportionally as well, so that nowhere in the proportion is an obol or a half-obol mentioned.

greek_sentence: πωροῖ γὰρ θᾶσσον καὶ ἀσφαλέστερον σύριγγας πάσας προσφάτους, παλαιὰς ὑποφορὰς, κόλπους, φύματα, παρωτίδας, τὰ ἐν μαστοῖς καὶ [775] μασχάλαις ἀποστήματα, ἢ ἵνα μὴ γένηται ἢ γενόμενα θεραπευθῇ.
english_sentence_A: For it forms callus more quickly and more safely over all recent fistulas, old sinuses (ὑποφοραί), hollows (κόλποι), phymata, parotid swellings, and the abscesses in the breasts and [775] armpits, either so that they do not arise or, once they have arisen, are cured.
english_sentence_B: For it brings to callus, more quickly and more safely, all recent fistulas, old burrowing ulcers (hypophorai), sinuses, phymata, parotid swellings, and the abscesses in the breasts and [775] armpits, either so that they do not arise or, having arisen, are treated.

greek_sentence: οὐ χεῖρον δὲ καὶ περὶ τοῦ δρακοντίου τό γε τοσοῦτον εἰπεῖν, ὡς ἐν τῷ θέρει ξηρανθέντος τοῦ καυλοῦ καὶ ὅλης τῆς πόας ἀναιρεῖσθαι χρὴ τὴν ῥίζαν, εἶτα τιθέμενον ἐν οἴκῳ ξηρῷ μὲν, οὐκ ἔχοντι δὲ ἥλιον, ὀλίγον ὕστερον μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἓξ ἢ ἑπτὰ τέμνειν τὴν ῥίζαν εἰς ﻿ [778] κυκλίσκους καὶ τούτους διείραντα λίνῳ κρεμᾶσαι πάλιν ἐν οἴκῳ ξηρῷ μὲν, ἀνηλίῳ δὲ, καὶ οὕτως ἐπειδὰν ἐθέλοις σκευάζειν τὸ φάρμακον, κόπτειν τὴν ῥίζαν.
english_sentence_A: It is no worse, however, to say at least this much about dracontium too: that in summer, when the stem and the whole plant have dried up, one should take up the root, then, having placed it in a room that is dry but does not receive the sun, a little later, after six or seven days, cut the root into [778] small disks, and having threaded these on a linen thread hang them again in a room that is dry but sunless, and so, whenever you wish to prepare the drug, pound the root.
english_sentence_B: It is not amiss also to say this much about dracontium: that in summer, when the stalk and the whole plant have dried, one must take up the root; then, having put it in a house that is dry but gets no sun, a little later, after six or seven days, one must cut the root into [778] little discs, and, threading these on a linen thread, hang them up again in a house that is dry but sunless; and so, whenever you wish to prepare the drug, pound the root.

greek_sentence: ἕψε ἐν λοπάδι μεγάλῃ ἐπὶ ἀνθράκων λιθάργυρον, ἔλαιον ὡς ἀμόλυντον κατὰ πᾶν εἶναι ἢ παρὰ μικρὸν, εἶτα ἄρας τὴν χύτραν, μίσγε ἰὸν καὶ λεπίδα καὶ ἕψε καὶ μὴ μολυνέτω κατὰ πᾶν, εἶτα πάλιν βαστάσας βάλε ῥητίνην καὶ ἀμμωνιακὸν σεσησμένα, κινῶν ἕως παύσηται ζέων, εἶτα ἐπιθεὶς καὶ μικρὸν ἐάσας βαστάσας ἔμπασσε χαλκὸν καὶ διφρυγὲς καὶ ἑψήσας πάλιν, ἕως μὴ μολύνῃ, ἔσθ’ ὅτε γὰρ [780] τούτων βληθέντων ἐπανίεται, εἶτα βαστάσας προσδίδου κηρὸν καὶ πάλιν ἕψε, ἕως ἀμόλυντος γένηται, ταχέως δὲ γίνεται, εἶτα ἄρας ἀποδώσεις πρόπολιν καὶ ἐπιθεὶς πάλιν, μικρόν τε ἐάσας καὶ ἄρας ἀποδίδου ἀλόην, μάνναν, δίκταμνον, ἀριστολοχίαν, γεντιανήν.
english_sentence_A: Boil in a large pan over charcoals the litharge and the oil, until it is non-staining entirely or very nearly so; then, having lifted off the pot, mix in the verdigris and the scale and boil, and let it not stain at all; then, having removed it again, put in the resin and the ammoniac, sifted, stirring until it stops boiling; then, having set it on again and left it a little while, remove it and sprinkle in the copper and the diphryges, and having boiled it again until it does not stain — for sometimes, [780] when these have been put in, it is loosened again — then, having removed it, add the wax and boil again until it becomes non-staining, and this happens quickly; then, having lifted it off, you will add the propolis, and having set it on again and left it a little while, lift it off and add the aloe, manna, dittany, birthwort, gentian.
english_sentence_B: Boil in a large pan over coals the litharge and the oil until it is entirely non-staining, or nearly so; then, lifting off the pot, mix in the verdigris and the scale and boil, and let it not stain at all; then, taking it off again, put in the resin and the ammoniac, sifted, stirring until it stops boiling; then, setting it back on and leaving it a little, take it off and sprinkle in the copper and the diphryges, and boil again until it does not stain, for sometimes, [780] when these have been thrown in, it slackens again; then, taking it off, add the wax and boil again until it becomes non-staining, and it becomes so quickly; then, lifting it off, you will add the propolis, and setting it on again and leaving it a little, lift it off and add the aloe, manna, dittany, aristolochia and gentian.

english_sentence_A: to reckon it, as others direct, knowing well that, if the drug should be boiled for a longer time—and this will happen when more [793] oil has been put in—it will become more drying, whereas if it should be taken quickly from the fire, because of the small quantity of the oil it will become less drying, but more emollient and more soothing; so that the six kyathoi must be rejected altogether, and six kotylai, each one of nine ounces, must be put in.

english_sentence_B: But in his text there stands written 'of omphacine oil, two choes'.

english_sentence_A: The Isis, which some call Epigonus' drug, is effective: undiluted, against separations of scales and thick exfoliations of bones; applied on lint and as a splenium, both against splinters and the blows and bites of all wild creatures, and it heals all the punctures and wounds inflicted by iron, in wars and otherwise, and fistulas, when applied on top and inserted as a collyrium, removing the callus of these and gluing them together; and this same drug, diluted, for every wound, applied on lint and as a splenium, and for malignant and chronic wounds and those spoiled by others, in which cases scrape beforehand and use the [795] diluted drug.
english_sentence_B: The isis, which some call Epigonus' isis, is effective.

greek_sentence: αἱ προγεγραμμέναι ἔμπλαστροι πᾶσαι διὰ τοῦτο πολύχρηστοι [809] γεγόνασιν, ὅτι φαρμάκων προσειλήφασι μαλακτικῶν, ἑλκτικῶν, διαφορητικῶν πεπτικῶν ἔτι τε τῶν ξηραινόντων ἀδήκτως· αἱ πλεῖσται δὲ αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν ἰσχυρῶς στυφόντων, ὧν δύναμίς ἐστιν ἀποκρουστικὴ τῶν ἐπιῤῥεόντων ὑγρῶν τῷ πεπονθότι μορίῳ.

lsj_entry_text: οἰκεῖος, α, ον, also ος, ον E. Heracl. 634 ; Ion. οἰκήϊος, η, ον : in or of the house, once in Hes. , δούρατ' ἀμάξης οἰκήϊα θέσθαι Op. 457 ; λέβης A. Fr. 1 ; κῆρυξ S. Tr. 757 ; of or for household affairs, domestic (for οἰκηΐη, v. οἰκία II), τὰ οἰ. household affairs, property, Hdt. 2.37 , S. Ant. 661 ; τὰ οἰ. ἀγαθά X. Oec. 9.18 ; τὰ οἰ. τὰ αὑτοῦ his household goods, Lys. 13.41 ; opp. πολιτικά, Th. 2.40 ; opp. τὰ τῆς πόλεως, Pl. Ap. 23b . Astrol., οἰ. ζῴδια domiciliary signs, Vett.Val. 37.21 , al. of persons, of the same household, family, or kin, related, ὥς οἱ ἐόντες οἰκήϊοι as being akin to him, Hdt. 4.65 ; οἰκεῖον οὕτως οὐδὲν . . ὡς ἀνήρ τε καὶ γυνή so closely akin, Men. 647 ; ἀνὴρ οἰ. kinsman, relative, near friend, Hdt. 1.108 ; οἱ οἰ. kinsmen, opp. οἱ ἀλλότριοι, And. 4.15 , cf. Th. 2.51 ; opp. ὀθνεῖοι, Pl. Prt. 316c ; οἱ ἑωυτοῦ οἰκηϊότατοι his own nearest kinsmen, Hdt. 3.65 , cf. 5.5 , D. 18.288 ; of the tie itself, κατὰ τὸ οἰ. Ἀτρεῖ because of his relationship to Atreus, Th. 1.9 . friendly, εἴχομέν ποτε . . τὸν τόπον τοῦτον οἰ. D. 4.4 ; οὓς ἂν ἡγήσαιτο -οτάτους τε καὶ ἑταιροτάτους Pl. Phd. 89e . of things. belonging to one's house or family, one's own (defined as ὅταν ἐφ' αὑτῷ ᾖ ἀπαλλοτριῶσαι Arist. Rh. 1361a21 ), οἰ. ἄρουραι Pi. O. 12.19 ; σταθμοῖς ἐν οἰκείοισι A. Pr. 398 ; γῆ, χθών, S. Aj. 859 , Ant. 1203 ; οἰκεῖον, ἢ 'ξ ἄλλου τινός ; born in the house, or . . ? Id. OT 1162 ; αἱ οἰ. πόλεις their own cities, X. HG 3.5.2 ; ἡ οἰ. (sc. γῆ), Ion. ἡ οἰκηΐη Hdt. 1.64 ; [ἀναθήματα] οἰκήϊα his own property, ib. 92 ; πόλεμοι οἰ. wars in one's own country, of the Helot war in Laconia, Th. 1.118 , cf. 4.64 ; σῖτος οἰ. καὶ οὐκ ἐπακτός homegrown, Id. 6.20 . = ἴδιος , one's own, personal, private, οἰκείων κερδέων εἵνεκα Thgn. 46 ; ἐὼν ἐν κακῷ οἰκηΐῳ Hdt. 1.45 , cf. 153 , Antipho 1.13 ; αἱ χεῖρες -ότεραι τοῦ σιδήρου Id. 4.3.3 ; μηδὲν -οτέρᾳ τῇ ἀπολαύσει with enjoyment not more our own, Th. 2.38 , cf. 7.70 ; ἀλλοτρίας γῆς πέρι οἰ. κίνδυνον ἔχειν Id. 3.13 ; οἰ. ξύνεσις mother wit, Id. 1.138 ; πρὸς οἰκείας χερός by his own hand, S. Ant. 1176 , etc.; for A. Ag. 1220 , v. βορά. in Stoic Philos., endeared by nature to all animals, including man, τὸ πρῶτον οἰ. what is earliest endeared, Chrysipp.Stoic. 3.43 , Hierocl. p.7A. proper to a thing, fitting, suitable, οὔτε . . καλὸν οὐδὲν [οὐδ'] οἰκήϊον Hdt. 3.81 , cf. D. 18.59 . c. dat. rei, belonging to, conformable to the nature of a thing, προοίμιον οἰ. ἑκάστῳ Pl. Lg. 772e , cf. R. 468d , al., and freq. in Arist. , as EN 1098a29 : also c. gen., τὰ αὐτῶν οἰ. Pl. Phd. 96d ; οἰ. τῆς διαλεκτικῆς Arist. Top. 101b2 , cf. EN 1096b31 , Rh. 1360a22 ; οἰ. πρός τι Plb. 5.105.1 . of persons, c. gen., a student of . . , σοφίας Str. 17.1.5 ; addicted to, καινοτομίας Iamb. VP 30.176 . proper, fit, οἰ. κατάγελως fit subject for ridicule, Men. 160 ; οἰ. ὄνομα a word in its proper, literal sense, opp. metaphor, Arist. Rh. 1404b35 . Adv. οἰκείως has the same senses as the Adj., οἰ φέρε bear it like your own affair, Ar. Th. 197 ; διαλέγεσθαι οἰ. τινί converse familiarly with him, Th. 6.57 ; οἰ. χρῆσθαί τινι to be on familiar terms, X. HG 2.3.16 ; οἰ. διακεῖσθαί τινι Id. english_sentence_A: And although others too have written this plaster of Hicesius, those who prepared it more accurately, in accordance both with the Tarentine and with the [prescription] judged by us through boiling to be the true one, have turned out in agreement; but those who [did so] more carelessly, whether in one only or two of the ingredients mixed in or even more, are seen to disagree with Heracleides.
english_sentence_B: And although others have also written up this plaster of Hicesius, those who prepared it more precisely have turned out to be in agreement both with the Tarentine and with the recipe judged by us to be truly correct by means of the boiling; but those who prepared it more carelessly appear to disagree with Heraclides either in only one or two of the ingredients mixed, or even in more.

greek_sentence: [Κυζικηνὴ τοῦ Ἥρα.] Τῶν ἐνδόξων ἐμπλάστρων ἐστὶ καὶ αὕτη, σχεδὸν ὑπὸ πάντων γεγραμμένη, τὰ πλεῖστα μὲν ἐν τῇ συμμετρίᾳ τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων ὁμολογούμενα γραψάντων αὐτῶν, ἐνίοις δὲ καὶ διαφωνησάντων, [815] ὡς ἔσται φανερὸν ὑπογραψάντων ἡμῶν ὡς ἕκαστος αὐτῶν ἀξιοῖ συντίθεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: [The Cyzicene of Heras.] This too is one of the celebrated plasters, written down by nearly everyone, these authors having for the most part written things that agree as regards the proportion of the simple drugs, but having also disagreed in some, [815] as will be evident when we have set down below how each of them thinks it ought to be compounded.

english_sentence_A: [The one through dittany, as Damocrates.] It has often been said by me that metrical writings are more useful than those written in prose, not only for memory but also for the accuracy of the proportion of the ingredients that are mixed.
english_sentence_B: [The plaster made with dittany, as Damocrates gives it.] I have often said that recipes written in verse are more useful than those written in prose not only for memory but also for exactness in the proportion of the ingredients mixed.

lsj_entry_text: ἔμ-πλαστρος, ἡ, salve or plaster, Dsc. 1.32 ; said to be later form of ἔμπλαστος, Gal. 13.372 ; also ἔμπλαστρον, τό, Hierocl. Facet. 221 , PSI 3.297 (V A. D. ).
greek_sentence: Τῶν περιβοήτων δ’ ἐστὶν ἐμπλάστρων μία, Μόνη τ’ ἔχουσα Κρητικὸν τὸ καλούμενον Δίκταμνον, ἰᾶται δὲ τὰς τῶν ἑρπετῶν, Ἰοβόλων πληγάς τε καὶ τὰ δήγματα Πάντων τετραπόδων, κᾂν λελυσσήκῃ τινὰ, Τετυλωμένα θ’ ἕλκη, τάς τε τῶν νεύρων φθοράς.
english_sentence_A: It is one of the celebrated plasters, and the only one containing the Cretan herb called dittany; it heals the strokes of venomous creeping things and the bites of all quadrupeds, even if one of them has gone rabid, and callused ulcers, and the corruptions of the nerves and of muscles and of the cartilages lying upon the bones, when they already have corruption in depth.
english_sentence_B: 'It is one of the celebrated plasters, and the only one that contains the so-called Cretan dittany. It heals the strikes of venomous reptiles and the bites of all quadrupeds, even if some of them have been rabid, and callused ulcers, and the corruptions of nerves, of muscles and of the cartilages that lie upon bones, when these already have corruption in depth.

Ch. 545 :—usage contradicts the statement of Gramm. that μαζός is the man's breast, μαστός the woman's:— breast, δεξιτερὸν κατὰ μαζόν Il. 5.393 ; of men's breasts, βάλε δουρὶ στέρνον ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο 4.528 ; βάλε στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν 8.121 , cf. Od. 22.82 , X. An. 1.4.17 , 4.3.6 . more freq. of a woman's breast, μαζὸν ἀνέσχε, of Hecuba pleading with Hector, Il. 22.80 ; εἴ ποτέ τοι λαθικηδέα μαζὸν ἐπέσχον ib. 83 ; γυναῖκά τε θήσατο μαζόν sucked her breast, 24.58 ; πάϊς δέ οἱ ἦν ἐπὶ μαζῷ Od. 11.448 ; σὺ δέ μ' ἔτρεφες . . τῷ σῷ ἐπὶ μαζῷ 19.483 ; so φαίνουσαι τοὺς μαζούς Hdt. 2.85 ; τοὺς μ. ἀποταμοῦσα Id. 4.202 ; ἐπὶ τοῦ μαστοῦ ἔφυ φῦμα Id. 3.133 ; προὔκειτο μαστῶν περονίς S. Od. 18.276 ; πατρὸς δ' εἴμ' ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μήτηρ Il. 21.109 , cf. Od. 4.611 ; κακὸς ἐξ ἀ. Thgn. 190 , cf. 57 sq.; πραῢς ἀστοῖς, οὐ φθονέων ἀγαθοῖς Pi. P. 3.71 , cf. 2.96 , 4.285 ; τίς ἂν εὔπατρις ὧδε βλάστοι; οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀ. κτλ. S. El. 1082 ; οἵ τ' ἀ. πρὸς τῶν ἀγενῶν κατανικῶνται Id. Fr. 84 ; τοὺς εὐγενεῖς γὰρ κἀγαθοὺς . . φιλεῖ Ἄρης ἐναίρειν ib. 649 , cf. E. Alc. 600 , al.: ἀγαθοὶ καὶ ἐξ ἀγαθῶν Pl. Phdr. 274a :—in political sense, aristocrats, esp. in the phrase καλοὶ κἀγαθοί (v. sub καλοκἀγαθός). brave, valiant, since courage was attributed to Chiefs and Nobles, Il. 1.131 , al.; τῷ κ' ἀγαθὸς μὲν ἔπεφν', ἀγαθὸν δέ κεν ἐξενάριξεν 21.280 ; cf. Hdt. 5.109 , etc. good, capable, in reference to ability, ἀ. βασιλεύς Il. 3.179 ; ἰητήρ 2.732 ; θεράπων 16.165 , 17.388 ; πύκτης Xenoph. 2.15 ; ἰητρός Hp. Prog. 1 ; προβατογνώμων A. Ag. 795 ; ἄρχοντες Democr. 266 : freq. with qualifying words, ἀ. ἐν ὑσμίνῃ Il. 13.314 ; βοὴν ἀ. 2.408 , 563 , al.; πύξ Od. 11.300 ; βίην Il. 6.478 ; γνώμην S. OT 687 ; πᾶσαν ἀρετήν Pl. Lg. 899b , cf. Alc. 1.124e ; τέχνην Id. Prt. 323b ; τὰ πολέμια, τὰ πολιτικά, Hdt. 9.122 , Pl. Grg. 516b , etc.: more rarely c. dat., ἀ. πολέμῳ X. Oec. 4.15 : with Preps., ἄνδρες ἀ. περὶ τὸ πλῆθος Lys. 13.2 ; εἴς τι Pl. Alc. 1.125a ; πρός τι Id. R. 407e : c. inf., ἀ. μάχεσθαι Hdt. 1.136 ; ἱππεύεσθαι 1.79 ; ἀ. ἱστάναι good at weighing, Pl. Prt. 356b . good, in moral sense, first in Thgn. 438 , cf. Heraclit. 104 , S. El. 1082 , X. Mem. 1.7.1 , Pl. Ap. 41d , etc.; ψυχῆς ἀγαθῆς πατρὶς ὁ ξύμπας κόσμος Democr. 247 : freq. with other Adjs., ὁ πιστὸς κἀ. S. Tr. 541 ; δικαίων κἀ. ib. 1050 :—ironical, τὸν ἀ. Κρέοντα Id. Ant. 31 . ὦ ἀγαθέ, my good friend, as a term of gentle remonstrance, Pl. Prt. 311a , etc. ἀ. δαίμων, v. sub δαίμων; ἀ. τύχη, v. sub τύχη; ἀ. θεός = Lat. bona dea, Plu. Caes. 9 , Cic. 19 . of things, good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη . . ἀ. κουροτρόφος Od. 9.27 , etc.; ἀ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει X. Cyn. 13.17 : c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀ. good for it, Id. Mem. 3.8.3 ; ἑλκῶν Thphr. HP 9.11.1 . of outward circumstances, αἰδὼς οὐκ ἀ. κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι Od. 17.347 ; εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν to good purpose, Il. 9.102 ; ὁ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀ. περ for his own good end, 11.789 ; οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη 2.204 :—ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it is good to do so and so<*> Il. 7.282 , 24.130 , Od. 3.196 , etc. morally good, πρῆξις Democr. 177 ; ἔργα Emp. 112.2 , cf. Ep.Rom. 2.7 , etc. ἀγαθόν, τό, good, blessing, benefit, of persons or things, ὦ μέγα ἀ. σὺ τοῖς φίλοις X. Cyr. 5.3.20 ; φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀ. εἶναί φασι Id. Mem. 2.4.2 , cf. Ar. Ra. 74 , etc; as term of endearment for a baby, blessing!, treasure!, Men. Sam. 28 :— ἀγαθόν τινα δεδρακέναι, πεποιηκέναι confer a benefit on . . , Th. 3.68 , Lys. 13.92 ; ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ τινος for one's good, Th. 5.27 , X. Cyr. 7.4.3 ; ἐπ' ἀ. τοῖς πολίταις Ar. Ra. 1487 ; οὐκ ἐπ' ἀ. for no good end, Th. 1.131 ; ἐπ' οὐδενὶ ἀ. τῆς Ἑλλάδος X. HG 5.2.35 :—in pl., ἡ ἐπ' ἀγαθοῖς γεναμένη (sic) κατασπορά PFlor. 21.10 (iii A.D.):—τὸ ἀ. or τἀ., the good, Epich. 171.5 , cf. Pl. R. 506b , 508e , Arist. Metaph. 1091a31 , etc.:—in pl., ἀγαθά, τά, goods of fortune, treasures, wealth, Hdt. 2.172 , Lys. 13.91 , X. Mem. 1.2.63 , etc.; ἀγαθὰ πράττειν fare well, Ar. Av. 1706 ; also, good things, dainties, Thgn. 1000 , Ar. Ach. 873 , etc.: good qualities, τοῖς ἀ., οἷς ἔχομεν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ Isoc. 8.32 , cf. Democr. 37 ; good points, of a horse, εἰ τἄλλα πάντα ἀ. ἔχοι, κακόπους δ' εἴη X. Eq. 1.2 . Comp. and Sup. are usu. supplied from other stems, viz. Comp. ἀμείνων, ἀρείων<*> βελτίων, κρείσσων ʽκάρρωνʼ, λωΐων (λώʽωνʼ), Ep. βέλτερος, λωΐτερος, φέρτερος:— Sup. ἄριστος, βέλτιστος, κράτιστος, λώϊστος (λῷστος), Ep. βέλτατος, κάρτιστος, φέρτατος, φέριστος:— later, reg. Comp. ἀγαθώτερος LXX Jd. 11.25 , 15.2 , D.S. 8 Fr. 12 , Plot. 5.5.9 , Diod.Rh. p.53.9H. : Sup. ἀγαθώτατος D.S. 16.85 , Hld. 5.15 , etc. ( -ότατος POxy. 1757.26 (ii A.D.)). greek_sentence: Δὶς δ’ εἴκοσι πέντε Ποντικοῦ κηροῦ δραχμὰς, Κολοφωνίας δὲ τῆς καλῆς, κηροῦ διπλοῦν, Τινὲς δὲ μᾶλλον, ταὐτὸ τῆς τερμινθίνης.
english_sentence_A: It contains litharge, twice one hundred drachmas, [822] and of old oil a quarter of a litra (though some say rather a quarter of a kotyle); twice twenty-five drachmas of Pontic wax; of good Colophonian resin, double the wax—but some rather [use] the same amount of terebinth resin; of verdigris of copper and of Indian aloe, of burnt copper and of good diphryges, sixteen and a half [drachmas] from each ingredient; twenty-four drachmas of galbanum; of manna and of frankincense equal amounts, twice twelve; of ammoniac twice five and twice twenty; sixteen drachmas of Attic propolis; of long aristolochia twice ten drachmas; twice six drachmas of scale of Cyprian copper, and of the driest gentian root an equal amount.

P. 8.20 ; στεφάνοισί νιν ποίας ἔρεπτον ib. 4.240 : hence, metaph., κεῖραι μελιαδέα ποίαν ib. 9.37 . the grass, i.e. a grassy place, πόα καθίζεσθαι grass to sit on, Pl. Phdr. 229b , cf. X. lsj_entry_text: κοῦφος, η, ον, light, nimble, Hom. only in neut. pl. as Adv., κοῦφα ποσὶ προβιβάς stepping lightly on, Il. 13.158 , cf. Hes. Sc. 323 ; κοῦφα βιβῶν Pi. O. 14.16 ; κ. ποσὶν ἄγ' ἐς κύκλον Ar. Th. 954 (lyr.); also κούφοις ποσί Pi. O. 13.114 ; κουφοτάταις πτερύγων ἀκμαῖς Ar. Ra. 1353 ; πήδημα κ. ἐκ νεὼς ἀφήλατο A. Pers. 305 ; κ. ἐξᾶραι πόδα S. Ant. 224 ; κ. ἅλμα E. El. 439 (lyr.); κ. αἴρειν βῆμα Id. Tr. 343 ; οὐ τοῖς κούφοις ὁ δρόμος LXX Ec. 9.11 : metaph., κουφότεραι . . ἀπειράτων φρένες too buoyant, Pi. O. 8.61 . metaph., easy, light, τελεῖν . . κούφαν κτίσιν to make achievement easy, ib. 13.83 ; κ. εἰ δοίης τέλος A. Th. 260 ; κ. νύξ an easier night, of a sick person, Jul. Mis. 342a ( Comp. ); περίπατος Sor. 1.46 ; τὸ ὅσιον ἅπαν κ. ἔργον OGI 383.120 (Nemrud Dagh, i B. C.); of government, light, κουφοτέραν βασιλείαν less oppressive, Isoc. 9.51 ; ἡ εὔκλεια κουφοτέρα φέρειν X. Cyr. 8.2.22 ; of an antagonist, easy-going, κουφότατος ἦν κρατήσας Id. Ages. 11.12 ; δεσπότην ἀπράγμονα καὶ κ. ἐξαπατᾷ θεράπων Men. Per.Fr. 1 . unsubstantial, airy, vain, τὸ νέον . . κούφας ἀφροσύνας φέρον S. OC 1230 (lyr.); οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν . . κούφην σκιάν Id. Aj. 126 ; ἐλπίδος τι εἶχον κούφης Th. 2.51 ; κ. καὶ πτηνοὶ λόγοι Pl. Lg. 717c ; κ. πρᾶγμα a trifle, ib. 935a ; κ. γράμματα a small letter, E. IT 594 ; of persons, = κουφόνους , Hdn. 5.7.1 ; τὸ κοῦφον τοῦ νοῦ levity, Paus. 5.21.14 , cf. Hdn. 7.8.6 . light in point of weight, opp. βαρύς, Pl. Phlb. 14d , R. 438c ( Comp. ), etc.; κούφα σοι χθὼν ἐπάνωθε πέσοι may earth lie lightly on thee, E. Alc. 462 (lyr.), cf. Hel. 853 ; κούφη σοι κόνις ἥδε πέλοι IG 14.1942.4 ; κούφη σεῖο γαῖ' ὀστέα κεύθοι ib. 329 (Himera); κ. πνεύματα light airs, S. Aj. 558 ; ὀστᾶ τε καὶ κ. κόνις Men. 538.3 ; τὸ κουφότατον . . τῶν κακῶν . . πενία Id. Kith.Fr. 2 . Medic. in various uses, σικύαι κοῦφαι dry cuppings, Philum. ap. Orib. 45.29.17 , cf. Sor. 2.11 , etc.; also κούφου μένοντος τοῦ ἰοῦ on the surface, Philum. Ven. 7.3 ; μὴν κ. the eighth month of pregnancy, Sor. 1.56 ; of food, easy to digest, light, Arist. EN 1141b18 , etc. of troops, light-armed, οἱ κ. τῶν στρατιωτῶν Hell.Oxy. 6.4 ; ὡπλισμένοι κουφοτέροις ὅπλοις X. Mem. 3.5.27 ; κούφη στρατιά Plu. Fab. 11 ; τὰ κ. τῆς δυνάμεως Plb. 10.25.2 . of ships, lightly-laden, Th. 6.37 , 8.27 . light, slight, ἁμαρτήματα Pl. Lg. 863c ; κουφότερα γυμνάσια, opp. ἀναγκαῖα, Arist. Pol. 1338b40 ; κ. ἐργασίαι ib. 1321a25 . empty, κεράμια Gp. 7.24.2 , cf. PLond. 5.1656.6 (iv A. D.), PFlor. 314.8 (v. A. D. ): hence as Subst., κοῦφον (sc. κεράμιον), τό, jar, in pl., POxy. 1631.16 (iii A. D.), PFay. 133.6 (iv A. D.), PStrassb. 1.10 (vi A. D.). Act. , relieving, assisting, χερὶ κούφᾳ Pi. P. 9.11 : prob. to be taken in this sense in Theoc. 11.3 . Adv. -φως lightly, nimbly, κ. ὀροῦσαι A. Eu. 112 ; κ. ἐσκευασμένοι, of soldiers, Th. 4.33 ; ὡπλισμένοι X. Mem. 3.5.26 , etc.; κ. ἔχειν to be relieved, Arist. Pr. 873a16 . metaph., lightly, with light heart, κουφότερον μετεφώνεε Od. 8.201 ; κ. νοῆσαι Sapph. Supp. 5.14 ; κ. φέρειν, opp. δεινῶς φ., E. Med. 449 , 1018 ; ὡς κουφότατα φέρειν Hdt. 1.35 ; διάγουσα κούφως doing well, of a patient, Hp. Epid. 1.26 .δ ́. lightly, with ease, A. Pr. 701 .
greek_sentence: λιθάργυρον δὲ μετ’ ἐλαίου βαλὼν, [823] Εἰς λοπάδα καινὴν κεραμίαν πλατύστομον, Ἕψε πυρὶ κούφῳ καὶ μαλακῷ, κινῶν σπάθῃ Ἕως γένηται μέλιτος Ἀττικοῦ πάχος.
english_sentence_A: and having put the litharge with the oil [823] into a new, wide-mouthed earthenware pan, boil over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it acquires the thickness of Attic honey.
english_sentence_B: Putting the litharge with the oil [823] into a new, wide-mouthed earthenware dish, boil it over a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it takes on the thickness of Attic honey.

lsj_entry_text: ῥητίν-η [ι], ἡ , resin of the pine, Hp. Art. 63 , Arist. HA 617a19 , Thphr. HP 9.2.1 , al., Nic. Al. 300 , 554 , Dsc. 1.71 , etc. (Prob. a foreign word.)
greek_sentence: Ἴσον δὲ καὶ τῆς λεπίδος προσβαλὼν πάλιν Ἕψε λαβρότερον, εἶτα κιῤῥοῦ γενομένου Τοῦ φαρμάκου, πρόσβαλε χαλκὸν καὶ διφρυγὲς, Ποιῶν τ’ ἀμόλυντον καὶ πεπηγὸς φάρμακον Πρόσβαλλε κηρὸν τήν τε ῥητίνην ἅμα.
english_sentence_A: And having added also an equal amount of the scale, boil again more vigorously; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, and, making the drug non-staining and set, add the wax together with the resin.
english_sentence_B: Then add an equal amount of the scale as well and boil again more vigorously; next, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, and, to make the drug non-staining and set, add the wax and the resin together. When these have melted together and you see that the plaster is blended, take the pot off the fire, and add some propolis and the galbanum, ammoniac, manna and aloe.

lsj_entry_text: ἔμ-πλαστρος, ἡ, salve or plaster, Dsc. 1.32 ; said to be later form of ἔμπλαστος, Gal. 13.372 ; also ἔμπλαστρον, τό, Hierocl. Facet. 221 , PSI 3.297 (V A. D. ).
greek_sentence: Ὧν συντακέντων, ὅταν ἴδῃς κεκραμένην Ἔμπλαστρον, αἴρεις τὴν χύτραν ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς Καὶ προσβαλὼν προπόλεώς τε καὶ χαλβάνην, Ἀμμωνιακὸν, μάνναν τε καὶ ἀλόην, τότε Ψύξας τὸ πυρῶδες καὶ ζέον τοῦ φαρμάκου, Ἀριστολοχίαν λειοτάτην προσεμπάσεις Καὶ γεντιανὴν, τήν τε δίκταμνον πόαν Καὶ προσανακόψας τῇ σπάθῃ τὸ φάρμακον Χερσὶ καὶ μαγδαλιὰς ποιῶν, ἔχε, Εἰς ἃς προεῖπον χρώμενος περιστάσεις.
english_sentence_A: When these have melted together, when you see the plaster blended, you lift the pot from the fire, and, having added propolis and galbanum, ammoniac, manna and aloe, then, having cooled the fiery and boiling heat of the drug, you will sprinkle in aristolochia, very finely ground, and gentian and the herb dittany; and having beaten the drug up further with the spatula and with the hands, and making it into cakes, keep it, using it for the circumstances I mentioned before.
english_sentence_B: Then, having cooled the fiery and seething heat of the drug, sprinkle in the aristolochia ground very smooth, and the gentian and the dittany herb. Beat the drug up further with the spatula, make it into rolls with your hands, and keep it, using it for the conditions I mentioned before.

lsj_entry_text: παρασκευ-ή, ἡ, preparation, δείπνου Hdt. 9.82 ; παρασκευὴν σίτου παραγγείλας having ordered corn to be prepared, Id. 3.25 , cf. Pl. R. 369e ; π. νεῶν Ar. Rh. 1382b3 ; μετὰ παρασκευῆς πλείστης ἠδίκησεν Id. Rh.Al. 1427a4 ; ἄνευ παρασκευῆς Pl. Ep. 326a . providing, procuring, φίλων καὶ οὐσίας Id. R. 361b ; ὑγιείας σώματι π. Id. Lg. 962a ; way or means of providing, τίς . . τέχνη τῆς π. τοῦ μηδὲν ἀδικεῖσθαι; Id. Grg. 510a ; δύ' εἶναι τὰς π. ἐπὶ τὸ θεραπεύειν ib. 513d ; in E. Ba. 457 , λευκὴν . . χροιὰν εἰς παρασκευὴν ἔχεις, ἐκ π. shd. be read. intrigue, cabal, for the purpose of gaining a verdict or carrying a measure, Cratin. 185 , Antipho 5.79 , And. 1.1 , Lys. 12.75 , al., D. 43.32 . that which is prepared, equipage, πλοῦτοί τε καὶ πᾶσα ἡ τοιαύτη π.
