english_sentence_A: Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the written texts not only unintentionally, but also deliberately on the part of some out of envy, who make the letter omicron a theta by drawing another, transverse, line through the middle of the round stroke, and the letter iota, likewise, by adding another transverse line, just as also, when one stroke is scraped away from the letter gamma (γράμμα in the text) and from rho, it happens that the shape of iota is left behind.
english_sentence_B: Menecrates did this because it often happens that errors are made in the writings not only by people acting unintentionally but also by some acting deliberately out of envy: they make the letter ο into θ by drawing another, transverse line through the middle of the round line, and alter the letter iota by adding another, likewise transverse, line; just as, when one line is scraped off from the letter [gamma?] and from rho, the result is that the character of iota is left.

lsj_entry_text: σύν-θεσις, εως, ἡ, putting together, composition, combination, Pl. Phd. 93a , R. 611b ; τῶν λίθων Arist. EN 1174a23 , cf. IG 42(1).103.56 (Epid., iv B.C.), 7.3073.92 (Lebad., ii B.C.); τῶν σπονδύλων Sor. 1.102 ; storage, τῶν μήλων (quinces in a ῥίσκος) Phylarch. 10 J. ; but ἐλαιῶν ς. a preserve of olives, Gp. 9.28.2 . in concrete sense, junction, ὀστῶν Arist. PA 658b19 ; συνθέσεις (λέγω τὰς γωνίας) Id. Pr. 910b14 . in various technical senses: in Grammar, composition, γραμμάτων τε συνθέσεις, i.e. syllables and words, A. Pr. 460 , cf. Arist. Metaph. 1092a26 ; ς. ἔκ τε ῥημάτων γιγνομένη καὶ ὀνομάτων, i.e. sentences, Pl. Sph. 263d , cf. Cra. 431c , Arist. Po. 1458a28 , Gal. 15.487 ; περὶ συνθέσεως ὀνομάτων, title of work by D.H. ; also, the juxtaposition of letters in a word, Arist. Rh.Al. 1434b34 ; of an author's composition, Isoc. 10.11 ; so ἡ τῶν μέτρων ς. metrical composition, Arist. Po. 1449b35 ; ἡ τῶν ἐπῶν ς. D.S. 5.74 ; ἡ τοῦ παίωνος ξ. the way the paeon is made up, Plu. 2.1143d ; the constitution of things, Hp. Virg. 1 . Math., synthesis of a problem (opp. ἀνάλυσις), Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.7 , explained in Papp. 634 ; ἡ κατὰ ς. ἀγωγή synthetic procedure, Id. 412.2 . Math., ς. λόγου transformation of a ratio known as componendo, Euc. 5 Def. 14 ; κατὰ -σιν, = componendo, Archim. Aequil. 2.9 . Math., addition, Ph. 1.11 , Plu. 2.1018c , Dioph. 1 Intr.; καθ' ἁντινοῦν -σιν however many times added, i.e. whatever number of times taken (multiplied), Archim. Spir. 1 :—also as Pythag. name for 2 , Anatol. ap. Theol.Ar. 8 . in Logic, union of noun and verb or of two objects of thought in a statement, Arist. Int. 16a12 , de An. 430a27 ; also ὁ παρὰ τὴν ς. [λόγος] the fallacy of composition, opp. διαίρεσις, Id. SE 177a33 . in Physics, composition of substances, parts of organisms, from their elementary constituents, Id. PA 646a12 , Top. 151a23 ; opp μίξις (combination), Id. GC 328a6 . in Medicine, compounding of essences and drugs, τῶν μύρων Thphr. Od. 14 , al., cf. D.S. 4.45 , Aglaïas 8 . combination of parts so as to form a whole, γενέσεις καὶ ς. Pl. R. 533b ; ἡ τῶν στρωμάτων ς. Id. Plt. 280b , cf. Arist. PA 645a35 , Metaph. 1014b37 ; in plants, Thphr. HP 5.5.2 . in concrete sense, a social or political combination, Arist. Pol. 1276b7 ; a military formation, Ael. Tact. 18.5 . agreement, treaty, Pi. P. 4.168 , Fr. 205 ; πὸς τὰς συνθέσις in accordance with the agreements, IG 5(2).343.41 , 60 (Orchom. Arc. , iv B.C.); ἐκ συνθέσεως by arrangement, D.S. 13.112 , etc.; συνθέσεις περὶ γάμων Plu. Sull. 35 . ς. λόγων making up accounts, Stud.Pal. 4.70.391 (i A.D.); so ς. alone, εἰς σύνθεσιν τῷ βασιλεῖ PTeb. 714.6 (ii B.C.). set, service (most freq. in Lat. synthesis): collection of clothes, wardrobe, Dig. 34.2.38.1 ; also, dress, gown, costume, suit, ς. τελείας λευκὰς δεκατρεῖς, γυναικείας ς. PHamb. 10.13 , 21 (ii A.D.), cf. POxy. 1153.23 (i A.D.), 496.4 (ii A.D.), PSI 10.1117.11 , 13 (ii A.D.), Mart. 2.46.4 , 5.79.2 ; synthesinam indutus, Suet. Ner. 51 . service of plate, ς. πινακίων BGU 781 i 5 (i A.D.), cf. Mart. 4.46.15 , Stat. Silv. 4.9.44 .

english_sentence_A: When, a muscle having been wounded, or some nerves, or even a membrane near a bone having been pricked, after the fourth day there comes an addition of frequent pains and inflammations and fevers with symptoms — much sleeplessness, derangement of mind, violent thirst, dryness of the tongue — inclining day by day towards the worse; a lees-like, thin ichor, red wounds, and all the bodies near them having turgors, distensions, inflammations, oedemata: then do not plaster them with variegated cataplasms.
english_sentence_B: [997] When, after a muscle or some nerves have been wounded, or a membrane near a bone has been pricked, there come after the fourth day frequent pains and inflammations, and fevers with symptoms; when there is an increase of much sleeplessness, delirium, violent thirst and dryness of the tongue, inclining day by day towards the worse; when the ichor is lees-like and thin, the wounds red, and all the parts near them have turgescences, distensions, inflammations and oedemas: then do not apply varied poultices.

greek_sentence: Τήξας δ’ ἐπιμελῶς ἐν λοπάδι τἀξούγγιον, Ἔπαιρ’ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοὺς ὑμένας καὶ τοὺς ἅλας, [999] Ἠθμῷ διηθῶν εἰς ἑτέραν μείζω χύτραν, Καὶ προσβαλὼν ἔλαιον ἀνάζεσον πάλιν, Μὴ πᾶν δ’ ἔλαιον, ἀλλὰ τὰ δύ’ αὐτοῦ μέρη, Τὸ τρίτον δ’ ὑπολιπὼν, ἔχ’ ἐν ἑτοίμῳ κείμενον, Ἄν ἐπειχθῇς προσβάλλειν, ἵν’ ᾖ σοι παρόν.
english_sentence_A: Having carefully melted the axunge in a dish, take off from it the membranes and the salts, [999] straining it through a strainer into another, larger pot; and, having added oil, bring it to the boil again—yet not all the oil, but two parts of it; leaving the third aside, keep it lying in readiness, so that, should you be pressed to add it, it may be at hand for you.
english_sentence_B: Having carefully melted the lard in a shallow pan, take off from it the membranes and the salts, [999] straining it through a strainer into another, larger pot; and, having added the oil, bring it to the boil again. Not all the oil, however, but two parts of it; leaving the third part aside, keep it lying in readiness, so that, if you are pressed to add it, you may have it to hand.

english_sentence_A: And when the drug, having been boiled for a moderate time, has taken on the thickness of a plaster and has likewise taken on the foul smell of a drug, quickly lift the pot from the fire, making it slightly harder in summer and soft in winter, yet nonetheless such that it does not stain; and stir it likewise until it has cooled down moderately, [1000] then again with firmer hands work (πρόσπασσε) the whole of it, once it has been softened, and so transfer it out of the pot.

greek_sentence: ὑστάτη δὲ ἡ τῶν ἀμολύντων, ὁμοία τῇ τῶν καλουμένων ἰδίως ἐπιθεμάτων· οἷς ἐφεξῆς ἐστιν ἡ τῶν ἐμπλάστρων σύστασις, ἐχουσῶν καὶ τούτων αὐτῶν, ἐν τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον οὐ μικρὰν διαφορὰν, ὥστ’ ἔνιοι τῶν ἰατρῶν, κηρωτομαλάγματά τινα προσηγόρευσαν, ἀπὸ τῆς συστάσεως μόνης οὕτως ὀνομάσαντες, ὅσα τῶν ἐπιτιθεμένων φαρμάκων οὐκέτι μέν ἐστιν ὑγρὰ, σκληρὰ δὲ εἰς τοσοῦτον οὐδέπω, καθάπερ αἱ ἔμπλαστροι.
english_sentence_A: Last is that of the non-staining ones (amolynta), similar to that of what are properly called epithemata; and next after these is the consistency of the plasters, these too having among themselves no small difference in the more and the less, so that some physicians have given the name kerotomalagmata to certain of them, naming them thus from the consistency alone, namely those of the drugs applied externally which are no longer fluid, yet not yet hard to such a degree as the plasters.
english_sentence_B: Last is that of the amolynta (non-soiling ones), similar to that of the things specifically called epithemata (applications). Next after these is the consistency of plasters, and these too have no small difference among themselves in degree, more and less, so that some physicians gave the name kerotomalagmata (cerate-emollients) to certain preparations, naming them thus from their consistency alone: namely those of the applied drugs which are no longer liquid, yet not yet hard to the same degree as plasters.

english_sentence_A: Now there is a naturally occurring simple drug that is a help for all fatigues, oil, which we also name without any addition, since in the ancient times it was in fact the only one; but later castor oil was added to it, among you at any rate.
english_sentence_B: Now there is a natural simple drug that helps against every kind of lassitude, namely oil, which we name even without any qualifying addition, since in ancient times it was also the only one.

PCair.Zen. 344.2 (iii B.C.), BGU 1185.13 (i B.C.), etc. quarters, lodgings for travellers or soldiers, Hdt. 7.119 , X. An. 1.8.1 , al., SIG 880.15 (Pizus, iii A.D.), etc.; soldier's billet, PStrassb. 92.4 (iii B.C.), etc. quarter of a town, PRyl. 102.8 (ii A.D.). in Persia, of stations or stages on the royal road, where the king rested in travelling, ς. βασιλήϊοι Hdt. 5.52 , cf. 6.119 , Plu. greek_sentence: ἐν θυείᾳ μείζονι Λίβανον καταθλάσας εἰς βραχεῖς χόνδρους πάνυ Ἀμμωνιακόν τε παραχέων οἶνον εὐθέως, Ἀφείς τε ταῦτα διαβραχῆναι συμμέτρως, Λέαινε τῷ δοίδυκι καὶ μέλιτος πάχος Ποιῶν, ἀποδίδου τὸ μέλι καὶ τὴν οἴσυπον Καὶ τὸν ἐλάφειον μυελὸν, εἶτα ταῦθ’ ἑνῶν Ἐν τῇ θυείᾳ, τῆκε κηρὸν ἐν χύτρᾳ Καὶ πᾶν ἔλαιον καὶ στέαρ καὶ χαλβάνην Τερμινθίνην τε καὶ τακῆναι πάντ’ ἀφεὶς, Κατὰ τῶν ἐνόντων τῇ θυείᾳ καταχέων, [1050] Καὶ μικρὰ δοίδυκι κινήσας, ἵν’ ὑποψυγῇ, Ταῖς χερσὶν ἀνάτριβε τότε ταῦτα πάνθ’ ὁμοῦ, Ἕως ἂν ἑνωθῇ πάντα καὶ μέλιτος λάβῃ Ὑγροῦ καλοῦ τε τὸ πάχος, οὕτως τ’ ἀποτίθου Εἰς κασσιτερινὸν σκεῦος ἢ καὶ πύξινον, Χρώμενος ἐπιμελῶς, ὡς κρατίστῳ φαρμάκῳ.
english_sentence_A: In a larger mortar, having crushed the frankincense into quite small lumps, and the ammoniac too, pouring on wine at once, and having allowed these to be soaked through in due measure, grind with the pestle and, bringing it to the thickness of honey, add the honey and the oesypum and the deer marrow; then, uniting these in the mortar, melt the wax in a pot together with all the oil and the fat and the galbanum and the terebinth, and having let them all melt, pour them over the things in the mortar, [1050] and having stirred a little with the pestle, so that it may cool somewhat, then rub all these together with the hands until everything is united and takes on the thickness of good liquid honey; and so store it away in a vessel of tin or even of boxwood, using it carefully as a most excellent drug.
english_sentence_B: In a rather large mortar, having crushed frankincense into very small grains, and the ammoniac too, pouring wine over them at once and letting these be moderately soaked, grind with the pestle; and when you have made it of the thickness of honey, add the honey and the oesypum and the deer marrow; then, having united these in the mortar, melt in a pot the wax and all the oil and the fat and the galbanum and the turpentine; and having let them all melt, pour them over the contents of the mortar, [1050] and having stirred a little with the pestle so that it may cool somewhat, then rub all these together with the hands until everything is united and takes on the thickness of good liquid honey; and so store it in a tin vessel or else a boxwood one, using it carefully as a most excellent drug.

greek_sentence: ἐν θυείᾳ μείζονι Λίβανον καταθλάσας εἰς βραχεῖς χόνδρους πάνυ Ἀμμωνιακόν τε παραχέων οἶνον εὐθέως, Ἀφείς τε ταῦτα διαβραχῆναι συμμέτρως, Λέαινε τῷ δοίδυκι καὶ μέλιτος πάχος Ποιῶν, ἀποδίδου τὸ μέλι καὶ τὴν οἴσυπον Καὶ τὸν ἐλάφειον μυελὸν, εἶτα ταῦθ’ ἑνῶν Ἐν τῇ θυείᾳ, τῆκε κηρὸν ἐν χύτρᾳ Καὶ πᾶν ἔλαιον καὶ στέαρ καὶ χαλβάνην Τερμινθίνην τε καὶ τακῆναι πάντ’ ἀφεὶς, Κατὰ τῶν ἐνόντων τῇ θυείᾳ καταχέων, [1050] Καὶ μικρὰ δοίδυκι κινήσας, ἵν’ ὑποψυγῇ, Ταῖς χερσὶν ἀνάτριβε τότε ταῦτα πάνθ’ ὁμοῦ, Ἕως ἂν ἑνωθῇ πάντα καὶ μέλιτος λάβῃ Ὑγροῦ καλοῦ τε τὸ πάχος, οὕτως τ’ ἀποτίθου Εἰς κασσιτερινὸν σκεῦος ἢ καὶ πύξινον, Χρώμενος ἐπιμελῶς, ὡς κρατίστῳ φαρμάκῳ.
english_sentence_A: In a larger mortar, having crushed the frankincense into quite small lumps, and the ammoniac too, pouring on wine at once, and having allowed these to be soaked through in due measure, grind with the pestle and, bringing it to the thickness of honey, add the honey and the oesypum and the deer marrow; then, uniting these in the mortar, melt the wax in a pot together with all the oil and the fat and the galbanum and the terebinth, and having let them all melt, pour them over the things in the mortar, [1050] and having stirred a little with the pestle, so that it may cool somewhat, then rub all these together with the hands until everything is united and takes on the thickness of good liquid honey; and so store it away in a vessel of tin or even of boxwood, using it carefully as a most excellent drug.

english_sentence_A: This too is a green akopon, very effective, [1051] which is why it acts better at the onsets of the pains; and it is beneficial to arthritics and to gout-sufferers who, before the baths, are rubbed with the drug on the feet and the sinews that have become thickened.

greek_sentence: Τινὰς δ’ ἐπέγνων στέασι πολλοῖς χρωμένους Μυελοῦ τε πολλοῦ καί τινων ἀρωμάτων, Ὀποῖς τε καὶ μύροισι κἀλαίοις τισὶν, Οἷς πάλιν ἀμέλει χρησάμενος ἔγνων ὅτι Ἀπειροκάλων τοιαῦτα καὶ μὴ κεκρικότων Τὰ μίγματα, τάς τε ἁπλὰς τούτων φύσεις.
english_sentence_A: But I have come to know some who use many fats, and much marrow, and certain aromatics, and juices and unguents and certain oils; and having in turn, of course, made use of these, I recognised that such things belong to men without taste, who have not judged the ingredients and the simple natures of these.
english_sentence_B: I have known some, however, who use many fats, and much marrow, and certain aromatics, and juices, and unguents, and certain oils; having in turn made use of these myself, I came, of course, to recognise that such things belong to men lacking in taste, who have not discerned the ingredients and the simple natures of these.

lsj_entry_text: ὀπός, ὁ, juice, distd. from χυλός, χυμός, in that ὀπός is prop. vegetable juice, the milky juice which is drawn from a plant by tapping it, ὀπὸν . . στάζοντα τομῆς . . κάδοις δέχεται S. Fr. 534 (anap.), cf. Thphr. HP 9.8.1 , etc. ; esp. the acid juice of the fig-tree, used as rennet (τάμισος) for curdling milk, Il. 5.902 , Emp. 33 , Hp. Morb. 4.52 , Menestor ap. Thphr. HP 1.2.3 , Arist. Mete. 384a21 , 389b10 , GA 737a14 ; generally, acid juice, Pl. Ti. 60b ; βλέπειν ὀπόν Ar. Pax 1184 : in pl., Antiph. 88.4 , cj. in Anaxandr. 41.59 (anap.); cf. ὀπίας, ὀποειδής, metaph., ὀπὸς ἥβης the juicy freshness of youth, opp. ῥυτίς, AP 5.257 (Paul. Sil.). ὀποῦ καρπός, = σιλφίου σπέρμα , Hp. ap. Gal. 19.126 ; and so prob. in Ar. Ec. 404 , Pl. 719 ; but ὀπὸς σιλφίου silphium juice, Hp. Acut. 23 , cf. 37 , Acut.(Sp.) 48 , Thphr. HP 6.3.2 ; so ὀπός alone, Gal. 12.90 . gravy, Ath. 9.402c . (Perh. cf. Lith. sakaĩ (pl.) 'resin', Slav. sok[ucaron] 'sap'.)

lsj_entry_text: μίγμα, ατος, τό, (μείγνυμι) mixture, compound, Emp. and Anaxag. ap. Arist. Ph. 187a33 , cf. Metaph. 1012a28 . μίγματα, τά , of drugs, Plu. 2.80a , Dsc. 5.44 , Apollon. ap. Gal. 12.655 ; μ. σμύρνης καὶ ἀλόης Ev.Jo. 19.39 ; of pigments, D.H. Is. 4 , Comp. 21 ; of condiments, Plu. 2.997a ; of amalgams, Zos.Alch. p.197 B.
